text: [T13] Use as few font sizes as possible in a form; differentiate size only between sections (labels/placeholders at one small size) and actions (the button label larger). The good mock uses 12 for both label and placeholder and 32 for the button label; the bad mock mixes 16 (label), 12 (placeholder), 32 (button).
why: Every extra size is another thing to decode, so the form takes longer to process.
check: count distinct computed `font-size` values inside one `form`; label and input/placeholder sizes should match.

text: [T31] Use one typeface across a card/page. The bad mock sets heading and body in a serif next to a sans eyebrow; the good mock sets everything in one sans.
why: Mixing faces creates confusion and hurts readability; a single face lets users learn the pattern.
check: set of distinct `font-family` primary families on page (expect 1, at most 2 with a clear role split) `[engine note on the "at most 2"]`.

text: [T35] Limit line width by characters per line, not by pixel width; wide full-width text lines bore users and hurt readability. Good mock: text column narrower with larger side padding than the card edge.
why: Long measures lose the reader's eye at line return.
check: measure chars per line of paragraphs (`ch`-based `max-width`); see T94 for the numeric range.

text: [T94] Keep paragraph line length in check: stick to 45-75 characters per line "if you want to play it safe". The good example is labelled 55-65 characters per line; the bad example is labelled ~120 characters per line.
why: Too-long lines make text harder to read.
check: `ch` count of rendered lines on `p`: 45-75, target 55-65.

text: [T86] Body text must be no smaller than 14pt. The page shows 12pt as the bad body and 16pt as the good body (the 16pt example also has visibly more leading than the 12pt one).
why: Small text is hard to read clearly.
check: computed `font-size` of body copy >= 14 (pt as the book uses it; read as px-equivalent 14+ in CSS) `[engine note: book says pt, web sizes are px; treat 14 as floor, 16 as default]`.

text: [T87] Do not set continuous running text in all caps; use sentence case and keep caps for moderate, short uses (the book's good mock sets a paragraph in normal case; bad sets the whole paragraph in caps).
why: All-caps blocks are difficult to read.
check: `text-transform: uppercase` should not be on paragraphs/long strings; flag uppercase runs > a short label.

text: [T17] Align description text to the title text, not to the icon. Good: icon sits in its own column, title and description share one left edge. Bad: description starts under the icon, so title and body have different left edges.
why: Unaligned text makes content hard to scan; aligning cleans up the design.
check: `getBoundingClientRect().left` of title and its description are equal.

text: [T95] Right-align numbers in tables so the decimal point is always in the same place; numeric column headers are right-aligned over their numbers too (good mock), text column (ticker symbols) stays left-aligned.
why: Aligned decimals let you compare values at a glance; ragged decimals look cluttered.
check: numeric `td`/`th` have `text-align: right` (`font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` is an `[engine note]` addition).

text: [T6] Break dense text into headed, scannable items: small letter-spaced uppercase grey eyebrow ("PROPERTY FEATURES"), then per feature an icon, a bold descriptive heading, and a short grey description of two lines. Do not show important features as one paragraph.
why: People scan; headings plus icons let them find a feature without reading the block.
check: no paragraph > ~3 sentences that contains multiple distinct features; visual.

text: [T1] Use human language that ties labels to values: "Only 7 left in stock!" instead of "In stock: 7"; "Add to Cart" instead of "Cart" on the button.
why: Robotic label/value pairs confuse; natural phrasing explains what the number and the button mean.
check: visual / copy review; button labels on commerce actions are verb phrases.

text: [T8] In confirmation dialogs make the options descriptive and consistent with the question. Bad: "Are you sure you want to cancel your upload?" answered by "OK" (grey) and "Cancel" (primary): ambiguous. Good: "Yes, Cancel" (grey) and "Don't Cancel" (primary).
why: "OK/Cancel" next to a "cancel?" question forces the user to decode which one does what.
check: dialog buttons are not generic "OK"/"Cancel" when the question itself contains "cancel".

text: [T29] Drop the verb from a navigation/menu label when the noun is already clear: "My address", "Order history", "Discounts", "Payment methods" instead of "Edit my address", "View order history", "View discounts", "Edit payment methods".
why: Verbs make labels long and over-detailed in a list that is already an action menu.
check: list-row labels are short noun phrases; visual.

text: [T47] Write opt-in button copy that makes users excited to join: "Join the Club!" instead of "Submit" on a subscribe form.
why: Generic words make people less interested in the program.
check: primary button label on sign-up/subscribe is not "Submit".

text: [T57] Button labels must state what will happen: "Create account", never "OK" or "Next" for the final form action.
why: Vague actions leave users unsure about the outcome.
check: submit button text is not in {OK, Next, Submit, Continue} without context.

text: [T42] Do not repeat the logo on the same page. When the hero shows the brand in the header and again as the hero headline, replace the hero text with a headline that conveys style and what you do (good: "MODERN STYLE"; bad: "LOOHOO FASHION" repeating the header logo).
why: Repetition wastes the most prominent text slot; a headline sells the offer.
check: brand name occurs in nav only, not also as the `h1`.

text: [T2] On dark UI limit saturation: keep brand colours at tone levels 200-500 (a Tailwind-style 50-950 scale); do not use fully saturated colours on dark cards. Good mock: title and button are a desaturated lavender; bad: vivid saturated blue title and button on the same dark card.
why: Highly saturated elements damage contrast and vibrate on dark surfaces.
check: HSL/OKLCH chroma of accents in `.dark` is lower than in light; accent lightness in the 200-500 band.

text: [T3] Build two colour palettes, one per theme: dark mode uses light pastel tones of each hue; light mode uses darker, deeper shades of the same hues. Do not reuse identical colours in both modes. (Good mock: lavender/mint/sky/salmon bars in dark; indigo/emerald/blue/coral-red darker versions in light.) The book adds "most people prefer light theme" (opinion).
why: The same swatch has different contrast on dark vs light backgrounds.
check: accent tokens differ between `:root` and `.dark`.

text: [T15] Avoid pure black (#000000) and pure white for surfaces; use a dark grey such as #333335.
why: Pure black/white can cause uneasiness in the eyes.
check: `background-color` or `color` not exactly `#000`/`#fff` on large surfaces and body text.

text: [T54] Build the colour scheme from one family: pick a few tones of the same hue (good: four steps from dark navy to pale periwinkle) rather than unrelated hues (bad: black, orange-red, mustard, magenta).
why: Too many inconsistent colours looks terrible.
check: palette hue spread: all brand/neutral tokens within a narrow hue range (excluding semantic colours).

text: [T55] Use the primary colour only on the most crucial components. In the good mock the header becomes light neutral, the tab bar becomes white with the primary colour only on the active icon, buttons and card titles carry primary; photos have no colour overlay. The bad mock floods header, tab bar, card backgrounds and image tints with primary.
why: Too much primary colour does not look nice and kills its signalling power.
check: share of page area filled with the primary colour is small (`[engine note]` rule of thumb under ~10% of viewport area); primary reserved for CTA, active, key accents.

text: [T19] Keep the colours used for navigation/state to two, one of which denotes the selection: good mock keeps active icon in blue and the others grey; bad mock gives every icon its own colour (blue, orange, green, purple).
why: Multiple colours in navigation add to the cognitive load.
check: distinct non-neutral colours among sibling icons <= 1 (the selected one).

text: [T92] Emphasise by de-emphasising: give inactive nav items a softer (lighter grey) colour so the active item (indigo/darker) pops. Bad mock: all links dark, active barely different.
why: The active item only stands out relative to the background of its siblings.
check: contrast/lightness delta between active and inactive nav link; inactive lighter but still readable `[engine note: still meet 4.5:1 for text]`.

text: [T88] Use accent colours to help users categorise sections: in the pricing mock, a 3-4px coloured top rule (violet on "Start", mint-green on "Pro") differentiates two otherwise identical cards.
why: Identical sections look the same and cannot be told apart at a glance.
check: sibling cards carry distinct accent token (rule/dot/icon); visual.

text: [T75] Add colour-based distinction to highlight significant classifications: status rendered as small uppercase coloured pills (SHORTLISTED violet, REJECTED red, IN-PROCESS green) with alternating row tint, not plain grey text.
why: Plain text statuses create no visual distinction between rows, so scanning is slow.
check: status cell uses a coloured badge, not default text colour.

text: [T12] Use red for destructive actions: the "Yes, Delete" button is red (bad: blue), the neutral Cancel is light grey.
why: Red alerts the user and acts as a warning sign; blue looks normal.
check: destructive buttons use the destructive/red token.

text: [T25] When text sits on a photo that is not dark enough, add a contrast overlay: good mock adds a darkening gradient behind the white "Hello, welcome to our academy" text; bad mock leaves white text on bright pink umbrellas, partly unreadable.
why: Without contrast the text does not appear clearly on a bright image.
check: contrast ratio of text vs the image pixels beneath >= 4.5:1 (`[engine note]` threshold).

text: [T26] Make gradients smooth by placing the gradient handle's start and end farther away from the object (outside its bounds); handles at the corners give a direct, sharp-looking gradient.
why: Close end points compress the transition and look harsh.
check: visual; the gradient's colour stops should not both be fully reached inside the element box.

text: [T21] Keep a second layer (e.g. dropdown) at least two shades or tints different from the layer behind it. Good: white dropdown over a grey page; bad: grey dropdown on grey page.
why: Similar shades for different layers are uneasy to the eyes and the layers blend.
check: luminance delta between popover bg and its backdrop element.

text: [T77] On dark themes communicate elevation with shades of grey (nearer/higher card is lighter, deeper ones darker), not shadows alone. Bad mock: stacked cards all the same mid grey with only blurred shadows.
why: Shadows are barely visible on dark surfaces and do not separate layers.
check: elevated surface tokens get lighter with elevation in `.dark`.

text: [T61] All shadows come from a single light source: same direction on every element. Bad mock: one button's shadow falls right, the next one's falls left.
why: Random shadow directions look odd and complicate the experience.
check: `box-shadow` x/y offset sign identical across components.

text: [T84] Never keep default shadows from design tools. Bad: X 0, Y 2px, blur 4px, #000000 at 50%. Good: X 0, Y 8px, blur 24px, #000000 at 15% (lower opacity, larger blur).
why: Default shadows look hard and dirty.
check: shadow blur >= ~3x Y offset and alpha <= ~20%; no `rgba(0,0,0,.5)` small-blur shadows.

text: [T43] Do not give inner elements the same corner radius as the container. Example: card 30pt outer, image inside 15pt (bad: 30 and 30).
why: Same radius for outer and inner looks uneven.
check: inner radius < outer radius (see section 5 for the 30 vs 15 vs "slightly" tension).

text: [T56] Avoid too many borders. Good mock: only the search input keeps a border; list rows have no row borders; the action footer is separated by a light grey fill. Bad mock: filled search band plus a bordered box around every row.
why: Too many borders complicate the experience and look cluttered.
check: count of elements with visible `border` per screen; list rows without `border-bottom` where tone/space can separate.

text: [T89] Create contrast between items with colour and space instead of divider borders: good mock alternates a light grey row tint with white rows and generous row padding; bad uses hairline borders between rows.
why: Borders for differentiation feel outdated.
check: list items without `border-top/bottom`; zebra or tonal fill used.

text: [T22] Use more padding and margin. Good mock: card content has larger insets, smaller hero image, clear room around title and photo; bad: title and image almost touch edges.
why: Too little margin/padding destroys visual hierarchy and looks cluttered.
check: card inner padding >= content-to-edge distance used elsewhere; visual.

text: [T20] Separate sections with spacing, not extra divider lines. Menu mock: "Options" group and "Settings" group split by an extra gap (good) rather than a hairline rule (bad).
why: Adding a new element (a line) just to create a division is not ideal.
check: group gap > intra-group gap; no `hr` between groups.

text: [T41] Leave space from edges and group related elements: card text inset visibly from the card edge, title/body spacing consistent, tag-title-description grouped. Bad: text hugging the left edge and title lines packed tight.
why: Less or inconsistent spacing hurts readability and grouping.
check: padding between content and card edge consistent on all sides; heading line-height not tight.

text: [T93] Avoid ambiguous spacing in forms: space between groups larger than between a label and its own input. Annotated: bad = 16px above label and 16px label-to-input; good = 16px above the label and 8px label-to-input.
why: Equal gaps make it unclear which label belongs to which input.
check: (gap between previous input and next label) > (gap between label and its input); good ratio 2:1 (16 vs 8).

text: [T67] Use consistent gaps in grids: same horizontal and vertical gap between tiles (bad mock: vertical gap noticeably larger than horizontal).
why: Uneven gaps give a bad experience and a sloppy grid.
check: `row-gap == column-gap` (or a deliberate token pair) across the grid.

text: [T58] Build on a grid and test it at different screen sizes; the layout must keep the same set of items and consistent columns across breakpoints. Bad mock: 3 columns on desktop, a 2x2 on narrow with one empty (crossed) placeholder tile. Good mock: 4 columns on desktop, 2x2 filled on narrow.
why: Irresponsive design has a negative impact on user experience.
check: screenshot at 375/768/1280/1440: no overflow, no empty slots, items preserved. (see section 7: image is ambiguous)

text: [T72] When several images share a screen, make some lead: good mock = one full-width hero tile, two half tiles, one full-width tile; bad = a uniform 2x3 grid of equal tiles.
why: With all images equal users cannot recognise the lead images.
check: tile area ratio between largest and smallest > 1 in a gallery.

text: [T73] Add dynamism to image layouts with multiple columns and tile sizes (mosaic: one big 2/3-width tile + two small stacked, then a narrow + a wide tile). Bad: a uniform 3x4 grid of equal tiles.
why: A uniform grid detracts from the appeal of the images and is boring to scroll.
check: more than one tile size; visual.

text: [T50] Prompt users to scroll by showing a glimpse of the next section at the fold. Bad: hero with big empty space below, so it looks finished; good: top edge of the next section peeks at the viewport bottom.
why: Too much spacing between sections makes users less likely to scroll.
check: next section's top within the first viewport at common heights (e.g. 1440x900, 375x812).

text: [T79] Overlap elements to add depth and clarity: good profile card has the avatar overlapping the cover image edge (half on photo, half on card) with the name below; bad has the avatar inline next to the name fully inside the white area.
why: Keeping all elements separate gives a basic look.
check: visual.

text: [T96] Scale hero images to fill the container so the visual content is visible across all display sizes. Bad: image scaled so its floating elements spill up onto the headline ("bills" collides with a coin); good: image is contained within its rounded frame, nothing overlaps the heading.
why: Scaling the image to the full screen feels different on different screen sizes.
check: hero image bounding box does not intersect heading; `object-fit` set; test at 375/768/1280. (see section 7)

text: [T49] Place the CTA at the end of the Z-shaped reading path (Gutenberg): 1 top-left logo, 2 top-right nav CTA, 3 diagonal to image/left-centre, 4 bottom-right CTA. Good mock mirrors the hero so image sits left and text + CTA sit bottom-right.
why: Eyes travel a Z from top-left to bottom-right, so the last stop gets the action.
check: primary hero CTA position in lower-right quadrant of hero; visual.

text: [T23] Maintain pattern repetition: all selectors of a kind share one shape and style. Good mock: footwear type, size and quantity controls are all pills with the same selected style (dark fill); bad: type = rounded pills, size = square boxes, quantity = pill.
why: Strange differences between visual elements make users re-learn controls for each task.
check: `border-radius` equal across same-role controls.

text: [T11] Keep the main CTA big and close to the thumb (Fitts' law): good mock puts a full-width tall button at the bottom of the card; bad has a small button at top right.
why: A small, distant target takes more time to hit.
check: primary action height >= 44px `[engine note]`; sits in bottom third on mobile.

text: [T28] Fill the CTA with the primary colour (white label) so it stands out: pricing card "Get Pro" filled primary, not a pale grey button with coloured text.
why: A dull CTA gets less attention and is harder to find.
check: primary button bg is the brand token, not neutral.

text: [T30] Use button hierarchy on a screen with two actions: "Log In" = filled primary; "Sign Up" = text-only primary-coloured link below. Bad: two identical filled buttons.
why: No hierarchy makes decisions hard.
check: at most one filled primary per view region; secondary uses outline/ghost/text.

text: [T51] Button padding: side padding = 2x the top/bottom padding (annotated x, 2x). Bad: label touches the left and right edges with ~no side padding.
why: Buttons with small padding do not look good.
check: `padding-inline / padding-block` ~ 2.

text: [T82] Never wrap a button label; keep it on one line and let the button grow ("Submit Form", not "Submit / Your Form" on two lines).
why: Wrapped button text is not good practice and looks cramped.
check: `white-space: nowrap`; button height == single-line height.

text: [T83] Differentiate button weight: neutral and negative buttons become outlined (grey border/text, red border/text), the positive action stays solid filled. Bad: neutral solid grey, negative solid red, positive solid blue, all competing.
why: Buttons with similar contrast compete for attention; the positive action should read as the clear one. (The book's caption says "lighter contrast"; see section 7.)
check: only one solid-fill button per button group.

text: [T98] On mobile make buttons full width within the system margins (good: Retry and Exit span the card minus margins; bad: ~60%-width centred buttons).
why: Small-sized buttons give an incomplete feeling.
check: button width == container inner width on viewport < ~480.

text: [T33] Make tappable cards look clickable by adding an actionable button that describes the action (good: small dark "Apply >" pill on each row; bad: bare rows).
why: Plain cards fail to indicate that they are clickable.
check: interactive card has a visible control or chevron/affordance.

text: [T48] Enhance the clickable area so it includes label plus icon plus padding: good mock shows the hit box around "Click Me ->" including text, around the radio including its label "I'm an option", and around the hamburger with padding; bad mock hit boxes are only the arrow, only the radio dot and a tight box on the icon.
why: Small hit areas make clicking buttons and elements difficult.
check: `<label for>`/wrapping `<label>` on radios; icon buttons >= 44x44 hit area `[engine note on 44]`.

text: [T65] Make text actions look clickable with colour or a button: "Read more" as a blue underlined link (bad: body-coloured plain text).
why: Users cannot identify clickable elements when they look like body text.
check: `a` elements differ from surrounding text by colour and/or underline.

text: [T4] Align forms vertically: labels left-aligned above fields, fields one edge, submit button on the same left edge. Bad: labels right-aligned beside fields at ragged offsets and the button centred, producing a zig-zag eye path.
why: Consistent alignment orients the user faster; inconsistent looks unprofessional.
check: labels, inputs and button share the same `left` coordinate.

text: [T14] Use a single column on small forms (group related fields otherwise). Bad: two columns of narrow fields.
why: Multiple columns disrupt vertical momentum.
check: inputs stacked, one per row, full width of the form.

text: [T16] Put social login first, then "or log in with" separator, then username/password and button, with "Don't have an account? Create here" at the bottom. Bad: registration form first, social option after.
why: Users see the one-tap option first and can log in without filling the form.
check: social buttons precede credential fields in DOM/visual order.

text: [T18] Checkboxes for multiple selections, radio buttons for a single choice (good mock: skills list uses squares with Design and Marketing checked; single-choice list uses circles with one selected).
why: The control shape tells the user whether one or many may be picked.
check: `input[type=checkbox]` for multi, `radio` for exactly-one groups.

text: [T24] Search fields need descriptive placeholder text that hints what can be searched: "Ebooks, audiobooks, and videos" vs bare "Search".
why: Without it the user is clueless about what kinds of things can be looked up.
check: search `placeholder` is more specific than "Search".

text: [T36] Fewer options for faster decisions (Hick's law): 8 radio options (bad) reduced to 3 plus "Others" which reveals a "Type Here" text field (good).
why: More options create complexity and delay choice.
check: radio group size <= ~5 with an Other/free-text escape `[engine note on 5]`.

text: [T38] Use input masks for phone numbers and dates: placeholders like (___) ____-____ and DD/MM/YYYY instead of generic "Number" and "Date".
why: Without a mask users are unsure about the format.
check: phone/date inputs have mask or format hint placeholder / `inputmode`.

text: [T39] When the user picks from 2-4 values, display all options side by side (radio rows), not in a dropdown. Bad: a "Light" dropdown for Light/Dark.
why: It is not ideal to hide 2-3 values inside a dropdown.
check: `select` with <= 4 options is a smell.

text: [T40] Avoid free typing when a control works better: price range with a dual-handle slider (value labels $47 and $150 above handles, green fill between) instead of From/To text inputs.
why: A slider makes the process fast and understandable; fields everywhere are not ideal.
check: range inputs use slider (see section 5 for precision caveat).

text: [T59] Keep forms short and clear: fewer fields (merge First/Last Name into "Name"; 4 fields became 3).
why: Every additional field lowers conversion and loses leads.
check: count of required inputs; flag unnecessary ones.

text: [T64] Use boxed fields: rectangles with visible borders and rounded corners, not underline-only fields.
why: It takes time for underline fields to be recognised as a form.
check: `input` has visible border on all four sides.

text: [T74] Do not use placeholder text as the label. Good mock: small grey labels above each filled field (Name, Surname, Address) with the entered value inside; bad: only "Name", "Email", "Address:" inside the empty fields.
why: Placeholder-as-label causes many usability issues (label disappears when typing).
check: each input has a visible `<label>`; placeholder is not the only identifier.

text: [T80] For selecting from a large multi-option list use toggle tokens (pills in a 2-column grid; selected = primary fill with white text, unselected = grey fill and grey text) instead of a long checklist.
why: A long list of checkboxes can make users abandon the form.
check: multi-select with > ~6 options uses chips/tokens.

text: [T90] Group form fields with section titles: bold "Personal Information" over First/Last Name, bold "Contact Information" over Address/City, with an extra gap between groups; do not leave one undivided list.
why: Ungrouped forms lack clarity; title plus grouping separates regions.
check: forms > ~4 fields have `fieldset/legend` or heading per group.

text: [T91] Differentiate the focused field: good mock shows a dark indigo thicker border on the active input (cursor in "Last Name"); bad shows the same grey border while the cursor blinks.
why: An obvious current-field state makes the form feel interactive.
check: `:focus` style differs in border colour from default.

text: [T99] Do not explain obvious fields (no "?" tooltip "Username is your user name"); when explanation is needed, put it directly below the field.
why: Stating the obvious in tooltips is noise.
check: helper text rendered inline below the field; no tooltip for self-evident labels.

text: [T100] Checkboxes must be squares ("boxes"), not circles. Bad: round checkbox with check looks like a radio.
why: Round checkboxes look too similar to radio buttons.
check: checkbox `border-radius` small (square/slightly rounded), radio fully round.

text: [T5] Use icon + label in menus for complex or abstract functions: each item (New Tab, New Incognito, Recent Tabs, Downloads, History, Bookmark) gets a leading outline icon plus its text; bad = label only.
why: Icon plus label gives rational and emotional impact.
check: menu items carry leading icon; visual.

text: [T37] Put the most important pages at the corners of the tab bar (serial position effect): good order Home, Search, Chat, Cart, Profile (Home first, Profile last); bad order Search, Home, Cart, Profile, Chat.
why: People remember the first and last items in a series.
check: primary destinations are first/last in tab bar.

text: [T81] The book recommends a hamburger menu instead of visible navigation links on the page shown ("visible navigation decreases conversion rate; hamburger increases it"). (opinion, no evidence on the page; see section 5)
why: Fewer competing links keep attention on the form/CTA.
check: visual.

text: [T9] Show a progress bar for multi-step flows: 3 steps with step 1 a green check, current step 2 a green numbered node, step 3 grey, solid green connector for done and dashed for remaining, step names below.
why: Without it users cannot track where they are in the flow.
check: stepper present in flows > 2 steps.

text: [T32] In mobile onboarding let users skip at any time and put "Skip" within thumb reach: centred at the bottom under the pagination dots, over a dark gradient scrim. Bad: tiny "Skip" in the top-right corner.
why: Top corners are hard to reach.
check: skip link in bottom half; present on every onboarding step.

text: [T34] Highlight the best plan: filled primary gradient card with white text and an inverted white button, next to a plain white card. Bad: both plans styled identically.
why: Same colour on both makes the most-used plan of no importance.
check: exactly one pricing card has the highlighted treatment.

text: [T44] Limit card content: truncate description with an ellipsis and add an "Explore More"/"See more" button; never make a card's text scroll internally (bad shows an inner scrollbar).
why: Scrolling within a card creates confusion.
check: no `overflow: auto/scroll` on card body; `line-clamp` used.

text: [T45] Use swipe actions on list rows (swipe reveals a red trash and a green star circle button) instead of a "..." menu button on every row.
why: Option buttons slow the process; swipe is fast and minimal.
check: visual.

text: [T53] For homogeneous content use a list (one container, hairline separators) instead of a stack of separate cards.
why: Cards do not give a sense of similarity; lists speed up scanning.
check: repeated identical items share one container.

text: [T85] Limit links in a card: one link or a limited set of actions. Good: plain body text, a filled "Primary Action" and an underlined "Secondary Action"; bad: also two inline blue underlined links in the paragraph.
why: Too many inline links look awful and give a negative impression.
check: inline `a` in card body = 0-1.

text: [T76] Avoid the super-minimal look in list rows: add detail ("Episode #1" instead of "#1", a progress bar with "42%" and a cancel x, rather than a bare bar).
why: Too little detail fails to describe the element and the process.
check: rows show secondary descriptor and progress value; visual.

text: [T68] Add a stroke (white ring) to avatars placed over photos or busy backgrounds.
why: Avatars without stroke blend with the background.
check: avatar over image has `border`/`ring` in surface colour.

text: [T7] Use one consistent icon set: the page's good example shows three coherent sets in rows (A filled circle, B outline ring, C plain line) while the bad mixes filled circle plus, outline trash and outline cart.
why: Inconsistent icons risk confusion and hurt brand credibility.
check: icons from one library, same fill style and size grid.

text: [T46] Use simple flat icons for UI (thin dark outlines), not glossy gradient "fancy" icons.
why: Fancy icons look unprofessional.
check: icons are single-colour line/solid glyphs.

text: [T70] Keep icons front-facing, not in perspective (good: flat-on image icon; bad: tilted glossy 3D icon).
why: Perspective views look complicated.
check: visual.

text: [T71] Use the same stroke weight throughout an icon set (bad pen icon mixes thick and thin strokes).
why: Inconsistent stroke weight is bad practice.
check: all SVG icons share one `stroke-width`.

text: [T66] Keep illustrations consistent: lock the figures' clothing colours to the brand palette (violet, charcoal, navy) rather than random red, yellow, green, blue.
why: Illustrations become part of the brand; inconsistent ones fail to define it.
check: illustration colours within brand palette hues.

text: [T69] Use high-resolution images, particularly where text goes over them.
why: Blurry or distorted images do not look appealing.
check: image natural width >= rendered width x devicePixelRatio.

text: [T78] Use supportive images that reinforce the message (credit-card visual for "The simplest way to pay your bills") instead of irrelevant stock (a wallet in a hand).
why: Irrelevant images fail to support the story and meaning.
check: visual / alt text matches the headline.

text: [T10] Show the user where and why an error occurred: red "!" inside the offending field and a small red message directly below it ("Username not valid!"); bad shows only a "1 error found !" summary above the form.
why: Users must locate the error and know the reason to correct it.
check: error text adjacent to its field and linked (`aria-describedby`).

text: [T27] Show the steps of a procedure visually: pagination dots under the button and copy "We just have one question" instead of "We have a few questions".
why: Users do not know how many steps remain.
check: progress indicator present.

text: [T52] Make selected items pop: selected row filled with primary gradient and white text vs unselected white rows (bad: only a tiny checkmark changes).
why: Users cannot tell that something happened.
check: selected state differs by fill from default.

text: [T60] Error/offline screens must name the error and suggest a solution: illustration, "You're offline" and a full-width "Retry" button with a refresh icon.
why: A bare spinner looks incomplete and gives no recovery path.
check: network failure state has message + retry action.

text: [T62] Use skeleton loading (grey blocks mirroring the layout with a shimmer sweep) instead of a spinner for content areas.
why: Skeletons are perceived as faster; spinners make loading feel slower and show nothing.
check: loading state has skeleton matching final layout.

text: [T63] Keep important guidance visible: show password rules as an inline checklist under the field ("More than 8 characters" met in green, "Include special characters or numbers" unmet) instead of a "?" tooltip.
why: Required info hidden under a tooltip is missed.
check: requirements rendered in the DOM, not in a hover-only tooltip.

text: [T97] Show a glimpse of an off-screen element in horizontal carousels (the next card peeks at the edge) rather than only a slider indicator.
why: Indicator alone gets ignored.
check: carousel item widths < container width with next item partially visible.

text: [T101] Create more than you consume: balance reading and inspiration with real designing.
why: More creation means more practice and better UI skill.
check: n/a. Not a UI rule.

text: [X1] Dark-mode recipe: base surface a dark grey not black (T15), accents at tones 200-500 (T2), separate palette from light mode (T3), elevation by lighter greys (T77).
why: These four rules together define dark theme tokens.
check: token audit of `.dark`.

text: [X2] Form recipe: one column (T14), left-aligned visible labels above boxed fields (T4, T64, T74), 8px label-to-input and 16px between groups (T93), titled groups (T90), focus ring (T91), errors under field (T10), rules inline (T63), masks (T38), full-width verb-labelled submit (T57, T98).
why: Collates the 10+ form rules into one build order.
check: run T-checks above.

text: [X3] Pricing recipe: highlighted best plan (T34), accent top rules to distinguish (T88), filled primary CTA (T28), consistent corner shapes.
why: Combines three pricing tips.
check: one highlighted card; visual.

text: [X4] Reserve the primary colour for CTA, active state and key accents (T55, T28, T92, T19) and keep everything else neutral.
why: Signal colour only works when scarce.
check: primary-coloured area share; sibling items have <= 1 coloured.

text: [X5] Do not rely on the book's mock pixel values as tokens; they are artboard numbers. Use the stated ratios (side padding = 2x vertical, 8:16 label gaps, inner radius < outer, 45-75 ch, 14pt floor).
why: The mocks use inconsistent sizes between good/bad (see section 7).
check: n/a

text: Before producing anything, restate the brief in your own words (goals, objectives, audience, deliverables) and surface it for confirmation or correction.
why: Misunderstandings and missing points are far cheaper to catch before creative work than after.
check: an explicit "brief restated" artifact exists before the first design/code step; it lists goals and objectives.

text: Ask clarifying questions up front until you can say exactly what the client wants; do not start on an ambiguous brief.
why: "Understanding what they want is critical; else, you won't be able to offer it" (p.87).
check: list of open questions is empty or each has a stated assumption before build.
source: (p.87) [engine note: when the founder cannot be asked, write each assumption down explicitly]

text: Ask "Why?" repeatedly about each requirement to find the underlying problem, ambition and motivation. Examine requirements before committing to a solution or budget, because the client may not understand why they need the website/app.
why: The stated request is often a proxy for a business problem.
check: each major requirement has a recorded "why".

text: Write the scope down first: what is delivered, what is NOT included, and what costs extra.
why: An explicit boundary lets you go back to the client when scope creeps or they ask for things "that weren't in your original proposal" (p.82-83, 85).
check: a scope doc with an explicit exclusions list exists.

text: State deliverables concretely: what will be produced, by whom, by when, how many meetings, and what the client must do to keep the schedule on track.
why: Many clients have never commissioned design; the process must be explained to them.
check: deliverables list with owner and date per item.

text: Include a realistic schedule that accounts for other work running in parallel, to avoid bottlenecks. "Above all, avoid over-promising."
why: Missed deadlines damage trust more than a longer honest estimate.
check: schedule exists; no item lacks an estimate.

text: When estimating time, add a buffer: example 7 days of work -> quote 10 days (add 2-3 days). Deliver early against the quoted date.
why: Early delivery against a padded promise reads as speed and wins ratings; (the book cites Walmart/Amazon delivery padding as the same trick).
check: quoted duration = estimate + 2 to 3 days on a 7-day job (~30-40% pad).

text: Split large projects into small pieces and complete one or two pieces per day; do not postpone starting a big job.
why: Procrastination on large jobs is the failure mode; small pieces make progress measurable.
check: task list granularity: each task completable in about a day.

text: Cut a project into essential stages (design concept, development, implementation, etc.) and close each stage explicitly (invoice/sign-off on completion).
why: Each stage gets a clean sign-off and protects against late or non-payment; also helps cash-flow forecasting (p.83).
check: stage list with completion criterion per stage.
source: (p.83) [engine note: for an agent, stage sign-off = review gate before next stage]

text: Involve the client in design decisions and learn their business and customers before proposing solutions.
why: An involved client is receptive to new ideas; they know their own customers better than you do.
check: decision points listed with who approves.

text: Do not accept projects you do not know how to finish; confirm you can reach the finish line first. Prefer genres you know, master them, then move to the next topic.
why: Taking work to "get the job first" leads to abandoned projects and bad ratings (the p.22-23 story: a freelancer claimed grid/Bootstrap skill, had none, ghosted for three days then quit).
check: capability self-assessment before accept.

text: If you cannot finish or will miss a deadline, say so immediately; do not waste the client's time.
why: Early notice lets the client re-plan.
check: blockers raised at first occurrence, not at deadline.

text: Answer client messages promptly and professionally: balanced tone ("not too strict or too funny"). On disagreement stay patient and composed; prefer a call/face-to-face over text.
why: Calls de-escalate; text hardens conflicts.
check: n/a mechanically. visual/manual.

text: Use plain, complete sentences and full words in client communication; avoid slang/abbreviations ("u", "DIY") because clients from other countries may not understand them.
why: Non-native readers misinterpret shorthand.
check: grep for "ur", "u ", "DIY" style shorthand in outbound text.

text: Keep communication short and specific: enough information for the other person to understand fully, no excess or useless information; double-check before sending (spell/grammar checkers are "not foolproof").
why: Brevity plus precision prevents misreads.
check: manual re-read of each outbound message.

text: Keep timesheets / track time per task; base future estimates on similar past projects; use them to explain cost and to detect a project running over budget.
why: Past data makes quotes faster and more accurate; shows which work types are profitable.
check: time log exists and estimates reference it.

text: Before the first working session write answers to: your process; why you take the work; which projects you will/won't take (and that "no" is allowed); your role in the client meeting; what success means to you AND the customer; what makes you stand out.
why: Undefined process/success criteria cause drift; this is the book's #1 recurring theme ("Define").
check: written answers to the 6 items exist.

text: Learn when to say NO: no time/capacity, unrealistic expectations of budget/timescale/results (do not start until aligned), unethical activity or request to violate copyright, no chemistry.
why: Protects brand, client relationship and sanity.
check: explicit accept/decline decision with reason.

text: Choose one skill path ("hill") first; learn the latest tools, techniques, methods for it; then expand into related skills.
why: Depth differentiates; chasing whatever earns money this month (3ds Max, Android) scatters effort.
check: n/a (planning).
source: (p.9-10) [engine note: for an agent, prefer depth in the user's stack over adding tools]

text: Make the basics strong before advanced techniques.
why: Newbies "don't get much grip on the basics".
check: n/a.

text: Do not switch tools/technologies as soon as they appear; learn it well, account for the slow early learning curve, then switch.
why: Early switching is slow and shallow.
check: n/a.

text: Add only skills related to your major skill (e.g., HTML/CSS with UI design), not unrelated ones.
why: Related skills compound ("tree" metaphor).
check: n/a.

text: Allocate a daily block of time for learning; never stop learning.
why: Technology and tooling move fast.
check: n/a.

text: Be able to explain, on request, the process, rationale and daily workflow behind a project; developers must be able to explain method/code choices.
why: Interviewers (and clients) always ask.
check: n/a.

text: Use a wide range of design stakeholders: collaborate with management, test users, technical department; be able to explain design concepts (user persona, testing, layout) to marketers, engineers, business analysts.
why: UX/UI is collaborative even for a department of one.
check: n/a.

text: Be honest about methodology experience (Lean, Agile, Design Thinking). A critical view is fine if backed by logical arguments.
why: The recruiter is testing workflow fit and reasoning.
check: n/a.

text: In job-search answers, explain why a project was best or worst; difficulty that forced a new approach is a good story.
why: Shows motivation and problem-solving.
check: n/a.

text: Evaluate job postings against your own tolerance: lists of every imaginable duty; weird or impossible requirements; absurd tasks; lack of company diversity; unrealistic wages; who the UX team reports to.
why: Employers often don't understand UX/UI; flags show mismatch.
check: n/a.

text: Check job boards regularly (the book suggests once or twice a week for IxDA). Boards named: Dribbble (full-time + contract; freelance listings PRO-only), Behance (international, no extra fee for freelance), IxDA (~300 ads at time of writing, mostly US), RemoteOK (remote), Ideate Labs (0-2 years' experience; small hard-to-read font), Design Jobs Board (long-standing; vivid colours), Remotive (~2000 listings; can hide US-only), AngelList (startups), Interns.Design (internships).
why: Different boards serve different regions/seniority.
check: n/a.

text: Stay visible: attend local meet-ups and conferences, write about design experiences, be active on social platforms (Twitter, LinkedIn, Instagram, Medium, Facebook, Slack, Dribbble).
why: Visibility builds personal brand and online communication skill.
check: n/a.

text: Network and keep in touch with clients, peers and coworkers; they refer and are sources for rates of comparable jobs.
why: Referrals; "best method to get good work is to produce good work and have other people tell others".
check: n/a.

text: Final checklist for a successful UI freelancer: be honest; know your UX/UI process; love helping people; deliver on promises; take pride in work; don't sell yourself short; weed out bad clients; define the scope first.
why: Book's own summary.
check: n/a.

text: Put a written proposal in place before starting work: delivery details (what, when, by whom, number of meetings), the client's role in keeping the schedule, deliverables, cost, payment dates, what is excluded/extra, a realistic schedule, and T&Cs covering permissions/releases, copyright and ownership.
why: The proposal sets expectations; T&Cs are the fallback for late payment or mid-project cancellation.
check: proposal contains each listed item.

text: Explain the project stages and ways of working in plain language; many clients have never commissioned design.
why: A client who understands the process cooperates better.
check: manual.

text: Invoice on completion of each stage, not only at the end.
why: Protects you if a client doesn't pay; aids cash flow and forecasting.
check: n/a.

text: Base bids on expected hours (from timesheets) so you have room to go back to the client when scope creeps.
why: Hours-based bids tie price to scope.
check: quote lists hour estimate per stage.

text: Compute a minimum hourly rate = annual survival budget (living costs + business overheads) / billable hours. Example: 8 h/day, 5 d/week, 4 weeks off = 1,920 h/yr; ~40% for operations (finding clients, books, planning) leaves 1,152 billable h.
why: Time is what a service business sells; undercharging loses money.
check: n/a.
source: (p.80-81) (see open question: the book's result does not match its numbers)

text: Test a rate against client reaction: if more than 1 in 4 people wince, slow down (ease off the rate); if fewer than 1 in 4 wince, raise it.
why: Wince rate is a market signal (Reichelt quote).
check: n/a.

text: When a client wants a quote on the spot, it is fine to gather needs, take notes and return the next day with a proposal.
why: Better to examine requirements before committing to a budget.
check: n/a.

text: Do not undervalue yourself because a job took less time; value = skill and impact, not minutes.
why: Quoted verbatim in spirit: "you are valuable as a person with skills and qualities" (p.45-46).
check: n/a.

text: Track hours on long engagements and keep detailed notes; they inform future estimates and mistakes.
why: Learning loop for estimation.
check: time log.

text: Make exceptions on rate only for a portfolio-growing project, a client you really want, or a cause you believe in; be wary of clients who bargain you down in exchange for promised future work.
why: Design is competitive; many clients exploit this.
check: n/a.

text: Weed out bad clients and "don't accept every project" (see also `brief-scope-and-delivery-process.md`).
why: Protects brand and sanity.
check: n/a.

text: Pick a niche when founding an agency: a specific vertical gives authority, a shorter learning curve, and a differentiator; verify enough demand exists and will grow.
why: Generalists have no value proposition beyond "we do good work" (Racki quote, p.65).
check: n/a.

text: If you offer one service, form referral arrangements with non-competing agencies offering complementary services.
why: Partners send you work they can't do.
check: n/a.

text: Choose an agency name with checks for: existing trademarks; incorporation availability in your state; domain and social handles; long-term fit (not restrictive). Law differs by country; seek a business attorney.
why: Name drives all branding; conflicts are costly.
check: domain and handle availability.

text: List what you do as a freelancer and identify what you cannot do when scaled; hire for each gap: workload -> assistant; finding customers -> salesperson/account rep; technical -> technical co-founder; managing staff -> partner/CEO; running the business -> accountant, attorney, VA.
why: Defines hiring in order of need.
check: n/a.

text: Pick partners with complementary skills or the same skills according to your gaps; split workload evenly; collaborate on design decisions even if one partner owns suppliers/dev.
why: Complementary abilities widen services; uneven load breaks partnerships.
check: n/a.

text: Choose suppliers who are specialists (not salespeople), share your vision and ethics, and nurture them as an extension of your team.
why: Output quality depends on suppliers; good ones handle problems professionally.
check: n/a.

text: Remote staff: state in advance whether in-office work will be required; use time-tracking tooling rather than frequent check-ins (book describes Hubstaff: time tracking, optional random screenshots, activity detection, payroll, invoicing, tasks with weekly sprints/checklists/daily standups; free up to 5 team members).
why: Check-ins are inefficient; surprises on office policy upset staff.
check: n/a.

text: Seek advice from an accountant/lawyer on taxes, licences, overheads, invoicing before going full-time freelance; keep company expenses deductible.
why: Legal/tax exposure.
check: n/a.

text: Present each design inside a realistic context mock-up (device frame for an app/site, table scene for a card) rather than as a bare artboard; present the final result as one complete package.
why: "Mock-ups allow clients to see your design in context and in real world", which affects their imagination and thinking.
applies: landing page | SaaS app UI | mobile (deliverable previews).
check: deliverable preview shows the design inside a device/frame or real surface; visual.

text: Prefer high-quality (premium) mock-ups over weak free ones when the impression matters; the book names ThemeForest-type marketplaces.
why: Quality of presentation lifts perceived quality of the work.
check: visual.

text: For a reading-first document (resume, CV, case-study page), do not overdesign: no bright colours, no striking shapes, no unconventional layouts; use a "sober & direct" version; let content lead.
why: Reviewers are "most likely tired and uninterested in a remarkable visual experience"; anything that diverts attention from the text is frowned on.
check: palette is neutral (text on plain background); no layout deviating from a single-column or simple two-column grid; visual.
source: (p.105-106) [numeric thresholds are engine notes; book gives none]

text: Prioritize readability and a clear visual hierarchy; no long paragraphs, no confusing layouts; the viewer must grasp immediately what they are looking at.
why: Scanning reviewers decide fast.
check: headings differ visibly in size/weight from body; paragraph length short (book gives no number).

text: Write each project entry to show how: "Instead of 'I designed the navigation system', show how you did it: how did you pull it off, what did it take, why was it important."
why: Process evidence beats task statements.
check: entry contains method + reason, not only a verb + noun.

text: Describe achievements and learnings, not tasks: what you completed, how long it took, what you learned and why it matters.
why: Recruiters want evidence, not job descriptions.
check: each project entry has an outcome statement.

text: Let writing reflect the author's voice (laid-back/funny or serious/direct) while remaining objective and concise; avoid grammar/spelling errors.
why: Personality survives even in efficient layouts.
check: spell/grammar pass.

text: Tailor emphasis to the target role/audience (e.g., data-driven research for UX, Agile for process-driven teams) but do not lie.
why: One golden opportunity justifies re-framing.
check: n/a (judgement).

text: Pair a portfolio (visual skill) with case studies (thinking). Make case studies easy to read; start with the strongest project; keep it basic and to the point.
why: Visual-only showcases (Dribbble/Behance style) omit problem-solving, empathy, business approach, data analysis.
check: first project in list is the strongest; each case study exists, not just images.

text: A case study answers five questions: what made the project difficult; how you overcame it; your logic and thought process; what you learned and how you apply it now; what effect the work had.
why: This is the structure the book gives for case-study content.
check: page contains five labelled sections or equivalents.

text: Highlight awards, certifications and work for known companies prominently on resume/portfolio.
why: They raise credibility and make you the first pick among similar candidates.
check: visual: proof element above the fold.

text: Prepare to explain your design process and the idea behind a project, and why you chose a method; also be able to explain design choices to non-designers (why a persona, why more testing, why a layout is better).
why: Interviews and clients ask for the reasoning, not only the output.
check: each major decision has a written rationale.
source: (p.14-15, 112-118) [engine note: an agent should attach a short "why" to each design decision it ships]

text: Keep written messages "short and specific"; reread before sending; use spellcheck but do not rely on it.
why: Intended meaning must survive transmission.
check: manual.

text: Keep the portfolio updated with new finished work.
why: "How quickly you get work depends on how unique and experienced your profile is"; new projects fix a thin profile (p.54-56).
check: latest entry date.

text: Never let the generating model pick between its own candidate directions. Deal them from outside: a seeded script chooses which candidate index is built, plus 2-6 challenger forms from different tiers (graphic system / instrument language / atmosphere world); store the seed and allow reproducible re-roll.
why: Measured 30/35 identical concepts across 16 prompt framings when the model chose. Same logic reduces Larpo's "5 of 7 concepts use Geist".
check: seed present in output comment + `grep` in the built HTML (Impeccable requires the seed key to survive the production build).

text: Keep a persistent ledger of structural fingerprints (macrostructure, nav archetype, footer archetype, type voice, ground band, accent hue, CTA silhouette, headline size band) and make the next build differ on >= 1 declared axis from the last three. Write the stamp into the page and into `ledger/`.
why: Hallmark does this; it is the only mechanism found that addresses cross-run sameness.
check: compare stamp to last 3 ledger entries (script).

text: Use a separate evaluator agent that renders the page (Playwright), scores Design quality, Originality, Craft, Functionality against written criteria that explicitly penalise stock components and AI-generated patterns, and is calibrated with several few-shot graded examples drawn from the ledger. Allow the generator to pivot aesthetic, not only refine. Cap iterations (5-15) and keep the best iteration, not the last.
why: Anthropic's harness; originality and design quality needed explicit weight; scores plateau; middle iteration sometimes better.
check: evaluator transcript + per-criterion scores stored with the ledger entry.

text: Before layout, produce >= 7 candidate world-references for the audience, including print/instrument/notation/identity-system artifacts from before the web; delete the category default and its predictable opposite; let the dice pick.
why: Forces source material that is not the web median; Arc/Irwin precedent.
check: artifact list present with one line each; no more than 3 of 7 share one material.

text: Write the direction contract (<= 150 words) as an HTML comment at the top of `<body>` in the emitted markup: THESIS (one idea + the category default refused), OWN-WORLD, FIRST VIEWPORT, signature interaction, seed. Grep the built output to prove it survived the build.
why: Makes the commitment auditable and lets a reviewer diff promise vs behaviour.
check: `grep` built HTML for seed key.

text: When generating options, ask for 5-8 with self-estimated "typicality" and require the build candidate to be low-typicality but high audience-fit (Verbalized-Sampling style).
why: Targets the preference-data typicality bias.
check: record the list in the ledger; run E-2.

text: Pre-build plan = 4-6 named colours, type roles, one-sentence layout concept + ASCII wireframe, "what makes it unique"; a review step compares it with the default look for that category and logs what changed.
why: Catches convergence before code exists, when changing is free.
check: plan file exists; diff vs the fingerprint ledger.

text: Write criteria wording deliberately and test it: adjectives such as "museum quality" or "premium" steer toward one look.
why: Observed convergence side effect in Anthropic's harness.
check: A/B the criteria on 3 briefs and compare fingerprints.

text: Use image-first exploration only when the comp is treated as a spatial contract and the code is verified against it; otherwise the code drifts back to template.
why: Taste-skill `image-to-code` (one image per section, extract layout/type/spacing/colour values, build, compare in a real browser) and Impeccable "comp is king" both flag that "generic coded reinterpretation after the image step" is the failure mode. Impeccable requires a pixel-overlap reproduction check of the first viewport (saved as `.impeccable/review/hero-repro.png`) before building further.
check: screenshot-diff vs comp at the comp's dimensions.

text: Bounded verification: build fully, inspect once in a batched round (desktop + mobile), fix everything in one batch, confirm with at most one more round, then stop; hand the remaining finds to a fresh-context reviewer.
why: Open-ended self-QA "burns the user's money doing worse what the finish handoffs do better"; a fresh reviewer finds more than the builder.
check: round counter in the run log.

text: Capture validity before critique: settle or disable entrance animation first, capture full-page from the document top, open every file and confirm it shows what its name says. An invalid capture invalidates the review.
why: An element hidden by animation timing reads as missing and gets "fixed" into a regression.
check: screenshot sanity (no blank/black regions; non-zero variance).

text: Do not use a font or palette because an "anti-slop" list recommended it. For every typeface and every ground/accent pair, check it against the current overused sets (Section 3) and against the last N builds; a recommendation list is a prior, not a decision.
why: The anti-slop skill ecosystem seeds Geist, "cobalt and cream", "terracotta and slate" into thousands of agents (Core idea 4).
check: D-FONT-1, D-COLOR-3, B-AXIS-*.

text: Ban lists must always be paired with a positive, specific, non-listed destination derived from the brief's own world; never "avoid X" alone.
why: Negative-only instruction relocates the mode (Space Grotesk after Inter; terracotta after purple; Anthropic cookbook line quoted above). Impeccable's self-check: "if someone could guess your aesthetic from the category alone, or from category-plus-avoidance, rework until neither answer is obvious" [verified-local, reference/new-work.md].
check: visual + guess-the-aesthetic blind test (process note P-7).

text: Treat the cream ground, italic/high-contrast serif display, and terracotta/coral accent as ONE combined tell, and near-black + single neon accent as a second. Allowed only if the brief pins it; otherwise the free axis must not be spent on them.
why: Named by Anthropic's own skill, Impeccable ("cream-palette" rule + "calibration" paragraph), and press coverage of "Claudian sameness".
check: D-COLOR-3 (cream bg test), D-FONT-3 (italic serif H1).

text: Keep display tracking at or above -0.04em (prefer -0.02 to -0.03em) and display size at or below 96px (6rem); a full-sentence H1 at >=72px that covers >=28% of viewport height or >=25% of viewport area is flagged.
why: Impeccable craft-floor: "display max 6rem, tracking floor -0.04em"; its detector fires `extreme-negative-tracking` at <= -0.05em and `oversized-h1` at >=72px with >=40 characters and viewport dominance. Larpo's observed -0.052 to -0.064em at 62-83px sits on the wrong side of both.
check: D-TYPE-1, D-TYPE-2.

text: No tracked all-caps eyebrow/kicker, no "WORD - fragment" labels, no middle-dot meta strings, no arrows appended to links and buttons, no monospace small labels as decoration, unless they encode real information.
why: Anthropic SKILL.md lists these as "template chrome". Impeccable `kicker-above-heading` is an outright ban ("no brief earns it back"). The reflexive arrow on the CTA is on Anthropic's list and was one of the rejected-yet-recurring Larpo items.
check: D-LAYOUT-5, D-CTA-1.

text: Do not accent a single word in the headline by switching font, italicising, or recolouring it.
why: Anthropic SKILL.md names it a tell; slop-cop `hero_font_mix` fires when the biggest heading near the top mixes two families, roman+italic, or two text colours (min 32px, <=140 chars).
check: D-TYPE-3.

text: Count tells per page and per batch; use pattern-count tiers (0-1 / 2-3 / 4+) as a triage signal, not a score to maximise.
why: In 1,590 Show HN pages 22% hit 4+ patterns; tiers are what the only open measurement used. False-positive rate 5-10%, so a single hit proves nothing.
check: run detector (Section 3 of detector note).

text: A page where **three or more sections end on a short rebuttal or manufactured contrast** ("X. No Y.", "Not a feature. A platform.", "Stop guessing. Start winning.") fails the copy check; one is fine.
why: Impeccable `aphoristic-cadence`; ban lists across several secondary sources flag "It's not X, it's Y", "No fluff. No filler. Just results.", manufactured-suspense hooks ("The secret?", "Here's the thing"), and openers ("In today's fast-paced...").
check: D-COPY-1..4.
source: Impeccable registry [verified-local]; Gartner community and other lists [secondary, anecdotal].

text: Numbers must be sourced or labelled sample. "Fake-perfect" stats (`99.99%`, `4.1x`, `10K+ users` rows) are tells.
why: taste-skill bans fake-precise numbers; slop-cop `stat_banner_row` (3-6 sibling cards, number font >=22px, text <=10 chars, row >=300px wide); Anthropic SKILL.md: don't default to big number + small label + supporting stats + gradient accent.
check: D-LAYOUT-6.

text: Do not add a FAQ accordion, numbered 1-2-3 steps, or a logo/stat strip by template habit; add only if the visitor's actual objection requires it.
why: Both are slop-cop patterns (`faq_accordion`: >=3 `<details>` or "FAQ"-headed uniform question items in the lower half; `numbered_steps`: >=3 ascending numeric markers). Larpo's playbook covers the template waterfall in prose; these are the measured forms.
check: D-LAYOUT-7, D-LAYOUT-8.

text: Style the browser-owned surfaces: text selection, caret, scrollbars, focus ring, underline offset, tabular numerals.
why: Impeccable craft-floor: the cheapest signal that a page was built rather than assembled, "the one models skip most reliably". Not on any other list.
check: D-CRAFT-1 (`::selection`, `caret-color`, `scrollbar-color/width`, `text-underline-offset`, `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` present in computed/stylesheet rules).

text: Pick light vs dark from a physical use scene (who, where, ambient light), not from category.
why: Impeccable: "Dark or light is never a default." Perma-dark + grey body is a slop-cop pattern.
check: visual; D-COLOR-4 for the grey-on-dark half.

text: Author every colour as `oklch(L C H)`; emit hex (sRGB-mapped) as the default declaration and optionally a wider `oklch()` or `color(display-p3 ...)` inside `@media (color-gamut: p3)`. Keep a fallback declaration first.
why: hex/rgb/hsl are sRGB-only in CSS; OKLCH has no gamut cap, and out-of-gamut values are mapped by the browser (CSS Color 4 specifies chroma reduction at constant L/H, which preserves hue; older engines clipped RGB channels and shifted hue) [verified: Evil Martians; browser behaviour has been changing, re-test].
check: every `oklch()` in CSS parses; a script converts it to sRGB and flags `max(r,g,b) > 1` unless it sits inside a `color-gamut: p3` block.

text: Gate text on WCAG 2.2 AND APCA: body/secondary text >= 4.5:1 (7:1 for ink-2 targets) **and** |Lc| >= 60 (75 for the primary reading colour). Large text (>= 18pt = 24px, or >= 14pt bold = ~18.7px) may use 3:1 under WCAG.
why: WCAG's formula treats light-on-dark mid-greys too generously; APCA models polarity (Lc 32 for the 4.5:1 grey on `#0f0f0f`) [computed]. Myndex thresholds: Lc 15 invisibility point for some viewers, 30 minimum for any spot/non-text use, 45 large fluent text or sub-fluent minimum, 60 medium text >24px, 75 minimum body text, 90 preferred body [verified]. Rounding is not allowed in WCAG: 4.499:1 fails [verified].
check: per pair: `wcag >= T && |apca| >= A`.
