text: Implement reduced motion at three layers: CSS (`@media`), JS libs (`MotionConfig reducedMotion="user"`, `useReducedMotion`, `gsap.matchMedia`), and media (autoplay video/Lottie/GIF).
why: CSS media queries don't affect JS-driven animation; web.dev: "For JavaScript animations you must listen for changes yourself".
check: emulate `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` (DevTools Rendering panel, or Command Palette; resets when DevTools closes) and walk every page: no slide/scale/parallax/autoplay remain.

text: Behaviour map under `reduce`:

Distance token trick: drive travel distances from a variable that collapses under reduce, so one keyframe serves both. [engine note] ```css :root { --travel: 16px; --reveal-ms: 600ms; } @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { :root { --travel: 0px; --reveal-ms: 200ms; } } @keyframes rise { from { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(var(--travel)); } } .hero > * { animation: rise var(--reveal-ms) var(--ease-out-expo) both; } ```

SSR-safe JS hook defaults to *reduced* on the server then corrects in an effect (Josh Comeau); in non-SSR apps read `matchMedia` synchronously. With Motion use `useReducedMotion()` (`boolean | null`).
Offer a site-level override where practical (Motion `reducedMotion={userSetting}`; GSAP `gsap.matchMediaRefresh()` after toggling).

Autoplaying/looping content longer than 5s next to other content needs a visible pause control (WCAG 2.2.2, Level A) regardless of OS setting; a mechanism that only stops while focused doesn't count; one control may serve the whole page. Preloaders can be "essential" when the user cannot interact during that phase.
check: any `animation-iteration-count: infinite` / looping video outside a loading indicator => needs control or `reduce` stop.

text: No flashing above 3 per second; avoid full-viewport strobe/fast alternating high-contrast transitions.

Vestibular triggers to avoid or isolate: parallax (differential speeds), large zoom/scale, full-screen slides, scroll-jacking, spinning/rotating large elements, swim/wobble effects, auto-scrolling carousels.
source: web.dev; WCAG 2.3.3; NN/g ("avoid flashing, parallax, scroll-jacking") (verified)

text: Motion is not the only information channel: pair with static cue; pair with focus management (focus moves to the new dialog/page heading regardless of animation).

Budget: 16.6ms/frame (60Hz), 8.3ms (120Hz) [engine note for 120Hz]. Profile with DevTools Performance (Summary > Rendering should be ~0 for transform-only animation) and the FPS meter ("Frames" ~99%). Check Paint flashing.

Eliminate layout thrash: never interleave DOM reads (`offsetWidth`, `getBoundingClientRect`, `scrollTop`, `getComputedStyle`) with writes in loops; batch reads, then writes, in `requestAnimationFrame`; use FLIP (First-Last-Invert-Play) rather than animating geometry (Motion `layout` and GSAP Flip do it). [engine note; standard practice, not fetched]
check: DevTools Performance "Forced reflow" warnings; Long Animation Frames (LoAF).

text: Scroll handling: no `scroll`/`wheel` listeners that read layout; use `IntersectionObserver`, CSS scroll-driven animations, Motion `useScroll`/`inView`, or GSAP ScrollTrigger; mark listeners `passive`. [engine note]

Keep animation work off the main thread when the main thread is busy: during page load, hydration, route change, data fetch. CSS/WAAPI animations continue; rAF-driven JS animations drop frames (Emil: Vercel dashboard tab animation dropped frames during page loads until moved to CSS).

Responsiveness (INP): animation must not delay the next paint after input. INP measures worst interaction latency (input delay + handler + next frame) at p75: **good <=200ms, needs improvement 200-500ms, poor >500ms**. Long tasks delay event handling; don't start heavy JS animation setup inside click handlers; yield (e.g., `scheduler.yield()`), and don't gate UI updates on animation completion.
check: field INP / CrUX; lab: DevTools "Interactions" track.
source: web.dev/inp (verified; yielding advice per page links, not detailed)

text: Limit simultaneously animating elements and layers: large blurred/shadowed elements and many `will-change` layers consume GPU memory; test on a low-end phone.
Never delay interaction: elements must be clickable/focusable during their entrance animation (don't set `pointer-events:none` for the whole stagger).
source: Emil: "never block interaction while stagger animations are playing" (verified)

text: No layout shift from motion: animate with `transform`; reserve space for skeleton->content swaps and image dimensions; `scrollbar-gutter: stable` (Motion layout docs).

Pick the indicator by expected wait (NN/g): **<1s: nothing** (a flash of skeleton/spinner is worse); **2-10s**: spinner (single module/card) or skeleton (full-page); **>10s**: progress bar with duration estimate; process tasks (upload/convert) use progress bars. Don't use skeletons for non-page processes and never as a substitute for performance work.

Skeletons mirror the real layout (header/footer-only frames are just spinners). Show only after a ~200-300ms grace period and keep at least ~400ms once shown, to avoid flash [engine note]. Shimmer: left-to-right linear gradient 1.5-2s loop (DoorDash example; NN/g warns pulse/shimmer can distract or cause a11y problems -> stop under reduce). ```css .skeleton { background: linear-gradient(90deg, var(--sk-a) 25%, var(--sk-b) 50%, var(--sk-a) 75%); background-size: 200% 100%; } @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) { .skeleton { animation: shimmer 1.6s linear infinite; } } @keyframes shimmer { to { background-position: -200% 0; } } ``` (animating `background-position` repaints; for many items animate a single transformed overlay instead [engine note]).
Content replacing skeleton: opacity cross-fade 150-200ms, same dimensions, no stagger, no slide.
why: Replacement happens on every navigation; frequency rule. [engine note]

text: Spinners: fast rotation (~0.8-1s per turn) reads as faster loading (Emil: same load time, different perception). `linear`.

Optimistic UI: apply the change instantly (<100ms), mark it subtly pending only if latency can exceed ~1s, reconcile silently on success, and on failure revert with a visible, non-modal explanation (toast + restore); do not animate the success path beyond the normal state change. React 19: `useOptimistic`. [engine note] ```tsx const [optimisticItems, addOptimistic] = useOptimistic(items, (state, next: Item) => [...state, { ...next, pending: true }]); async function onAdd(next: Item) { addOptimistic(next); await save(next); }   // revert is automatic when the action settles ```
Progress that tracks reality: match animation duration to the real operation (upload animation duration matches file size, IxDF "Timing" principle). Fake progress bars that stall at 99% look cheap.

Button loading state: keep width (no layout shift), swap label for spinner with opacity/blur/scale (0.25->1, opacity 0->1, blur 4px->0, `spring duration .3 bounce 0`, per make-interfaces-feel-better) or keep label + inline spinner.

Plan the load as a short, ordered sequence with one focal point at a time (Disney "staging"): (0) navigation and layout are static; (1) background/media settles (0-150ms); (2) eyebrow -> headline -> sub (80-100ms apart, 600-700ms each, `ease-out-expo`); (3) primary CTA; (4) hero visual; (5) secondary elements below the fold wait for scroll. Total <= ~1.2s to final state; user can interact at t=0.

Prefer **CSS keyframes (with `animation-fill-mode: both`) for the first-paint hero** over a hydration-dependent JS library: CSS runs before hydration and off the main thread, so it starts at first paint. Use Motion/GSAP for what happens after load (interaction, scroll, layout).
why: Emil's observation that CSS beats JS animation while the page is busy; hydration-gated entrance makes content pop in late.
check: Performance trace: first animation frame near FCP; no long task overlapping the entrance.

text: Do not hide the LCP element behind `opacity:0`: Chrome ignores `opacity:0` elements for LCP, so a 700ms fade-in on the LCP candidate is added to the metric. [engine note, based on the web.dev LCP definition, not fetched this session] Animate the LCP element with transform only (or a very short fade <=150ms), and animate the non-LCP supporting elements more freely.

SSR: render the *initial* hidden state in CSS/HTML only if the animation is guaranteed to run; otherwise render the final state and add motion as enhancement (no-JS and reduced-motion get the final state). `initial={false}` on `AnimatePresence`; Motion server-renders `initial` styles.

Wait for fonts before animating text (or `font-display: optional/swap` with size-adjusted fallbacks) so glyph reflow doesn't happen mid-animation; split by line/word, not by character, for headlines longer than ~3 words (per-character stagger at 30ms*40 chars = 1.2s). `document.fonts.ready`.
Run the hero entrance once per session/visit; skip on same-session repeat navigations (frequency rule). Reveal below-the-fold sections on scroll with `once`.
Keep total JS cost of motion libs in the budget: `LazyMotion` + `m` (~4.6kb) or CSS-only for marketing pages. GSAP core + ScrollTrigger only if scroll storytelling is the product.

Enhance native scroll, never replace it: keep the real scrollbar, wheel/trackpad speed, keyboard (Space/PgDn/arrows/Home/End), in-page anchors, find-in-page, back button, and focus-into-view working. If a smooth-scroll library is used, disable it under reduced motion and for keyboard focus jumps.
check: Tab through the page: focus ring is never offscreen/hidden by a pinned layer; browser find works; `scroll-behavior`/lib off under `reduce`.

text: Every beat's content must be reachable without the animation: in reduced-motion, no-JS, and unsupported-browser states render a stacked static version. Never hide essential text behind scrubbed opacity.

One idea per scroll beat; pin length <= ~2 viewport heights per beat; total pinned journey short enough to scroll past in seconds; always provide a way to skip (anchor links, nav). Animation overload is the most common failure (distracting, slow, fatiguing).

Size sticky stages with `svh` (or `dvh`) with a `vh` fallback and test with the iOS address bar visible; `100vh` overflows the visible area on phones. WebKit bug 266835 (dvh scroll jank, NEW at capture) means test on a real iPhone; avoid `dvh` on elements that also use scroll-snap. ```css .stage { height: 100vh; height: 100svh; position: sticky; top: 0; } ```

Scrub on `transform`/`opacity` only; prefer CSS scroll-driven animations or Motion `useScroll` (GPU `ScrollTimeline` path) or ScrollTrigger with `scrub: 0.5-1`; call `ScrollTrigger.refresh()` after fonts/images load; use `invalidateOnRefresh` for computed starts.
Parallax: small differential only (<= ~10-20% speed delta) on decorative layers, never on text or controls, off under `reduce` (WCAG 2.3.3 AAA calls it out). Mobile: usually remove.

Decide mobile strategy up front: keep the scroll interaction (consistent, works when transitions carry meaning) or stack content (The Pudding's two options). Phones have less perf headroom; test on real devices.
Scroll-snap: avoid `mandatory` on content taller than the viewport (traps users); use `proximity`.
Time content to reading speed, not scroll distance: text that disappears before it can be read at normal scroll speed is a failure; allow dwelling (no auto-advance).
Contrast over moving media must hold in every frame (check worst frame), text over video needs a scrim.
Do not animate keyboard-initiated actions (command palette open/close, shortcut toggles, list navigation by arrow keys, tab switching via keyboard).
why: Repeated hundreds of times/day; animation makes the UI feel delayed and disconnected from input. Rauno found removing motion from frequent keyboard actions made the UI feel faster even when the animations had been tuned.
check: For handlers fired by `keydown`/shortcut libs, no `transition`/`animate` on the result; `visual`.

text: Run the frequency table before writing any animation: 100+/day = none; tens/day = remove or <=100ms opacity/color only; occasional = standard tokens; rare = may add delight.
why: The "initial delight fades and the animation slows users down".
check: `visual` review against the table.

text: Motion must never be the only carrier of state. Pair every animated change with a static cue (color, icon, label).
why: Reduce Motion users, fast users who interrupt, screenshots.
check: Disable all animation (`*{animation:none!important;transition:none!important}` in devtools): every state change is still legible.
source: Apple HIG "optional" (third-party mirror of official page); make-interfaces-feel-better skill

text: UI transitions <=300ms; target by role (section 3.1). Exceed 300ms only for large-distance movement, hero/marketing orchestration, or drawers/sheets that mimic native (500ms).
why: Perceived responsiveness; NN/g says >500ms drags.
check: Parse computed `transition-duration`/`animation-duration` of interactive components; flag >300ms on non-hero elements; `visual` for JS springs (estimate settle time, section 3.3).

text: Make exit shorter than enter (roughly 60-75% of enter).
why: Entering needs a moment for the eye to register; leaving is the system getting out of the way.
check: `exit duration <= enter duration` for every paired overlay.

text: Scale duration with distance/area travelled, not one value for everything. [engine note] Tiers: <=48px move: 120-150ms; 48-200px: 180-250ms; 200-500px: 250-350ms; full-screen: 300-400ms; never >500ms without a stated reason.
why: Perceived speed should be roughly constant; larger objects need longer to read as the same velocity. NN/g: 400ms only for big movement on large screens.
check: `visual`; lint max duration by element area.

text: Hover-in is fast, hover-out may be slower (Josh Comeau: 125ms in / 450ms out for a lift-on-hover) for forgiving, non-flickery feel. (opinion)
why: Action-driven timing: user intent is clear on enter, uncertain on leave.
applies: landing page hover effects only; skip for dense app UI.
check: `visual`.

text: Enter and most exits: custom strong ease-out. Default token `--ease-out: cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1)` (ease-out-quint, Penner CSS values).
why: Starts fast (responsive), settles softly.
check: Computed `transition-timing-function` is not the keyword `ease-in`/`linear` on enter/exit of UI; prefer not the bare keyword `ease-out`/`ease` either (weak).
source: Emil, emil-design-eng skill (verified); curve identity verified against Penner CSS easings

text: On-screen movement/morph (element moves between two visible positions): strong ease-in-out `cubic-bezier(0.77, 0, 0.175, 1)` (ease-in-out-quart) or a spring.
why: Needs both acceleration and deceleration.
check: `visual`.

text: Use `ease-in` (or M3 emphasized-accelerate `0.3,0,0.8,0.15`) only for an element that exits the viewport entirely and ends invisible.
why: Accelerating away is natural only when leaving; Josh Comeau: "ease-in rarely right unless the element ends off-screen".
check: `ease-in` present => element must end off-screen or at opacity 0.

text: `linear` only for constant-speed things: spinners, marquees, progress fills, scrub-bound scroll animations, hold-to-confirm press.
why: Linear motion looks mechanical otherwise.
check: `linear` outside those uses is a smell.

text: Avoid bouncy/elastic/back easings on UI chrome; reserve overshoot for playful or gesture-momentum moments.
why: Apple: bounce only when the gesture has momentum.
check: `cubic-bezier` with y>1 or <0, `bounce > 0.3`, `back`/`elastic`/`anticipate` named easings.

text: Start every spring at no overshoot (Motion `bounce: 0`, i.e. damping ratio 1). Add `bounce` 0.1-0.25 only for drag-release, swipe-dismiss or deliberately playful elements; never above 0.3 on product UI.
why: Apple: damping ratio 100% for taps; ~80% (= Motion bounce 0.2) for momentum gestures. Motion maps `bounce` to damping ratio as `1 - bounce` (verified in motion-dom 14.0.0 source: `bounceToDampingRatio`).
check: grep `bounce:` > 0.3; grep `stiffness`/`damping` pairs and compute ratio = damping / (2*sqrt(stiffness*mass)) >= 0.7 for chrome.

text: Prefer duration-like spring params (`visualDuration` + `bounce`) over raw stiffness/damping/mass in product code; keep raw physics only when matching a reference.
why: Designer-legible; `visualDuration` states when the bulk of motion is done. Note raw `stiffness`/`damping`/`mass` override `bounce`/`duration` (verified, docs + source).
check: Springs in code are tokens from `motion-tokens.json`.

text: Do not use the Motion default transition on x/y by accident: its implicit transform spring is `stiffness 500 / damping 25` (damping ratio 0.56, ~12% overshoot), `scale` is critically damped `550/~47` (verified in source `default-transitions.mjs`).
why: The implicit x/y overshoot is the single most common "bouncy template" look.
check: Every `animate`/`whileX` with transform props specifies a `transition` (or a `MotionConfig transition` default is set).

text: Springs for opacity/color are usually wrong; use tween (`duration`, ease-out) for opacity/color.
why: Spring overshoot on opacity clamps or causes flicker; Josh Comeau avoids springs for color/opacity (opinion).
check: `type:"spring"` on `opacity`/`color`.

text: Pressable elements: `transform: scale(0.97)` on `:active` (allowed band 0.95-0.98), 100-160ms ease-out. Never below 0.95.
why: Immediate feedback that the UI is "listening". Sources differ: Emil 0.97, make-interfaces-feel-better 0.96 (opinion).
check: `:active` rule exists with scale in [0.95, 0.98].

text: Hover animation only behind `@media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)`.
why: Touch fires hover on tap = false positives. (Motion's own `whileHover` already ignores `pointerType === "touch"`, verified in source `gestures/hover.mjs`; CSS `:hover` does not.)
check: every `:hover` that moves/scales is inside the media query.

text: Tooltips: first one delayed (hover intent), subsequent siblings open instantly with no animation (`data-instant` in Base UI). Tooltip animation 125ms ease-out, `scale(0.97)` + opacity.
why: Prevents accidental activation yet makes the whole toolbar feel fast.
check: `[data-instant]{transition-duration:0ms}` present; open delay token.

text: Popovers/menus/selects set `transform-origin` to the trigger (`var(--transform-origin)` in Base UI, `--radix-*-content-transform-origin` in Radix); modals stay `center`.
why: Growth from the trigger shows causality.
check: computed `transform-origin` != `50% 50%` for anchored popups.

text: Never `scale(0)`; start at 0.9-0.97 + opacity 0.
why: Nothing real appears from nowhere.
check: grep `scale(0)`, `scale: 0`, `initial={{ scale: 0 }}`.

text: Gesture UI: show immediate 1:1 tracking during the gesture, animate only after commit; dismissal by velocity (Sonner: swipe distance >= threshold OR velocity > 0.11 px/ms), with friction (not a wall) past boundaries.
why: Delay in tracking = "disconnected"; hard stop at a boundary reads as broken.
check: `visual` + test on a real device.

text: Destructive/irreversible commits wait for release (pointer up); lightweight reversible ones may fire mid-gesture.
why: Change-of-mind costs.
check: `visual`.

text: Stagger sibling entrances 30-80ms per item for routine lists; ~80-120ms for a staged hero/semantic chunks; cap the total cascade at ~400ms for lists (clamp index: `delay = min(i, 8) * step`) and ~1s for a hero.
why: Cascade guides the eye in reading order; long cascades block perceived readiness. Emil: 30-80ms; make-interfaces: ~100ms for staged chunks; the cap is [engine note].
applies: landing page; lists on first load only.
check: `step <= 120ms`; `last delay + duration <= 1200ms` on heroes.
source: Emil skill; make-interfaces-feel-better skill (verified); cap [engine note]

text: Never stagger on high-frequency or user-triggered repeat updates (filter results, typing, tab switch). Never block interaction while a stagger plays.
why: Attention cost repeats each time.
check: `visual`.

text: Prefer the library's stagger over hand-written `nth-child` delays: Motion `delayChildren: stagger(0.05)`; GSAP `stagger: 0.05`; CSS `--i` custom property + `animation-delay: calc(var(--i) * 50ms)`.
why: Survives item-count changes.
check: no >10 hardcoded `nth-child` delays.

text: Design each microinteraction as Trigger -> Rules -> Feedback -> Loops & Modes. Feedback must reveal the (invisible) rules; give feedback within ~100ms of the trigger [engine note: the 0.1s figure is the classic Nielsen response limit, not fetched here]. Long-lived loops should decay: the 50th occurrence must be quieter than the 1st.
why: Rules are invisible; feedback is how users learn them (Saffer).
check: each interactive component has trigger state, feedback state, and a repeat-use behavior defined in its spec.
source: search summaries of Saffer's *Microinteractions* (O'Reilly 2013); book itself NOT read, see section 7.

text: List properties explicitly. Never `transition: all` (and never `transition-property: all` via utility classes).
why: Unexpected properties (width, filter, color from a later rule) start animating; also hides cost.
check: grep `transition:\s*all|transition-all`.
source: Vercel Web Interface Guidelines; Josh Comeau (verified) ```css .btn { transition: transform 160ms var(--ease-out), background-color 150ms ease, box-shadow 150ms ease; } @media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine) { .btn:hover { background-color: var(--accent-hover); } } .btn:active { transform: scale(0.97); } ```

text: Keyframe animations that should hold their end state need `animation-fill-mode: both` (or `backwards` for delayed starts); otherwise the element is fully visible during `animation-delay`.
why: Without `backwards`, the base styles show during the delay and the element flashes then animates.
check: any `animation-delay` on an entering element must come with fill-mode `backwards|both`.

text: Put per-element variation in custom properties, not duplicated keyframes: `animation-delay: calc(var(--i) * 60ms)`, `--bounce-height`. Keep keyframes generic and reusable; keyframe names are global. ```css @keyframes rise-in { from { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(var(--rise, 16px)); } } .reveal > * { animation: rise-in 600ms var(--ease-out-expo) both; animation-delay: calc(var(--i, 0) * 80ms); } ``` (React: `style={{ "--i": index } as React.CSSProperties}`.) Cap `--i` at ~8 [engine note].

Timing functions in keyframes apply per segment, not to the whole animation (use `linear` for spinners; set easing on each keyframe if shaping a multi-step path). `alternate` halves keyframe work for back-and-forth. (Josh Comeau, verified)

Delay-on-leave trick for hover menus: 300ms `transition-delay` on the hidden state, 0 on the shown state, so diagonal mouse travel toward a submenu does not close it. ```css .dropdown { opacity: 0; transition: opacity 400ms; transition-delay: 300ms; } .wrapper:hover .dropdown { opacity: 1; transition: opacity 100ms; transition-delay: 0ms; } ```
Don't let the animated element be its own hover trigger when it moves away from the cursor (flicker loop). Hover the stationary parent, transform the child.
Set `transform-origin` deliberately (trigger-anchored for popovers; `center` for modals). For SVG, put transforms on a `<g>` wrapper with `transform-box: fill-box; transform-origin: center`.

Order matters: a standalone `@starting-style` block has the same specificity as the rule it modifies and must come **after** it; nested form is `selector { @starting-style { ... } }`. It applies only to CSS transitions (CSS animations don't need it). It supplies "from" values on first render and on `display:none` -> visible. It is **not** used on the way out; exit goes to the element's default state, so entry/exit can differ.
To animate exit of `display` or top-layer elements, transition `display` and `overlay` with `allow-discrete` (shorthand `transition: all 0.7s allow-discrete` also works).
why: Without `overlay` the element leaves the top layer immediately, so the exit looks broken.
check: popover/dialog exit works: close it and watch it fade rather than vanish.
source: MDN @starting-style (verified) ```css /* Popover / dialog entry+exit in pure CSS  (MDN pattern, tuned to our tokens) */ [popover], dialog { opacity: 0; transform: scale(0.96); transition: opacity 150ms var(--ease-out), transform 150ms var(--ease-out), overlay 150ms allow-discrete, display 150ms allow-discrete; } [popover]:popover-open, dialog[open] { opacity: 1; transform: scale(1); transition-duration: 200ms;           /* enter slower than exit */ } @starting-style { [popover]:popover-open, dialog[open] { opacity: 0; transform: scale(0.96); } } [popover]::backdrop, dialog::backdrop { background-color: transparent; transition: background-color 200ms, overlay 200ms allow-discrete, display 200ms allow-discrete; } [popover]:popover-open::backdrop, dialog[open]::backdrop { background-color: rgb(0 0 0 / 0.25); } @starting-style { [popover]:popover-open::backdrop, dialog[open]::backdrop { background-color: transparent; } } ``` (MDN notes nesting with `&` is not supported for pseudo-elements, so the backdrop starting style is a standalone block.) The `dialog[open]` selector is the MDN dialog pattern; not re-fetched this session.

text: Base UI / Radix components expose `data-starting-style`, `data-ending-style`, `data-instant`, `--transform-origin`; use those instead of re-implementing. (verified) ```css .tooltip { transition: transform 125ms ease-out, opacity 125ms ease-out; transform-origin: var(--transform-origin); } .tooltip[data-starting-style], .tooltip[data-ending-style] { opacity: 0; transform: scale(0.97); } .tooltip[data-instant] { transition-duration: 0ms; } ```

Animating to `height: auto`: set `interpolate-size: allow-keywords` on `:root` and transition `height` between a length and `auto|max-content|fit-content`; one end must be a length. MDN status: **Experimental / limited availability**, so provide a fallback (instant change, or `grid-template-rows: 0fr -> 1fr` trick [engine note, unverified here]). ```css :root { interpolate-size: allow-keywords; } .panel { height: 0; overflow: clip; transition: height 220ms var(--ease-out); } .panel[data-open] { height: auto; } ```

Generate `linear()` springs from physics rather than hand-typing; keep ~20-40 points; first point `0`, last `1`; values may exceed 1 for overshoot; percentages must ascend. Use Jake Archibald's generator (linear-easing-generator.netlify.app) or sample your own spring. Fixed duration = settle time.
why: Real springs (Motion) keep velocity on interruption; this does not. Use for static hover/entry states, not drag release.
check: `linear(` used on transitions that can be interrupted by gesture => switch to Motion.
source: MDN linear() (verified syntax); generator named by MDN. The three curves below were generated for this file by sampling the same mass-spring model (stiffness/damping, mass 1) at 21 points; check visually before shipping. ```css :root { /* ~209ms, zeta 0.9, no visible overshoot  == M3 "standard default spatial" (k700, c47.6) */ --spring-snappy: linear(0, 0.034, 0.114, 0.216, 0.325, 0.432, 0.531, 0.619, 0.696, 0.76, 0.814, 0.856, 0.891, 0.919, 0.941, 0.957, 0.97, 0.98, 0.987, 0.992, 1); --spring-snappy-duration: 210ms; /* ~400ms, zeta 0.7, peak 1.045 (Motion visualDuration .3 / bounce .3) */ --spring-bouncy: linear(0, 0.053, 0.176, 0.331, 0.489, 0.636, 0.76, 0.859, 0.933, 0.985, 1.018, 1.036, 1.044, 1.045, 1.041, 1.035, 1.028, 1.021, 1.014, 1.009, 1); --spring-bouncy-duration: 400ms; /* ~570ms, zeta 1.0 (Motion visualDuration .4 / bounce 0) */ --spring-gentle: linear(0, 0.057, 0.176, 0.312, 0.443, 0.559, 0.657, 0.736, 0.8, 0.849, 0.887, 0.916, 0.938, 0.954, 0.966, 0.975, 0.982, 0.987, 0.99, 0.993, 1); --spring-gentle-duration: 570ms; } .card { transition: transform var(--spring-snappy-duration) var(--spring-snappy); } ```

text: Fallback: declare a `cubic-bezier` `transition` first, then override inside `@supports (transition-timing-function: linear(0, 1))` if you need to guard older engines (support is widely available since Dec 2023, so usually unnecessary).

Timelines: `scroll(<scroller> <axis>)` with scroller `nearest|root|self`, axis `block|inline|x|y`; `view(<axis> <inset>)` for an element's progress through its scrollport. Named: `scroll-timeline-name`/`view-timeline-name: --x` + `animation-timeline: --x`; `timeline-scope` hoists names to an ancestor (support lagged: Chrome 116 flag at first).

`animation-duration` must be `auto` (the default in the shorthand when omitted; if you set it for the fallback, scroll-driven code needs `auto`/`1ms` per MDN's example); **declare `animation-timeline` after the `animation` shorthand** because the shorthand resets it to `auto`.

Use `animation-range` to define the active window: names `cover | contain | entry | exit | entry-crossing | exit-crossing` (plus offsets: `entry 0% cover 40%`, `entry 10% exit -25%`). A bare name means 0%-100% of that range. Use `animation-fill-mode: both` to hold styles outside the range.
source: MDN animation-range/animation-timeline; Chrome docs (verified) ```css /* Scroll progress bar */ @keyframes grow { from { transform: scaleX(0); } to { transform: scaleX(1); } } .progress { transform-origin: 0 50%; animation: grow linear both; animation-timeline: scroll(root block); }

text: No-support state (Firefox stable): the `.reveal` element must be visible and in place (the snippet only sets `animation` inside `@supports`). Never ship a pattern where JS-less/unsupported browsers see `opacity:0`.

Animate only `transform`/`opacity` (and `clip-path`/`filter` sparingly) with scroll timelines, to stay compositor-driven. - JS: `new ScrollTimeline({ source: document.documentElement, axis })`, `new ViewTimeline({ subject, axis, inset })`, `el.animate(kf, { timeline, rangeStart: "entry 25%", rangeEnd })`.

Same-document: feature-detect, then wrap the DOM update. If page visibility is `hidden` the transition is skipped. Duplicate `view-transition-name` values at once reject `ready` and skip the transition. ```js function go(update) { if (!document.startViewTransition) return update(); document.startViewTransition(() => update()); } ``` (React: wrapping `flushSync` for the DOM update is the usual companion; or use React's `<ViewTransition>` inside `startTransition`, see `motion-library-react.md`/React docs where `enter/exit/update/share/default` props map to CSS classes and React does NOT auto-handle reduced motion.)

Default animation is cross-fade + smooth geometry; customise with `::view-transition-group(name)`, `-image-pair`, `-old`, `-new`. Targeting `*` styles all snapshots. Keep durations to the motion tokens: 250-350ms for route changes. ```css @keyframes fade-in  { from { opacity: 0; } } @keyframes fade-out { to   { opacity: 0; } } ::view-transition-group(root) { animation-duration: 280ms; animation-timing-function: cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1); } ::view-transition-old(root) { animation: 140ms ease-in both fade-out; } ::view-transition-new(root) { animation: 280ms var(--ease-out) both fade-in; } @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { ::view-transition-group(*), ::view-transition-old(*), ::view-transition-new(*) { animation: none !important; } } ``` The reduced-motion block is my application of React's documented approach (their docs set `animation: none` under the media query) [engine note: for a minimal-change variant keep a crossfade only].

Cross-document (MPA): add `@view-transition { navigation: auto; }` on both pages (same origin). Name shared elements in `pageswap` (outgoing) and `pagereveal` (incoming), and **clear the names afterwards** (`await e.viewTransition.finished`) so bfcache back-navigation doesn't produce duplicate names. For stable first frames use render blocking: `<link rel="expect" href="#lead-content" blocking="render">` and `<script blocking="render">` in `<head>`, optionally with `media` per viewport. `PageSwapEvent.activation` is `null` if the redirect chain includes a cross-origin URL.

Custom JS animation on the pseudo-elements (e.g., circular reveal for theme toggle) requires `transition.ready.then(() => documentElement.animate({ clipPath: [...] }, { duration, easing, pseudoElement: "::view-transition-new(root)" }))` and neutralising the default (`animation: none; mix-blend-mode: normal; display: block` on old/new; `isolation: auto` on image-pair).

Use shared-element names for hero image -> detail, nav indicator, grid filter reorder; otherwise stay with root cross-fade. Don't name 100s of elements (each is a snapshot). - Transition **types** (`transition.types`, `:active-view-transition-type()`) and `view-transition-class` exist for per-direction animation (React's `ViewTransition` maps them); not read in detail this session, see 7.

Animate `transform`/`opacity` only. If a layout property must change (accordion height), prefer `interpolate-size` / grid-rows trick, contain the subtree (`overflow: clip`, `contain: layout paint`), and keep it short.
why: 60fps = 16.6ms budget; layout+paint each frame blows it. web.dev measured a `top/left` example at 37ms rendering and 50% dropped frames vs 0 and ~1% for `transform`.
check: Chrome DevTools Performance: Rendering time in summary should be ~0; Rendering tab "Frame Rendering Stats"; Paint flashing.

text: `will-change`: only on elements that are about to animate and only when you've observed first-frame stutter; values limited to `transform`, `opacity`, `filter`; never `will-change: all`. For occasional animations, set it just before via JS and remove after; keep it permanently only for always-changing elements. Each promoted layer costs GPU memory (matters on low-end phones).
CSS variables inherit: updating a custom property on a container (e.g., `--swipe-amount` on a drawer root) invalidates style for all descendants; write `transform` on the specific element instead.
Blur: <=20px, short-lived; heavy blur/backdrop-filter animation is expensive, especially in Safari. `filter: blur(2px)` crossfade masking is fine.

Prefer CSS/WAAPI for predetermined animations (off-thread), JS for dynamic/interruptible ones. WAAPI snippet with `fill: "forwards"` and a custom easing string is hardware accelerated for compositor properties: ```js el.animate([{ clipPath: "inset(0 0 100% 0)" }, { clipPath: "inset(0 0 0 0)" }], { duration: 600, fill: "forwards", easing: "cubic-bezier(0.77, 0, 0.175, 1)" }); ``` - CSS property cost cheat sheet [engine note, from the well-known CSS Triggers model; not fetched]: composite-only = `transform`, `opacity` (and `translate/scale/rotate`); paint-only = `color`, `background-color`, `box-shadow`, `border-radius`, `outline`, `visibility`; layout+paint = `width/height/top/left/margin/padding/font-size/border-width/flex-basis`. Josh Comeau also ranks `background-color` as moderately expensive and `height` as to-avoid (verified).

`clip-path: inset(top right bottom left)` is a high-quality animatable reveal (hold-to-delete overlay: press 2s `linear`, release 200ms `ease-out`; image reveal on scroll from `inset(0 0 100% 0)`; comparison slider; tabs with duplicated "active" layer clipped to the active tab for perfect colour transitions). (Emil skill, verified)
Set one app-wide `MotionConfig` with `reducedMotion="user"` and a default `transition` token, so no component falls back to the implicit 500/25 spring.
why: Implicit defaults are bouncy and ignore reduced motion unless configured.
check: `MotionConfig` exists at the root; grep `<motion.` usages with transform props and no `transition`.
source: motion.dev/docs/react-accessibility; source default-transitions.mjs (verified) ```tsx // app/providers.tsx   (motion@14.0.0) "use client"; import { MotionConfig } from "motion/react"; export function MotionProvider({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) { return ( <MotionConfig reducedMotion="user"   // "user" | "always" | "never" transition={{ type: "spring", visualDuration: 0.3, bounce: 0 }} > {children} </MotionConfig> ); } ```

check: no literal `stiffness:`/`damping:` outside this file.

why: M3 uses non-overshooting "effects" springs for color/alpha; overshoot on opacity is meaningless.

text: Headline 48-64px at 1440 is the default; to be distinctive, go to <=40px *or* >=84px, never in between. Cap fluid type (`clamp`) at 64px for default-range sites; sites above 80px scale with vw (Darkroom ~13.9vw, Pitch, Granola, Notion).
why: 48-64 is the shared template zone (25% to 75% quartiles = 48 to 64).
check: computed `font-size` of the hero headline.

text: Headline line-height 0.9-1.15 (median 1.07), never the 1.3+ body ratio. Below 0.95 only above ~64px (Pitch 0.8, Darkroom 0.8, Granola 0.93).
why: large display type reads as a shape; leading is the gap between lines, which looks wider as size grows.
check: `lineHeight / fontSize` on h1; flag >1.25.

text: Headline tracking -0.02em as default, tightening to -0.04..-0.06em for big/regular-weight display (Vercel -0.06 at 64px/400; Notion -0.048 at 96px/600; Resend h2 -0.05 at 56px). Positive tracking only for uppercase/mono/labels (Rive +0.01, TBC +0.15em, Darkroom labels).
why: large type opens up optically; tight tracking restores density.
check: `letterSpacing / fontSize` on h1/h2.

text: h2 about 0.74x the h1 (IQR 0.64-0.81); absolute median 44px (range 24-56). Section heading size changes <=1 step across the page (Linear: 48 on all four chapters).
check: h2/h1 and distinct h2 sizes per page.

text: Hero lede 16-20px (median 18), lh 1.3-1.5, colour at 60-70% of the ink (Linear `#8a8f98` on `#08090a`; Resend `#a1a4a5`); column 350-640px, not the container width.
why: muted contrast makes the headline the first read.
check: lede colour contrast vs headline (1.5-2.2x less).

text: Nav height 64px (IQR 64-72; range 42-102 incl. banners), sticky or fixed, transparent or bg-matched, with a 1px hairline or `backdrop-filter: blur(16-20px)` *or* nothing; link text 13-16px at weight 400-500. Reserve tall navs (>=96) for brand devices (Arc's 96px blue bar).
check: `getBoundingClientRect().height` of the fixed/sticky ancestor of `header`.

text: Hero primary CTA height 38-48px (median 41; range 34-58), 14-16px label, weight 400-600. Radius is one of {pill 7 of 22, 5-8px 7, <=4px 4, 9+px 4}. Pick one radius and use it for CTAs, inputs and chips together.
check: CTA `height`, `border-radius`; consistent across button/input/chip.

text: Content container 1200-1360px at 1440 (median 1274, range 1048-1392), expressed as `max-width` ~1280 + 24-40px side padding. Narrow text columns inside it: hero text 480-740px.
check: width of h1 ancestor chain.

text: Section vertical padding 96-128px (median 104, range 60-160); the set clusters on 96 / 120 / 128 / 160. Keep it uniform across sections (Resend 96 x9, Linear 128 x4 with near-identical section heights 1220-1232px, Framer 120).
check: padding-top/bottom of top-level `section`s; stdev across them.

text: Card radius 8-16px (median 12; 29 sites: min 4, max 24); controls 4-8px; pills only for chips/CTAs. Nested radius = outer minus padding.
check: histogram of `border-radius` on elements >180x100.

text: Borders: 1px at 6-12% white on dark, `#e5e5e5`-class on light; shadows only for floated media/popovers (Cursor `0 28px 70px .14`; Stripe `0 30px 45px -30px` tinted `50,50,93`).
check: count of non-"none" box-shadow vs 1px borders.

text: Type scale is small and sparse: 7-21 distinct font sizes sitewide (median ~11); Vercel uses 7, PostHog/Neon/Dub ~20.
check: `new Set(computed font-sizes)`.

text: Pair a display voice with a mono or utility voice: a monospace face is loaded on ~25 of 38 sites (Linear Berkeley Mono, Cursor Berkeley, Vercel Geist Mono, Resend Commit Mono *outweighing* its body font, Rive/Tomorrow, Darkroom mono at weight 200).
check: `@font-face` families.

text: Motion: transitions 150-300ms (200ms is the mode), `ease-out` or a strong bezier: `cubic-bezier(.16,1,.3,1)` (Anthropic, Ramp, OpenAI), `(.22,1,.36,1)` (OpenAI, v0), `(.32,.72,0,1)` (Linear, Granola, Supabase), `(.25,1,.5,1)` (Stripe), `(.23,1,.32,1)` (Raycast, Locomotive), `(.33,1,.68,1)` (Clerk, Mercury). Reserve >=500ms for entrances and decorative loops.
check: parse `transition-duration` and `-timing-function`.
source: measured n=40 (top durations 200ms x31, 150 x26, 300 x21, 400 x8, 100 x8).

text: Responsive headline: size at 390px is 0.44-0.89x desktop (median 0.63x); big-type sites scale continuously (Notion 42 -> 89.7 @1024 -> 96; Granola 48 -> 68 -> 110; Darkroom 104 -> 142 -> 267) while default sites step and cap (Vercel/Linear/Stripe cap at 64/64/48 beyond 1440).
source: measured n=24. One site (Mercury) had horizontal overflow at 1024 and 1920: verify `scrollWidth <= innerWidth`.

text: Use `text-wrap: balance` on headings: present in 33 of 40 CSS bundles (Notion 84 uses, OpenAI 99, Vercel 41, Linear 28).
check: computed `text-wrap` on h1/h2.

text: Evaluate each interaction against three things: the specific action performed (for example entering text into a web form), the physical attributes of the device (size, shape, weight of a phone), and how the user interacts with information on the device in context (p.84).
why: These variables determine whether a product lets users work quickly and efficiently (p.84).
check: process: each flow lists device, action, and context.

text: Size touch controls to reduce incorrect actions; if testing shows users struggle to hit certain buttons, enlarge them. Measure the error rate during user testing (p.84-85).
why: Mobile ergonomic design aims to reduce the possibility of incorrect actions (p.85).
check: touch target width/height from computed layout; process: error rate in test. The book gives no minimum size; see section 5 engine note.

text: Internal consistency: apply the same conventions and visual appearance to all UI elements throughout the interface (p.85-86).
why: A consistent design lets users transfer an acquired ability to other parts of the product; it is essential for pleasant encounters (p.85).
check: computed style variance for components of one role across all pages (button height, radius, font-size, colour); the set of distinct values per property should be small and tokenised.

text: External consistency: use the same design for the product on all platforms, desktop and mobile alike (p.86).
why: Same reason as internal: skills and expectations transfer (p.85-86).
check: compare component styling, labels and flows across breakpoints; same label strings, same iconography.

text: Use one name and one appearance per concept across screens (see also PU-DIF-06 in why-systems-fail.md) (p.47, 85).
why: Inconsistency forces rote learning (p.47).
check: synonym clustering of labels.

text: Prefer familiar concepts and metaphors; do not reinvent conventional patterns for novelty's sake (Jakob's Law). Full rule: PU-MOD-02 in memory-models-learning-effort.md (p.86).
why: Users get accustomed to conventions from other products and expect them (p.86).
check: see PU-MOD-02.

text: Give proper feedback: use visual and audio cues so users comprehend the present state of the system (p.87).
why: Control of information by the user is at the heart of HCI design; the user, not the system, should be in charge (p.87).
check: every async action has visible in-progress and completed states (spinner/skeleton/disabled/toast); focus, hover and active states exist on interactive elements.

text: Let users control system operations, including interrupting or terminating them (p.87).
why: Control is the user's, not the system's (p.87).
check: long-running operations (upload, export, generation) have cancel; modals and flows have close/back; no auto-advancing content without pause.

text: Personalise content using what you know about the user, to give the appearance that the system responds to their requirements (p.87).
why: Perceived responsiveness raises the sense of control (p.87).
check: process: personalised content has a visible, changeable source (e.g. shows name, recent items, saved settings) and a way to reset or control it.

text: Break difficult tasks into simple steps (p.88).
why: Simplifies decision-making and reduces complexity (p.88).
check: count fields/decisions per step; long forms are sectioned or stepped. No number in the book.

text: Remove every unnecessary action and keep navigation paths to a minimum so the user's attention and brainpower go to the task, not the interface (p.88).
why: Interaction should not take a lot of brainpower (p.87-88).
check: click depth from landing to each core task; count of optional fields and interstitials.

text: Give users the information they need to learn the system up front, and anticipate where they will need extra help (p.88).
why: Reduces learning cost at first use (p.88).
check: help text, empty states and contextual hints exist at known confusing points (format requirements stated before input, not after).

text: Combine related information and arrange UI elements so the most critical information is highlighted; use Gestalt principles to organise information on screens (p.88-89).
why: Grouping and emphasis cut search and cognitive effort (p.88-89).
check: see PU-PER-01/02/06.

text: Offer shortcuts for experienced users, for example keyboard shortcuts that perform tasks without a mouse (p.89).
why: Raises seasoned users' productivity (p.89).
check: visible shortcuts for repeated actions (command palette, kbd hints in menus); focusable controls in logical order.

text: Prevent errors where possible: map user journeys and analyse them to find places where users are likely to have issues (p.89-90).
why: Errors are human; the way a system handles them strongly affects users (p.89).
check: input constraints and formatting hints present (input type, masks, inline validation); process: journey walkthrough.

text: Stop users from making deadly mistakes with protective layers: confirm dialogs for deleting files or an entire account (p.90).
why: Fatal error states should be unreachable by accident (p.90).
check: destructive actions (delete, remove, cancel subscription, overwrite) trigger a confirmation that names the object, or are undoable.

text: Support "undo": allow actions to be reversed (p.90).
why: Reversibility makes trial and error safe (see PU-DIF-05) (p.46-47, 90).
check: delete/archive/edit actions expose undo (toast with Undo, trash, history).

text: When an error occurs, write messages that help users resolve it (p.90).
why: Users need to regain control (p.89-90).
check: error text states what is wrong and how to fix it, is adjacent to the field, uses no codes or jargon only; no "Error" alone.

text: Never hold users responsible for errors; treat them as the design's defects (p.90).
why: User-centered design: it is not the users' fault but design defects that cause mistakes (p.90).
check: copy lint on error text: no "you entered an invalid", "you failed", "your mistake"; phrase as what the system needs.

text: Design every decision point for three to four items held at once, not seven; treat Miller's 7 +/- 2 as an outdated upper bound (p.59-60).
why: The book reports estimates declining from Miller's seven and a half to three to four items (Koyani et al., 2004) and falling with age (p.60).
check: count items users must hold or compare simultaneously (steps in a flow visible at once, options in a primary choice, items in a nav level); flag >4 ungrouped.

text: Do not make users remember information across screens or steps; keep everything needed to complete the job in close proximity (p.62-63). People can only recall a few items for 3 to 4 seconds (p.62).
why: Short-term storage lasts 5 to 30 seconds (lower likely) (p.60) and is erased by competing activity (p.60-61).
check: multi-step flows repeat or summarise prior choices needed later; inputs with instructions put the instruction adjacent, not on another screen.

text: Place information that must be compared next to each other (p.63).
why: Avoids straining memory (p.63).
applies: landing page (pricing plans), SaaS app UI (tables, diffs).
check: compared items (plan features, before/after) appear in the same viewport and aligned rows.

text: Do not require working-memory tasks while the user needs to read fast: when screen-reading speed is critical, avoid asking for other jobs that use memory (p.63).
why: Short-term memory is overwritten by thinking, reciting or listening (p.60-61).
check: visual: no instruction text that disappears (auto-dismiss toast carrying required info; placeholder-only labels).

text: Organise, structure and present knowledge meaningfully and in familiar terms; give the user control over how information is presented (p.62).
why: Structured, meaningful, familiar information transfers to long-term memory and reduces demand on short-term (p.61-62).
check: headings/groups present; data views offer sort/filter/density control where tables exceed the chunk budget.

text: Make significant items unique or unusual (highlight crucial elements) to increase the chance they are remembered (p.63).
why: Distinctiveness aids recall (p.63).
check: one or two highlighted elements per section; if more than that are highlighted none is (see section 5).

text: Prefer recognition to recall: present lists of alternatives (menus, selects, suggestions, recent items) instead of requiring users to produce names or commands from memory (p.61-62, 80).
why: Active vocabulary (recallable) is about 2,000 to 3,000 words, passive vocabulary (recognisable) about 100,000; recognition provides memory cues for searching long-term memory (p.61-62). A GUI cut cognitive load by replacing commands to remember and format with menu commands only recognised (p.79-80).
check: free-text inputs where a finite option set exists (country, plan, role, date) should be a select/combobox/picker; commands exposed in menus not only via typed syntax.

text: Use words from the user's passive vocabulary: familiar words recognised at a glance; chunk size depends on the user's familiarity (p.60-62).
why: Familiarity enlarges chunk size (p.60).
check: copy review; jargon list.

text: Match the user's existing mental model: use familiar visual and usage expectations from other systems; a design that follows existing models is much easier to learn (p.73-74, 86).
why: Users carry expectations and prejudices from other systems and daily tasks; when the system matches, the model is reinforced and use feels intuitive; if not, interference arises (p.73-74).
check: compare nav placement, icon semantics, form patterns, checkout, auth flows to common conventions; deviation requires a stated reason.

text: Use familiar concepts and metaphors rather than inventing new ones (Jakob's Law): users spend most of their time on other products and expect conventional patterns; reinventing lengthens the learning curve (p.86).
why: Unfamiliar usage forces more time learning (p.86).
check: visual/pattern review: standard patterns for navigation, search, cart, forms.

text: When the existing mental model does not fit your goal, do not bend the design to it; give the user a clear and consistent new model to learn (p.74).
why: "Never compromise your goals or design to fit into pre-existing mental frameworks" (p.74).
check: process: new concept has one consistent name, one visual treatment, introduced once with onboarding.

text: Make targets for critical functions large; time to acquire a target depends on its distance and size (p.75-76).
why: Larger or closer targets are acquired faster (p.75); large buttons beat small buttons because they give a broader target (p.76).
check: computed bounding box of primary actions and touch targets; primary action larger than secondary actions; no numeric minimum is given in the book.

text: Use the screen's sides, top, bottom and corners ("pinning") for frequent controls, and let controls extend ("bleed") to the screen edge instead of leaving a one-pixel non-clickable border (p.75-76).
why: The edge stops the pointer at the control, so movement is much faster; a one-pixel edge needs careful positioning (p.76).
applies: SaaS app UI (toolbars, sidebars, top bars), desktop.
check: edge-docked bars: clickable area reaches the viewport edge (no padding between hit area and edge).

text: Size touch controls to reduce the possibility of incorrect actions; in testing measure error rate and enlarge buttons users miss (p.84-85).
why: Physical ergonomics: touch targets that are too small cause errors (p.85).
check: touch target dimensions and spacing; process: error rate in test.

text: Do not justify a complex design by users' ability to learn; where a simpler pathway exists, use it (p.76-77).
why: Humans can learn almost anything given time (the tightrope example), but unproductive learning time is usually avoided (p.76-77).
check: process: for each flow, compare the actual number of concepts to learn to the minimum.

text: Support jump-in, explore-and-experiment use: let people act immediately and discover; do not front-load massive amounts to learn (p.77).
why: People prefer to be active and experiment; the prospect of learning massive volumes deters some from using a system at all (p.77).
check: time/steps to first meaningful action; mandatory tutorials before first action are a flag.

text: Keep interface changes between versions or screens minimal; people are very sensitive to even modest changes (p.77).
why: Such changes cause problems when switching systems (p.77).
check: diff across screens/versions for moved or renamed primary controls.

text: Make the location of recurring items predictable by design consistency, so experienced users can start moving the cursor to a target before it appears (p.78).
why: Anticipating location is a by-product of learning; achieved through consistency, detailed and timely feedback, and phased learning (a person need only know what is required at that point) (p.78).
check: the same control occupies the same position/size across screens (compare bounding boxes of header, primary CTA, nav across routes).

text: Transfer skills: where possible let abilities learned in one setting apply in a similar situation elsewhere (p.77).
why: Learning is boosted by transfer (p.77).
check: same component = same behaviour everywhere.

text: Design screens so skilled performance can grow: allow gradual learning of shortcuts and better ways of working, and keep consistency so lower-order skills become automatic (p.78-79).
why: Skill is precise execution in exact time sequence; skills are hierarchical and lower ones become automatic (p.78-79).
check: frequent actions have keyboard shortcuts or quick paths; shortcut shown in menus/tooltips.

text: Cut cognitive load: keep screens free of noise and superfluous information; format and organise information properly; provide tools that rely on recognition not recollection; automate memory-intensive tasks (p.80).
why: The greater the effort required, the less likely a task is completed (p.79).
check: visual: count of distinct elements/weights per viewport; autofill/defaults/remembered values for memory-heavy fields.

text: Cut kinematic load: reduce the steps to complete tasks, minimise control actions and movements, automate mundane jobs (p.80).
why: Physical effort has a cost like mental effort; the GUI replaced multi-letter commands with one click (p.80).
check: click/keystroke/field count per task; pointer travel distance between consecutive controls.

text: Make the first use feel low-effort: a quick first impression that effort is not worth the reward ends in rejection, and so does merely believing it will take a lot of effort (p.81).
why: Perceived effort drives adoption as much as actual effort (p.81).
applies: landing page (above the fold), SaaS signup.
check: visual: first screen shows the job and one clear entry step; required fields at signup minimised (no number in the book).

text: Put related items closer to each other than to unrelated items; use gap size to encode relatedness (proximity) (p.55).
why: Near items are perceived as belonging together (p.55); this is the primary grouping cue.
check: measure inter-item gap within a group vs between groups; within-group gap < between-group gap for every adjacent pair (ratio of the two is the metric; book gives no number).

text: Give items that function alike the same visual feature (colour, size, shape, brightness, orientation) and give items that function differently a different one (similarity) (p.55).
why: Shared visual feature reads as belonging together (p.55).
applies: all (buttons of the same level, cards, nav items, tags).
check: computed style comparison across sibling components of the same role: same font-size/weight/colour/radius; differing roles differ in at least one property.

text: Do not draw every grouping explicitly; let closure and continuity complete shapes and lines, but enclose items with a border or container when they must read as one unit (unity) (p.55-56).
why: Perception creates logical wholes even from incomplete closed shapes; closed shapes are viewed as groups (p.55-56).
check: visual: groups containing 2+ related controls share a container or alignment axis.

text: Prefer vertical, horizontal and right-angle alignment for structure and keep layouts balanced (p.56).
why: These angles are "most visually pleasing and easy to look at"; people seek stability or equilibrium (p.56).
check: share of elements whose edges align to a small set of x/y axes (count distinct left edges per section); visual for balance.

text: Use depth cues consistently: overlapped, smaller or darker objects read as further; shadows and shading imply light from above (p.56).
why: Top-down lighting is natural; other orientations are unnatural (p.56).
check: computed `box-shadow` offset-y > 0 (shadow falls downward) for raised elements; inset shadows shade top.

text: Make the important element (the signal for the user's current task) distinguishable from its surroundings; reduce similarity between signal and background noise (p.57-58).
why: "Noise obstructs signal perception to the extent that they are similar to one another" (p.58); even an important signal can be obscured by noise.
check: contrast of primary CTA / key data vs adjacent elements (colour, size, weight, whitespace); visual: a squint/blur test should still reveal the primary element.

text: Let element prominence follow task phase: screen title is the signal when a screen first appears, data becomes the signal during use and the title recedes (p.58).
why: Elements change role between signal and noise as user needs change moment to moment (p.58-59).
check: visual: page title is smaller/quieter than the data region once content is on screen; heading is not the loudest thing in a data view.

text: Give every element on a screen a clear function; remove elements without one (p.64).
why: Reducing interface noise makes crucial details less likely to be overlooked; excessive, repeated stimulation causes habituation and the user can no longer tell important from irrelevant (p.64).
check: for each visible element: label its function; unlabelled elements are candidates for removal; count of distinct visual-weight levels per viewport.

text: Do not repeat attention-grabbing stimuli (repeated banners, pulsing badges, constant alerts) so often that users stop seeing them (p.64).
why: Habituation: sensory storage becomes less alert and cannot discriminate crucial from irrelevant information (p.64).
check: count of simultaneously animated or flagged ("new", red dot, pulse) elements per viewport; the book gives no number.

text: Treat the zone around the fixation point as a small "visual chunk" and make screen groups roughly that size or smaller; screens contain very few such chunks (p.64-66).
why: Relative acuity is half at 2.5 degrees from fixation; the optimum area is a 5-degree diameter circle (p.64-65). At 19 in (475 mm) viewing distance this is 1.67 in (41.8 mm) in diameter, holding 88 characters (15 on the widest line, seven rows) (p.65). Optimum viewing distance with modern screens is roughly 24 inches (p.66).
check: visual; angular-size calculation is possible: diameter = 2 x distance x tan(2.5 deg).

text: Avoid fill patterns of closely spaced lines or dots (hatching, fine dots, moire-like stripes) that shimmer; choose fill patterns carefully (p.66-67).
why: Eye tremor aids edge detection but makes close line/dot patterns shimmer, which is "distracting and upsetting" (p.66-67).
check: visual; flag repeating patterns with period under a few px. The book gives no number.

text: Use peripherally visible patterns, shapes and alignments to lead the eye through a screen in a methodical order (p.67-68).
why: Peripheral vision gives hints of where the eye should go next in visual search (p.67-68).
check: visual: consistent alignment axes and repeated shapes create a path; count distinct left-edges (fewer = stronger).

text: Do not put moving or dynamic content beside content the user is actively reading or working in (p.68).
why: Mori and Hayashi (1993): with peripheral windows present, performance on the foveal window deteriorates, and degradation is greater when the peripheral information is dynamic or moving (p.68).
applies: landing page (auto-playing carousels, tickers beside copy), SaaS app UI (live feeds beside forms).
check: detect CSS animations/autoplay media/marquee within the same viewport as primary text or forms; require pause control or reduced-motion respect.

text: Make each screen visually distinct in shape and structure so familiar users can recognise it with a glance instead of reading it. Avoid cluttering screens until they lose individuality (p.69-70).
why: Lower-level processing handles familiar information quickly without conscious effort; clutter forces slower, thought-interrupting reading (p.69-70).
check: visual: blur test, each page type has distinct layout skeleton; repeated layout across pages of different purpose is a flag.

text: For unfamiliar screens, give concrete identifying aspects: a title, the controls and the information it provides (p.69-70).
why: Unfamiliar users must use higher-level processing and rely on these cues to check "this is the right screen" (p.69-70).
applies: SaaS app UI (new users), landing page (h1).
check: each route has an `h1` or title that names its purpose.

text: Do not use colour that contradicts meaning (stop interference): no green for stop/destructive, red for go/confirm (p.71).
why: Naming the colour of a word printed in a different colour takes longer; a green Stop sign with a red Go sign creates mental conflict (p.71).
check: destructive buttons/states use red-family hue; success/confirm use green-family; no reversed semantics; label text colour does not name a different colour.

text: Avoid code combinations that cause distraction, such as colour and iconography meaning different things (p.72).
why: Interference arises when perception and cognition must reconcile opposing mental processes (p.71-72).
check: visual: icon meaning and its colour agree (e.g. no green "x" for delete).

text: Follow the conventions of previously learned systems; do not reuse a familiar pattern with a different meaning, and expect old habits to interfere with new rules (proactive interference), and new learning to disturb old (retroactive) (p.71-72).
why: Prior interaction procedures hamper learning new ones; learning a new system disturbs a learned one (p.71-72).
check: compare controls (icons, gestures, shortcuts) against platform/industry convention; flag reuse of a standard icon for a nonstandard action.

text: Before designing, write a problem statement that is about the user and their need, not about technology, revenue or product specs. Book's example: not "boost food sales to seniors by 5%" but "elders need meal delivery to have access to nutritious meal alternatives" (p.17-19).
why: A human-centered statement steers every later decision toward the user; a business-metric statement steers toward the company's bottom line (p.19).
applies: all (landing page: the hero/offer; SaaS: each screen's job).
check: process: brief contains a one-sentence user-need statement; it contains no KPI percentages, tech names or feature specs.

text: Keep the problem statement in a middle band: broad enough not to prescribe the solution or include technical requirements, narrow enough to be manageable. "Improve the human condition" is too broad (p.18).
why: Too narrow kills alternative solutions; too broad overwhelms the team (p.18-19).
check: process: statement does not name a UI pattern or technology; statement could be tested with a concrete task.

text: Evaluate any design on three axes at once: human attractiveness, business viability, technical feasibility. Failing the first means the other two cannot rescue it (p.11-12).
why: An unappealing product to its audience cannot generate profit (p.12).
check: process: critique output scores all three; visual for attractiveness.

text: Build an empathy map with four quadrants (Says, Thinks, Does, Feels) around the user before the first web design phase, and give *Does* (observed behaviour) more weight than *Says* (p.1, 9).
why: Cover tagline: attention to what users do. Stated and actual behaviour diverge.
check: process: four filled quadrants exist; each design claim traces to one.

text: Ask what users want, how they behave, where their pain points are, what their online habits are, and which wants must be met, before choosing a direction (p.9). Empathy techniques listed: What-How-Why, the 5 Whys, empathic interviews, photo/video studies, brainstorming, engaging users, journey map, analogies (p.11).
why: Answers give a strong start and prevent solving the wrong problem (p.9, 12).
check: process: list of the above answers present in brief.

text: Lay aside assumptions and own biases; examine what you see instead of rejecting it and do not seek only evidence that confirms prejudices (p.8, 10).
why: Biases enter how we interpret the world and the scenarios we investigate (p.10).
check: process: critique step lists at least one assumption that was tested rather than assumed.

text: Generate many candidate directions before selecting one; judge viability only afterwards. Ground rules: one conversation at a time; quantity over quality; encourage wild ideas; no judgment during generation; visualise (p.20-24).
why: Creativity appears when volume is prioritised; judgment blocks it (p.20, 23).
check: process: more than one distinct direction logged before commit. The book gives no number.

text: When mapping ideas, use keywords not long sentences, link every item to the central problem, and use images, colour and radial hierarchy for emphasis (p.25).
why: A map must give a quick cue to the concept; reading long statements wastes time (p.25).
check: visual.

text: Start with low-fidelity prototypes (storyboarding, drawing, Wizard of Oz, card sorting; paper-based, cheap). Use high-fidelity, computer-based prototypes when the product nears completion, because they give more genuine performance data (p.28-29).
why: Cheap models test many concepts without extra money, time or effort (p.31).
check: process: low-fi artefact precedes hi-fi render.

text: Test early and often, and treat test findings as grounds to revise the problem statement and loop back; do not treat the process as linear (p.33, 36).
why: Planned products rest on designer assumption until tested; later insights change earlier decisions (p.33, 36).
check: process: at least one render-critique-revise iteration recorded.

text: In moderated usability testing, let the moderator ask clarifying questions and ask participants to think aloud; most valuable with a high-fidelity prototype (p.34, 92).
why: Reveals why participants act the way they do (p.34).
check: process.

text: Use focus groups of six to nine members to study attitudes toward a specific solution (for example how onboarding makes users feel) (p.34).
why: Group debate surfaces feelings, not task performance.
check: process: group size 6-9.

text: Critique with precise, practical recommendations (constructive criticism) rather than verdicts (p.34).
why: It is the most effective way to give input on design solutions (p.34).
check: process: each critique item carries a concrete fix.

text: Use testing to find where cognitive load is high; if high, the experience gets less pleasurable (p.34-35).
why: Load is the amount of brainpower required (p.34).
check: visual + process (task walkthrough).

text: Pick method by phase: Wizard of Oz in user research (p.91); cognitive walkthrough in prototyping, working through tasks from the user's perspective (p.92); moderated testing with hi-fi prototype (p.92); contextual inquiry after launch, observing users in their natural setting (p.92).
why: Each keeps focus simple or realistic for its phase (p.91-92).
check: process.

text: For every user goal, make all three stages visible: (1) what the goal can be, (2) what controls carry it out, (3) what the outcome was. After any control activation, show a perceivable outcome that can be compared with what the user expected (p.40-43).
why: The user perceives the result, interprets it by expectation, then compares it with the goal (p.42); if any step is opaque, cycles repeat or goals are dropped (p.43).
check: for every `button`, `a[role=button]`, form submit: a DOM or visual state change within the interaction (loading/disabled/success/toast/navigation); script a click and diff DOM.

text: Minimise the steps and time the interface adds to a task's action cycle; design for the cycle to finish quickly and precisely (p.43).
why: Cycle length ranges from seconds to hours; interface should not add to it (p.43).
check: count clicks/fields from landing to goal completion; compare against baseline of the simplest flow.

text: Give each goal one obvious route, or if several routes exist, make them behave identically. Do not make the same outcome depend on when or how an action is performed (p.43, 46).
why: "Exceptional differences" (different results from the same action depending on timing) are minor, hard to notice and cause errors (p.46).
check: same-label controls resolve to same destination/behaviour across the site; visual.

text: Do not cram functionality in when user needs are not understood. Each added function adds complexity; "as a system's versatility grows, its usability declines" (p.44-45).
why: Higher complexity needs more learning and lowers performance efficiency (p.45).
applies: SaaS app UI, landing page (feature lists).
check: count of top-level actions per screen and nav items; flag screens where primary action is not distinguished from the others.
section: Causes of difficulty (what makes systems hard)

text: Use the user's vocabulary, not system jargon. Book's examples of opaque terms: filespec, abend, segment, boot (p.45).
why: Learning a system should not require learning a new language (p.45).
check: lint copy against a jargon list; nav and button labels use words a first-time user would produce; visual/copy review.
section: Causes of difficulty (what makes systems hard)

text: Make cause and effect evident: show results immediately and visibly; avoid hidden prerequisites and invisible overall architecture (p.45-46).
why: Unexpected design is non-intuitive; results are then not linked to the acts that produce them (p.45-46).
check: every state-changing control has visible result; disabled controls state why (text or tooltip adjacent).
section: Causes of difficulty (what makes systems hard)

text: Avoid distinctions that have no practical importance and make the important distinctions at the point where they matter (p.46).
why: Book's example: a user said difficulties came from pressing Enter "in the wrong way" (p.46).
check: visual: no two near-identical controls with different outcomes.
section: Causes of difficulty (what makes systems hard)

text: Support trial-and-error: let people act, observe, and correct. Do not rely on them reading instructions first (p.46-47).
why: People learn by practice, often do not read instructions, and solve problems by "error-correcting" (p.46). Early systems used an "error-prevention" approach assuming people would act only when sure, which left people in one-way situations that were hard or impossible to escape (p.47).
check: every destructive or navigational action offers undo, cancel, back or an exit; no modal without a close/cancel; keyboard Esc closes.
section: Causes of difficulty (what makes systems hard)

text: Use one label, one behaviour, one information order per concept. Bad: "Save" vs "keep", "write" vs "list" for the same action; "not legal" vs "not legitimate" for the same outcome; same data in different order on different screens (p.47).
why: Inconsistency turns learning into rote memorisation; meaningful learning becomes very difficult (p.47).
check: collect all button/link/label strings; cluster synonyms; same concept = one string. Table columns/fields in same order across screens.
section: Causes of difficulty (what makes systems hard)

text: Treat every error, delay or confusing state as having outsized weight: users remember what went wrong, not what went right (p.47-48). Budget polish accordingly: error states, empty states, slow states.
why: Problems get abnormally high priority in memory (p.47-48).
check: each flow has designed error, loading and empty states; no raw browser/stack error visible.

text: Never let a response to an action be irreversible and unexplained; frustration rises when an unanticipated response cannot be reversed or what happened cannot be determined (p.49).
why: Named cause of frustration (p.49).
check: destructive actions: undo or confirmation; result messages state what happened.

text: Avoid the named causes of annoyance: roadblocks to tasks or requirements, design inconsistencies, slow response times, difficulty accessing information fast, outdated information, visual screen distractions (p.48-49).
why: Annoyance becomes frustration when annoyances accumulate or goals cannot be communicated (p.49).
check: performance budget (slow responses); stale content/date check; visual for distractions.

text: Do not leave users waiting under pressure without response: long response times while the user has a deadline or an unhappy customer create panic and anxiety (p.49). Also avoid underload: slow pace and long download times cause boredom, and "a bored person is more likely to make mistakes" (p.49-50).
why: Both overload and underload harm concentration (p.49-50).
check: measure interaction latency; any wait has a loading indicator; visual.

text: Keep perceived effort below perceived reward. When effort plus negative emotions exceed the reward, people abandon the system, use only part of it (the easiest or highest-benefit tasks), use an intermediary, change the task, add compensatory work (manual reformatting), abuse the system, or reprogram it (p.50-52).
why: People want the advantages to outweigh the expense or effort (p.50).
check: visual + process: for each task, list effort (fields, steps, reading) against reward; flag features that will be "partly used".

text: Never trust designer intuition about user skill. Assume users lack the context clues and system knowledge the designer has; assume they will not "think" the system is usable just because the designer can use it (p.44, 52-53).
why: Specialised knowledge creates a false sense of security; the designer cannot imagine someone unable to use the system they built (p.44, 53).
check: process: test with a naive task walkthrough ("first-time user, no context").

text: Design for users whose main goal is to get a task done, who are busy and may be hostile or technically unsophisticated. Do not require them to learn technology (p.53).
why: "He or she would rather use a computer than learn how to utilise one" (p.53). Many people also now expect a certain amount of design expertise (p.53).
check: visual: primary task visible without scrolling/explanation.

text: Treat visual design (colour patterns, typography, buttons, interactions) as the UI deliverable, and apply it to a structure and content plan that already exists. Do not invent information architecture while styling; if the structure is missing, define it first (sections, content priority, flows) and then style it.
why: UI without UX structure is arbitrary decoration (p.15); the UI designer's job is to receive "all of the needs and structure" and present them attractively (p.24).
check: process: a written section/content structure exists before visual styling begins.

text: Make the interface express exactly what the company/product is, through the UI itself (the interface carries the brand: colour, type, tone), without turning the task into logo/brand-identity design.
why: The UI designer "implements" the brand; they are not a branding designer but are closely tied to it.
check: visual: a viewer can name the brand/product category from the UI with logo covered.

text: Design for every screen size and resolution the product will be viewed on (the book names desktop, mobile device and an Xbox 360); the layout must "look good on each".
why: Adapting to every screen size and resolution is part of the UI designer's responsibility.
check: render at multiple viewports (e.g. desktop and mobile) and verify no overflow/broken layout. Specific breakpoints are not given in this chapter.

text: Include inner animations, interactivity and prototyping in the UI scope, not only static visuals.
why: "Nowadays it's a standard for UI designers to also think about inner animations, interactivity, prototyping."
check: visual/process: interactive states (hover, press, transitions) are defined for interactive elements.

text: Cover the full GUI element set: menus, tabs, widgets, input controls, navigational components and informational components.
why: This is the book's enumerated list of what UI/UX designers design.
check: inventory of components present vs this list.

text: Do competitive/market research (what is standard in the related market) before settling the look and feel, so the product "makes sense" in its category.
why: Look and feel is the biggest UI element; the designer analyses market standards "to insure that the product make sense".
check: process: reference set exists (and see examples/ layer).

text: Put the user first in structure and content decisions ("always user comes first... ALWAYS"), and strategize how content is applied and received, since "content is king on the web".
why: UX is a user-first discipline; content strategy is a large part of the UX role.
check: process.

text: Close the loop with the people who built and who use the product: incorporate customer feedback, usage metrics and usability findings; collaborate with developers so what ships looks and works as designed.
why: The designer is responsible for the voice of the customer and for design-to-build fidelity.
check: process.

text: Make the purchase/engagement journey feel personal and appealing to the particular user (the book's example: a customer looking for shoes should find the experience equally appealing to engage with; the purchase "must be a delightful one").
why: UX is about how the experience makes people feel, not only how it looks.
check: visual/process (user-journey walkthrough).

text: Use the UI/UX/CX lens as a checklist of qualities beyond appearance: UI (colour theory, typography, design patterns, interactivity and animations) inside UX (desirable, valuable, findable, accessible, credible) inside CX (attraction, awareness, advocacy, purchase, discovery, cultivation).
why: Scope diagram, p.13.
check: process: review a design against each ring.
