text: Design the layout in grayscale first; only then choose a single brand colour, then choose the other colours that suit it.
why: Greyscale "forces a layout of the elements and a renewed focus on spacing" and makes a complex visual element simpler (p.57).
check: visual (render the page with `filter: grayscale(1)`; hierarchy and grouping must still read).

text: Choose colours that are consistent with the brand's personality; never use colours that contradict what the brand is trying to portray.
why: Colour sets the brand's mood, tone, concept and meaning, and the user connects it to the brand only if it agrees with it (p.36, p.57).
check: visual / brief review: each palette colour can be justified by a brand attribute.

text: Before committing to colour, define: brand personality, likely customers (the book names gender), tone to project, value proposition, and company age ("fresh and exciting" or "tried and true").
why: The goal is a hue that becomes synonymous with the company later (p.58-59).
check: the brief records these five answers before a palette is chosen.

text: Keep the goal as "a simple UI with sensible colors" rather than maximal colour.
why: Stated as the overall objective of colour selection (p.59).
check: visual; count distinct hues (see 2.2).

text: Match each hue's connotation to what the brand or product says (see the table in section 3): trust/security = blue, calm/regeneration = green, excitement = orange, joy = yellow, wealth/royalty = purple, energy/passion = red, mystery/modern = black, purity/clarity = white.
why: Hues provoke particular emotions and "help to get the desired response" (p.38); technology brands choose blue to establish trust (p.42).
check: visual / brief.

text: Keep in mind that meaning depends on culture and context; the same colour can mean opposite things (red = love and anger; black = mystery and death; warm colours = comfort or rage).
why: Each colour has "a unique meaning and connotation", partly culture-dependent (p.38, p.39-40, p.46).
check: visual; confirm with target-market review.

text: Run colour options past potential clients/users before launching a website or a new corporate logo.
why: Cheap validation; the book frames it as "never a bad idea" (p.70).
check: process (ledger of the review).

text: Take colour inspiration from nature and art (e.g. the many greens of grass); natural-looking colours are chosen by people and "appear to be user-friendly".
why: Colours that appear natural feel familiar and friendly (p.69). (opinion)
check: visual.

text: Use a deliberate UX palette to help readability, strengthen CTA buttons, improve navigation and meet subconscious aesthetic needs.
why: Appropriate colour aids information readability and elicits intuitive responses (p.37).
check: visual.

text: Distribute colour 60% / 30% / 10%: 60% a neutral ("any justifying neutral color"), 30% the secondary brand colour, 10% the main brand colour. The book writes it as 6:3:1 and calls it the Golden Rule / Golden Ratio of Colors.
why: Produces a neat, harmonious interface, soothes the eye, and lets the viewer flow from one place to the next naturally (p.59, p.60).
check: sample rendered pixels by colour family (neutral share about 60%, secondary about 30%, main brand colour about 10% of visible area).

text: Use no more than three primary colours.
why: Keeps the design from becoming jumbled and maintains equilibrium, especially with 60/30/10 (p.60).
check: cluster dominant hues on the rendered page; non-neutral hue families of brand role <= 3.

text: Apply it as: neutral for 60% of the design, secondary brand colour for 30%, main brand colour for 10% of the UI (the book's wording for a logo and for UI).
why: Same proportion, stated for both logo and UI (p.60).
check: as above.

text: Reference pattern (Amazon, p.61): white page background = 60%; blue (dark navy in the screenshot) header/footer = 30%; yellow buttons and star ratings = 10%. The accent colour sits on actions and ratings, i.e. the elements the user should act on.
why: The book presents it as good UI using the rule "to arouse people" (p.61).
applies: SaaS app UI | e-commerce landing page.
check: the 10% colour appears only on CTAs/key signals.

text: Avoid overcrowding and disorder; minimalism is "always preferable in user interfaces"; do not ignore colour combinations entirely.
why: Crowded colour use produces a disordered interface (p.59).
check: visual.

text: Prefer a simple scheme: two contrasting hues, or a monochromatic scheme. Do not put many colours in many locations.
why: Simple schemes are less distracting to the eye and make material easier to assimilate; too many colours "generates a convoluted interface that confuses the user". If the mind finds an app easy to look at, "half of a designer's job is done" (p.68).
check: count distinct non-neutral hues on a screen (target <= 2 in the book's "simple" version; <= 3 in the 60/30/10 version).

text: Monochromatic: use tints, shades and tones of one hue, including black and white. Expect lower contrast than other schemes; compensate so the result is not lifeless.
why: Full spectrum of one colour is cohesive but "the contrast is often lower ... making our creations appear lifeless" (p.50).
check: contrast ratios between element tiers (see 2.7).

text: Triad: three colours equally spaced on the wheel, used when the design needs more colours; make one colour prominent and the other two accents.
why: Keeps balance in a three-hue scheme (p.51).
check: one hue family covers the majority of coloured area; others limited.

text: Complementary: pair colours directly opposite each other for significant contrast. It is "the polar opposite of similar and monochrome". Example: an orange button on a blue background is difficult to overlook.
why: Opposite hues give maximum contrast and so make a CTA stand out (p.52).
check: hue difference about 180 degrees between CTA and its surroundings.

text: Analogous: use hues immediately adjacent on the wheel where there is little need for contrast, such as page backgrounds or banners.
why: Adjacent hues give "comparable harmony" with low contrast (p.53).
check: hue spread of the scheme narrow (adjacent wheel segments).

text: Tetradic (rectangle): four colours as two complementary pairs forming a rectangle on the wheel. It is the hardest to balance and "reserved for skilled designers"; works only if synchronised well.
why: Many hues compete; payoff is rich result when done well (p.54).
check: visual; keep one hue dominant.

text: Square: four colours evenly spaced around the wheel. Works best when one colour dominates; also balance warm and cold hues.
why: Evenly spaced hues have equal weight unless one is made dominant (p.55).
check: one hue holds the largest area share; both warm and cool present.

text: Split-complementary: base colour plus the two colours adjacent to its complement. Same high visual contrast as complementary but "less tense".
why: Keeps the contrast while softening the tension of an exact opposite pair (p.56).
applies: CTAs/accents where complementary feels too harsh.
check: hue offsets of accent colours about 150 and 210 degrees from base.

text: (figure-derived, not stated in the text) In every scheme mockup the type-and-button kit is built the same way: title and subheading are set in the scheme's darkest hue (near-black tinted with the scheme), body text is a neutral grey, the primary button is a solid fill in the strongest hue, the secondary button is a second hue (or a lighter tint) fill, and the tertiary button is an outline (or text-only) in the same hue.
why: Visible across pp.50-56: hierarchy is carried by fill > tinted fill > outline.
check: at most one solid fill per button group; lower tiers use tint/outline/text.

text: Create variants of a hue on the wheel by: adding white = tint; adding black = shade; adding a mix of black and white (grey) = tone.
why: These give systematic, harmonious variants of one hue ("extremely useful indicators for guiding the human brain to specific conclusions") (p.62, p.63).
check: tokens derive from one base hue by mixing with white/black/grey.

text: Use shades, tints and tones to enhance major design elements "in a subtle way", not as new unrelated colours.
why: Keeps the palette cohesive while giving emphasis (p.62).
check: visual.

text: To make a dark variant, increase saturation while lowering brightness; to make brighter variants, do the opposite (HSB terms).
why: Stated as the way to make dark/brighter colour variations (p.63). (Note: this is the HSB model shown on p.35.)
check: HSB of dark variants: S up, B down vs the base.

text: Use strong contrast (colours on opposite sides of the wheel, black next to white) to create tension and make viewers focus; use light contrast for delightful, relaxing, laid-back feel. Decide by intent.
why: Contrast between opposite hues is "always the most noticeable"; strong contrast creates tension and focus; light contrast relaxes (p.63, p.64).
check: visual; contrast of focal element vs surroundings higher than of non-focal elements.

text: Contrast is also a way to create a simple interface and elicit emotional responses.
why: Stated as a "simple approach" (p.63).
check: visual.

text: Combine a highly saturated hue with less saturated colours; do not saturate everything. "Saturation overload kills color vibrancy"; less is nearly always more.
why: One saturated colour among muted ones looks vivid (the Instagram logo is the example); many saturated colours cancel each other (p.64).
check: only one hue family has high saturation; rest neutral or desaturated.

text: Use interactive colours for anything the user touches or clicks (links, buttons, other controls). Keep primary interactions to a single hue.
why: "For the user, that color will begin to have a single meaning" (p.64).
check: all primary buttons/links share one hue (computed `background-color`/`color` of `a`, `button`).

text: Provide the interactive colour in dark and light variants and use these shades for states: pressed/hover (darker), disabled (lighter/washed).
why: Shades express status of UI elements; pressed and hover are named examples (p.65). The figure (p.64) shows default = saturated violet gradient, hover/pressed = darker indigo with cursor, disabled = pale lavender; loading = pale blue with spinner or progress bar.
check: four states exist per interactive component with the same hue.

text: (figure-derived, not stated in text) Purchase actions can have their own colour language. The p.64 figure shows a dark charcoal pill with yellow label ("ADD TO CART"), yellow pills with dark labels ("CHECKOUT", "PayPal" logo) and a blue pill ("Submit"); the pairs are high-contrast (yellow on charcoal, charcoal on yellow).
why: Shown, not explained; the text only says to keep primary interactions to one hue.
check: visual; each button's label/fill pair is a strong contrast.

text: Define a state palette: error, success, warning (the figure also has info). Red, green and (in the figure) yellow/amber and blue are used. Each status card has a tinted background, a tinted border, a solid-colour circular icon with white glyph, bold title, grey description, and a close X.
why: Denotative colours "have meaning" and must be defined for states (p.65).
check: tokens `--success`, `--warning`, `--error`, `--info` exist; each pairs colour with an icon glyph.

text: If a brand colour is red, do not use that red for error messages.
why: A brand colour carrying a status meaning makes errors indistinguishable from branding (p.66).
check: error colour differs in hue from brand primary.

text: When picking the disabled-state colour, make sure it has sufficient contrast; users must be able to read it.
why: Disabled does not mean unreadable (p.66).
check: contrast of disabled text/label vs its fill (see 2.7).

text: Check the contrast and accessibility level of the palette while choosing colours, so colourblind users can use the product. Use contrast checkers and accessibility checkers (WebAIM contrast checker, noCoffee, Accessibility Scanner).
why: "You are creating an interface for the use of public" (p.66, p.67).
check: computed contrast ratio per text/background pair. Book's own reference figure: WebAIM result 4.83:1 for a light violet foreground (about #9095FE) on a dark grey background (about #323232), which shows WCAG AA Pass and AAA Fail for normal text, AA Pass and AAA Pass for large text (p.67).

text: Do not rely entirely on colour distinctions. Use light and dark hues (value difference) and techniques like cross-hatching to distinguish parts of the interface.
why: Colour-blind people cannot use products that depend on colour alone (p.67).
check: desaturate the screenshot; elements and states must remain distinguishable.

text: Let hierarchy survive greyscale: in the book's example the bad version fills both "Skip" (pink) and "Continue" (teal) buttons, which become two near-identical grey fills in greyscale; the good version keeps "Skip" as an outline (pink border/text) and "Continue" filled, so greyscale still shows outline vs solid.
why: Colour-blind users and greyscale rendering lose hue, so primary vs secondary must differ in form (fill vs outline) too (p.66 figure).
check: greyscale screenshot; the primary and secondary controls differ in fill/weight, not hue only.

text: (claim) Treat colour as a primary driver of first impressions: the book cites the "Institute for Color" saying customers assess online purchases in about 90 seconds, that colour influences 62% to 90% of product evaluations on a subconscious level, and "up to 85%" of customers say colour is the most important purchase factor.
why: Used to justify care in logo, brand and packaging colour (p.36, p.57). No primary source given.
check: n/a (motivation only).
section: 2.8 Claims about colour effectiveness (source-stated; weak evidence)

text: Judge balance by perceived visual weight, not by element count, pixel area alone or real-world object weight.
why: The eye weighs distinctiveness and attention-pull; similar-looking competition means balance even when the "real" weights differ (basketball vs bowling ball).
check: visual (squint / blur test).

text: When two elements should feel equal, make them compete for attention equally; to make one dominant, raise its weight on purpose through size, color, contrast or density.
why: Visual weight is a metric of how distinctive an element is compared to its surroundings.
check: visual; mechanical proxy: compare area, background-contrast ratio, saturation and ink coverage of the two elements.

text: Size: the larger element carries more weight (book's figure: a large rounded square left of a roughly half-width rounded square of the same pink, bottoms on a shared baseline, left clearly dominant).
why: Most obvious weight lever.
check: bounding-box area ratio of the elements flanking an axis.

text: Color: saturated/hot colors (the book's hot pink-red) carry more weight than a pale yellow-lime of the same size on a light neutral ground. Treat this as a tendency, not a law.
why: Perception of a color depends on the colors around it; the red "commands our attention".
check: visual; compare saturation/chroma against the surrounding background.

text: Contrast: weight follows contrast against the element's own background. Darkening the background behind an element reduces its contrast and its weight; raising contrast on a neighbour shifts focus to that neighbour.
why: Figure p.75: same pink and yellow squares on a mid pink-red panel. The pink square (low contrast vs panel) fades, the lime-yellow square (high contrast) now wins. The reverse was true on the light background (p.74).
check: contrast ratio of each element vs its immediate background.

text: Density: when two elements share size, color and contrast, the denser one (more ink, less internal gap) is heavier. Open up gaps/white space inside the heavier one to bring it back into balance.
why: Figure p.75: two squares built from identical grids of small pink squares; the left grid has visible gaps, the right grid is nearly solid. Right looks heavier. "White space can help to achieve equilibrium."
check: ink-coverage ratio (non-background pixels / area) per element; icon fill vs outline.

text: Combine levers: tiny changes in size, color, contrast or density visibly change weight; use them together to tune balance.
why: The levers are additive.
check: visual.

text: In a centered hero, do not load one half of the page. If centered text keeps vertical-axis symmetry, the left and right halves still need similar weight (logo + a left-hand CTA vs nothing on the right reads lopsided).
why: Figure p.76: purple hero (logo top-left, four nav items top-right with the last wider, centered headline "The Conversion Platforms for Marketers", 3-line centered paragraph, ONE outlined CTA "PREVIEW THE PAGE BUILDER" sitting left-of-centre). The text is centered, but the single CTA makes the left half "visibly heavier", producing tension and a sense that "something appears strange".
check: compare ink/weight left vs right of the page's vertical center line; visual.

text: Fix the lopsided hero by adding a counterweight on the light side of the same visual size: a second outlined CTA to the right of the first ("HOW UNBOUNCE HELPS YOU"), so the pair sits symmetrically about the center line.
why: Figure p.77: same hero, now two equal outlined buttons side by side, centered as a pair; the page is "evenly balanced on both sides". "Our brains prefer balance over stress."
check: the pair's combined center aligns with the text's center axis; visual.

text: Create hierarchy between a primary and a secondary button without breaking balance: make the primary stronger through color/fill, but give the secondary a comparable *density* (a solid fill, e.g. white) rather than leaving it as a thin outline next to a solid primary.
why: Figure p.78 shows three attempts, each a pair "Secondary Button" (left) / "Primary Button" (right): (a) "Insufficient Contrast": secondary = dark navy outline, white fill, dark text; primary = outline only in the brand purple, purple text on light. Primary is harder to read, and the secondary now looks heavier. Wrong. (b) "Too Much Tension": secondary unchanged (dark outline); primary = solid purple/blue gradient fill with white text. Contrast fixed, but the primary is now "significantly too heavy" next to a thin outline. (c) "Balance & Tension": secondary = solid white filled pill/rounded rect, no outline, dark text; primary = solid purple fill, white text. The densities match and the color difference carries the hierarchy. Correct.
check: both buttons filled (or both comparably dense); primary differs by color, not by fill vs outline; visual.

text: Use tension deliberately and sparingly: avoid visual strain from accidental loss of equilibrium; use visual tension only "with care and purpose" to get a desired effect.
why: Brains prefer balance; deliberate tension can direct attention.
check: visual; ask whether each point of imbalance is intentional.

text: Symmetrical/formal balance: mirror the visual weight across the axis (vertical, horizontal or any line through the middle). Use it when you want stability, order and a clear, strong message.
why: Equal weight on both sides makes the composition stable and orderly and gives the viewer a stronger sense of what is being communicated.
check: reflect the layout across the axis; compare bounding boxes and colors.

text: In a symmetrical layout, keep value (lightness) matched on both sides; a light-valued side opposite a dark-valued side breaks the balance even if shapes and positions mirror exactly.
why: Figure p.80: top = three purple squares left and three purple squares right of a tall light-grey bar, dashed center axis through it ("perfectly balanced"); bottom = the identical layout with the left three squares in pale grey. Now the dark right side feels heavier.
check: compare mean luminance of left vs right of the axis.

text: Do not rely on pure mirror symmetry alone; mirror the weight but vary the techniques on each side to keep the design from being boring.
why: "Symmetrical balance doesn't always relay an interesting design."
check: visual.

text: Asymmetrical/informal balance: use unequal elements on each side, balanced by position and stacking, like a seesaw or beam scale. Options: several small elements against one large; smaller elements placed further from the center.
why: Weight times distance. It keeps balance while adding visual interest, movement and tension.
applies: all (hero with big illustration vs stacked small items, feature sections).
check: visual; weigh each side by area x contrast x distance from the axis.

text: In an asymmetric layout one side may feel heavier, as long as the whole is still balanced; expect to experiment because the two sides cannot be matched exactly.
why: Perfect matching is impossible, feel must be tuned.
check: visual iteration (step back, blur).

text: Radial balance: arrange objects, colors or textures at equal distances around a single point (usually the center, not always), like a snowflake or seesaw about a pivot.
why: Equal distribution about a point balances without any left-right axis.
applies: all (logo marks, orbit/diagram layouts, circular galleries).
check: radial distribution; equal radii for equal weights.

text: Mosaic/crystallographic balance: for "organized chaos" with no focal point, give all elements some uniform emphasis so it works together on close inspection.
why: Uniform emphasis across many parts replaces a focal point.
applies: all (dense galleries, pattern backgrounds, icon walls).
check: no element outweighs the rest; visual.

text: Step back and judge the whole composition; if one piece draws too much attention, redistribute weight by changing size, color, contrast, density.
why: Balance is a whole-composition property.
check: blur/squint test; thumbnail view.

text: Combine types of balance (e.g. symmetrical frame with asymmetrical content) for a more dynamic, lively design.
why: Single-type compositions are static.
check: visual.

text: Align elements to shared edges or center-lines; every element should line up with something else on the page.
why: Shared lines give the eye predictable stops, reading as organised, professional and unified.
check: collect the left/right/top/bottom/center coordinates of sibling elements (getBoundingClientRect); count distinct x-positions per column and distinct y-positions per row; flag near-misses of 1-3 px.

text: Connect related items by aligning them in the same row or column, as a table does; use this to make information scannable.
why: Row/column alignment signals relatedness without borders or labels ("without the need for external helpers").
applies: SaaS app UI, tables, forms, pricing.
check: items in a group share one x (column) or one y (row) edge.

text: When a list repeats a pattern (marker + title + description), start every row's marker on one x and every row's text on one x.
why: Figure p.98: left = "In Alignment": four rows, each a blue dot + bold title bar + two grey description lines; dots all on one dashed vertical guide, title bars all start at the same x. Right = "Out of Alignment": the dots are staggered on the guide (row 2 shifted right, row 3 slightly right, row 4 shifted left of the guide) and the text start moves with each dot, so the left edge zigzags. The book states the aligned version is "more pleasing to look at".
applies: all (lists, feeds, settings rows, notification lists).
check: `left` of the icon/avatar element identical across rows; `left` of the text block identical across rows.

text: Elements that belong to one brand/identity block (logo + slogan, heading + subheading) should share one alignment edge (both left-aligned) and sit close together.
why: Figure p.99: left = Pixsel Academy logo (round icon + wordmark) with the two-line slogan "Teaching the foundations of design" left-aligned beneath, left edges flush with the logo; right = same pair but the slogan is right-aligned (ragged against the logo), "looks like elements of different designs". Goal: "bring unity in the branding" and show both elements are one design element. "Common alignment and proximity with design elements can unify them."
check: left edge of subline == left edge of logo/wordmark block.

text: Align a row of items on a common top, bottom or center line; you need not align all three.
why: One consistent horizontal line is enough to read the row as ordered. Figure p.89: three identical cards (image-header on top, text lines below) with three dashed horizontal guides at the top edge, image/text boundary, and bottom edge; all three cards coincide on all lines.
check: equal `top` (or `bottom` / vertical center) across siblings.
section: Vertical alignment (items on a shared horizontal line)

text: If the items' heights differ dramatically, align by top (or bottom).
why: Figure p.90: main body (tall) and sidebar (short) share the top edge, and their headings align too, which establishes the connection. Tops-align avoids a floating short block.
applies: main + sidebar layouts, columns of unequal length.
check: `top` of both containers equal and first heading baselines equal.
section: Vertical alignment (items on a shared horizontal line)

text: If heights differ only somewhat, align by center.
why: Figure p.91: header nav bar with a round logo, three text links and a filled CTA, all centered on one dashed horizontal line across the bar even though the pieces have different heights.
applies: headers/navbars, icon + label rows, buttons with leading icons.
check: vertical center of each item within the row within 1 px (`align-items: center`).
section: Vertical alignment (items on a shared horizontal line)

text: Align items on a common left, right or center vertical line; again one of the three suffices.
why: Figure p.91: 2 x 3 grid of identical cards. Guides show the left edge, center and right edge of each card as vertical dashed lines: columns line up across both rows.
applies: card grids, sections stacked vertically, forms.
check: same `left` per column across rows.
section: Horizontal alignment (items on a shared vertical line)

text: Set a max-width on all content from the start; content then aligns to the same left and right edges regardless of push left/right.
why: The "invisible box" guarantees consistent edges. Figure p.92: whole landing-page mock with two vertical guides marking the content column; logo, nav end, hero text, hero image, cards, banner, and footer columns all start/stop at those two guides, while the header and footer bars extend full width.
check: every section's content box shares the same container left/right (same max-width and padding); no section uses a different gutter.
section: Horizontal alignment (items on a shared vertical line)

text: Use center alignment only when there is a single element in the row (the standard case: a call-to-action block: heading, short paragraph, button, all on one center axis).
why: Figure p.93: one purple panel with a dashed vertical center line passing through "Call to Action" heading, 3-line centered paragraph (bold "Lorem ipsum", "Cras nulla risus") and a white pill "Button"; all pieces share the center axis.
applies: landing page CTAs, empty states, hero.
check: items' horizontal centers equal the container center (+-1 px).
section: Horizontal alignment (items on a shared vertical line)

text: Left-align body text and multi-line text when the audience reads left to right.
why: With left alignment the eye jumps from the end of one line to the start of the next predictably; after a few lines readability degrades with centered or right alignment.
check: computed `text-align` on `p`, `li`, multi-line blocks is `start/left` (or `right` for RTL); flag `center` on paragraphs of more than ~3 lines.
section: Horizontal alignment (items on a shared vertical line)

text: Media objects (icon + text rows): center each icon on a common vertical axis and left-align all text on a second vertical axis; align like items with like items.
why: Icons of variable width otherwise cause misalignment. Figure p.94: "PROPERTY FEATURES" card: small caps label top-left; three rows each with an icon of different width (pin, key, car) centered on one dashed vertical guide, and to the right a bold title ("Beautiful Waterfront Location", "Fast check-in experience", "Free secure parking") plus 1-2 grey description lines, all text starting at one dashed guide. The result "gives a perfect look and balance".
check: icon center x equal across rows; text block `left` equal across rows.

text: Use edge alignment: anchor one or more corners of neighbouring blocks to shared horizontal and vertical lines (top edge of the text block with top edge of the image, bottom of the button with bottom of the image, inner edges with container edges).
why: Anchoring items "in each corner" guides the eye from one piece to the next. Figure p.94: purple banner; left = headline bar, two description lines, a white "Button" pill; right = wireframe image placeholder. Horizontal guides: headline bar top == image top; button bottom == image bottom. Vertical guides: text/button left edge and image right edge sit on the container's content edges.
applies: hero sections, split sections, cards with media.
check: `top` of text block == `top` of media; `bottom` of last element == `bottom` of media; left and right edges on container.

text: Where exact geometric alignment looks wrong, optically align: nudge the shape until it looks centered/aligned, rather than trusting the numbers.
why: An element's uneven visual weight distribution makes a mathematically centered shape look off. Figure p.95: two circular buttons with a play triangle. Left, "Center Alignment": the triangle's bounding box is centered, so the gaps left and right of the triangle (marked x and x) are equal; it looks shifted left. Right, "Optical Alignment": gaps marked x (left) and y (right), unequal: the triangle is deliberately moved right (by roughly a tenth of its width, measured from the figure; no number in the book), so the visual mass sits at the circle's center.
applies: icons in circles/buttons, play/arrow glyphs, asymmetric logos, text inside pills.
check: visual; compare bounding-box centering vs centroid centering and nudge by eye.

text: Left-aligned text is the easiest to read; default to it.
why: Figure p.96: three identical paragraph cards (8 lines each) labelled Left / Center / Right Alignment. Left is easiest; center "not so bad but a bit odd"; right is difficult.
check: `text-align`.

text: Center alignment is acceptable for short text of a few sentences: headings and slogans.
why: Few lines remove the ragged-start problem. (The paragraph in the figure was nevertheless judged harder than left.)
check: centered blocks <= ~3 lines (book: "after a few lines" it suffers).

text: Do not right-align running text in LTR languages; right alignment is the default for right-to-left languages, where left alignment would look weird.
why: Right-ragged starts make each new line hard to find; but RTL scripts invert the convention.
check: `dir` and `text-align` consistent.

text: Justified text is for print/multi-column text composition; the justification acts as the separator between columns. Avoid on short web columns.
why: Newspaper columns use it; long unseparated lines make readers lose their place. Figure p.97: two narrow columns of lorem ipsum in a rounded outlined box with both edges flush; uneven word and letter spacing is visible (line 3 of column 2 is visibly squeezed, lines in column 1 widely letter-spaced), showing the cost.
check: `text-align: justify` only with hyphenation and wide columns; visual rivers.

text: Right-align numeric columns (prices, totals); also align decimal points.
why: Units, tens, hundreds (and cents) stack in the same columns so magnitudes are comparable at a glance; with left alignment the decimals become confusing.
check: `text-align: right` on numeric cells and `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums`; decimal-places constant.
source: (p.99, p.100, p.101) Figure p.100: two invoice cards, "Item Description | Price (USD)": Clay Pot 100.54, Sharpie 5.00, Pencil 24.24, Key Chain 24.00, Eraser 4.99, dashed rule, Sub Total: 158.77, Tax: 0.00, dashed rule, Grand Total: 158.77 (bold). Left card: prices flush right (cents stack under cents). Right card: prices flush left (decimal points zig-zag; 100.54 vs 5.00 lose their column). Descriptions and header labels left-aligned in both. Labels "Sub Total:", "Tax:", "Grand Total:" right-aligned next to the value column in both.

text: Use layout grids (design-tool column grids) so that every layout element snaps to a column and gutter width stays consistent across the screen.
why: Grids guarantee consistent alignment and gutters. Figure p.101: bank/hotel app mockups on two phones overlaid with lavender column bands: four columns, three white gutters of equal width, margins at both sides; list items, titles, prices and cards start and end on column edges (left phone: Notification list with circular status icons, titles "Payment Sucessful!", "E-Wallet Connected", "Hotel Booking Cancelled", "2 Step verification"; right phone: hotel list with thumbnail, name, location, rating and price at right edge).
applies: mobile, SaaS app UI, landing page.
check: element left/right edges coincide with CSS grid track edges; constant `gap`.

text: Misalign only on purpose, to draw attention, and only when you can pull it off; the book calls it difficult but feasible with practice.
why: An off-grid element is conspicuous against an otherwise strict alignment.
check: visual; count deviations: at most a few intentional ones.

text: Header font size = body font size x 1.618. 16px body -> 16 x 1.618 = 25.88, round to 26px.
why: Sizes related by one constant ratio read as a proportionate system rather than arbitrary picks.
check: computed font-size of h1/h2 divided by body font-size is about 1.618 (tolerance suggest +-0.05).

text: Body line height = font size x 1.618 (16px body -> 26px line height, i.e. about 1.625).
why: The book's figure shows the 26px version (heading 26px / body 16px / line-height 26px) reads easier than the compared 18px heading / 16px body / 19px line-height version ("the increase in line height makes reading easier").
applies: all (short to medium text blocks; see next rule for long lines).
check: line-height / font-size on `p` is about 1.6.

text: Increase line height as line length increases; do not hold line height fixed when the measure gets longer. Use a golden-ratio typography calculator (font size + line width in, optimum line height out) if you want to derive it.
why: Long lines make the eye struggle to find the start of the next line; extra interlinear space lets it "readily detect the next line below" (2004 University of Reading).
check: line-height grows with the `ch` width of the text column.

text: When cropping a photo, place its main subject at the golden spiral's focal end. In the book's example the crop is a landscape rectangle whose spiral tightens into the lower right; the red tree sits in the upper-right square and the small figure sits in the spiral's innermost square, with open sky filling the large left square.
why: Gives the image a compelling composition with the focal point off-centre.
check: visual (subject centre falls near the spiral eye, roughly 61.8% across and about 61.8% of the way down/up depending on spiral orientation; derived).

text: For a two-column page, split the viewport rectangle (golden, e.g. roughly 1024 x 633) into a square (main content) and a smaller golden rectangle (sidebar).
why: The square/golden-rectangle division gives main-content-plus-sidebar "structure and balance"; book calls the result "perfect for a main content area and sidebar".
applies: landing page, SaaS app UI (sidebar plus content).
check: sidebar width : main width is about 1 : 1.618 (see Numbers).

text: Build a layout from the ratio in four steps: (1) draw a 1 : 1.618 rectangle as the browser window (roughly 1024px x 633px); (2) duplicate it, rotate it vertically, keep proportions locked, resize it to fit inside the larger rectangle; (3) repeat inside the new rectangle until the grid structure you want exists; (4) align elements (logo, global navigation, local navigation, main content) to that grid.
why: Gives a repeatable, proportionally related set of regions.
check: visual / measure that element edges coincide with the derived grid lines.

text: Only "loosely follow" the golden layout. Do not try to enforce it at every viewport; set up a basic ratio grid, align components to it, and take the benefit at the screen sizes where it holds.
why: Responsive layouts cannot keep fixed ratios across viewports.
check: visual at desktop width; do not fail breakpoints below it.

text: Treat whitespace as a content-bearing design element, not leftover. Do not fill empty areas just because they are empty; defend it against "use the space for more information" requests.
why: Whitespace balances design features, organises content and prevents cluttered pages; under information overload users get irritated and bail (call the helpline, per the manual example).
check: visual; (as a guard) no section where every region is filled edge to edge.

text: Use macro whitespace to organise material in the layout and guide the user through content blocks: page margins to the left and right of the content, and the space between content blocks.
why: It acts as a container for the whole design; large-picture structure.
check: measure outer page margins and inter-section gaps; they should be clearly larger than any in-component gap.

text: Use micro whitespace inside design elements: between text lines, between paragraphs, between grid pictures, between menu links, between the image, label, heading and body of a card.
why: It directly drives legibility; the amount of micro whitespace governs reading speed and comprehension.
check: line-height, paragraph margin, gap between list/menu items, card internal padding and stacked-element gaps; each should be non-zero and consistent.

text: Give card contents room: the book's "good" card has visible padding on all sides and distinct gaps between category label ("Travelling"), headline ("Why Travel the World this year?") and body text; the "bad" card has the label touching the image bottom, text hugging the left/right edges and almost no gaps between label, heading and body.
why: Cramped micro spacing makes the same content look cluttered and harder to scan.
applies: cards, SaaS app UI, landing page.
check: card padding > 0 on all sides and consistent; gap label-to-heading, heading-to-body nonzero (the book gives no values; the visual ratio of good card padding to card width is about 8-9%: derived from the figure, about 28px on a 335px-wide card).

text: As content volume rises, macro whitespace shrinks and micro whitespace must grow; keep the balance so pages are not "solid slabs of data".
why: News and information-dense sites rely on micro whitespace to stay comprehensible (Boulton, 2007); user reading comfort is critical.
check: in dense layouts compare line-height/paragraph spacing before cutting them.

text: Choose the macro/micro mix from four factors: content, design (the style the designer chooses), user (demographics, audience research), brand message.
why: The book's explicit list of drivers; there is no universal rule of thumb.
check: the brief states audience and brand tone before spacing is chosen.

text: Do not apply one "ideal" whitespace ratio across audiences; test with the target users.
why: "There is no rule of thumb to apply consistently between audiences"; "They are the only ones who can tell you how they feel about your creations".
check: n/a (process).

text: Pick the macro amount by tone: large macro whitespace for minimalism and elegance; smaller macro whitespace for sites meant to look informative (news).
why: Whitespace contributes to the overall tone (Kyrnin, 2015).
check: visual.
source: (p.125; softened p.126 "These signs aren't forged in stone")

text: Make passive whitespace do legibility work: build in space between characters (tracking/kerning), between lines (leading) and between paragraphs. Text with almost none ("crushed and compressed") is "quite difficult to read".
why: Figure comparison, left column of p.123: no whitespace is a wall of text.
check: letter-spacing/line-height/paragraph margin not collapsed to zero; see p.123 columns.

text: Add active whitespace on top of passive: use gaps, indents, sidebars/pull-outs and pull quotes to guide the reader through a long text, turning the "wall of text" into a navigable layout.
why: Active whitespace improves page structure and leads the user through the information.
check: visual: long text has more than uniform paragraph spacing (headings, pull quotes, margin notes).

text: When choosing font, size, colour, style, leading, kerning and tracking, account for the whitespace they create.
why: Micro whitespace is critical to legibility; changing the whitespace arrangement significantly changes reading performance and user experience; happy readers stay on the page.
check: n/a (process); computed leading/tracking reviewed with the type choice.

text: Use whitespace around an element to create a focal point: more space around the thing you want noticed.
why: Prioritising features is strategy; space is one of the visual techniques to draw attention; used in branding and print to focus brand messages.
check: visual: key CTA has more clearance than surrounding items.

text: On a nearly empty page, give a cue that the page is complete (the Google example: a copyright notice at the bottom told users the page had loaded).
why: Users unaccustomed to so much whitespace waited for more content to download.
check: visual.
source: (p.120) *(book states what Google did; applying it as a rule is the engine's reading of that story.)*

text: Remember whitespace can be any colour/texture/pattern/background image; the point is "no UI elements or specific content", not white pixels.
why: Definition.
check: n/a.

text: Place related elements near each other; separate unrelated elements with clearly larger gaps. Gap *between* groups must be visibly larger than gap *within* a group.
why: Closeness is read as relatedness before any text is read.
check: measure intra-group gap vs inter-group gap on siblings; inter-group should be clearly larger. (The book gives no ratio; see judgement calls.)

text: Use different amounts of whitespace to express group membership, including within one row. Example: put the Search field on the same line as the primary navigation but with extra whitespace to its left, so it reads as a different function even though it shares the nav's font treatment.
why: Spacing alone can differentiate functions when type styling is identical.
check: gap between last nav item and Search > gap between nav items.

text: If the separating gap cannot be preserved at a smaller viewport, move the item out of the group instead of letting it merge. TfL-style example: on smaller screens the Search was moved up and away from the main nav; on tablet it was shifted up and grouped with the utility-menu items.
why: Cramped space would make Search look like part of the main navigation.
check: at each breakpoint the separation still exists or the item has moved to a different group/row.

text: Group an icon with its label by proximity or shared region (the book's own criticism of the sample site: Search label and its icon are not grouped).
why: The label-icon pair is one control and should read as one unit.
check: icon-label gap smaller than gaps to neighbouring controls.

text: In text, group sentences into paragraphs divided above and below by whitespace; put a heading closer to the text beneath it than to the preceding section's text.
why: The spacing around headings tells you which paragraphs they belong to; groupings are discernible even without reading (the grey-bar version of the figure still shows heading+paragraph chunks).
check: space above heading > space between heading and its first paragraph; paragraph gap > line gap.

text: Cluster related form fields. 12 fields as one block look too difficult; the same 12 fields as three groups of four look straightforward.
why: Chunking makes the form easier to skim and complete.
check: forms with more than about 6-8 fields have visible group breaks (the book's example is 12 fields into 3 x 4; the threshold is derived, not stated).

text: Make the groupings meaningful: shipping information in one group and billing information in another. Do not group arbitrarily just to create gaps.
why: Groups must reflect real relationships to help.
check: each group has a label/heading or a clear single purpose.

text: Keep a top-aligned label very close to its own field and put a bigger gap before the next label-field pair.
why: Minimal spacing label-to-field makes that relationship obvious; the bigger gap after separates pairs.
check: label-to-field gap < field-to-next-label gap.

text: Never place a button or control among unrelated controls. Group only related actions; put the primary on-page action next to the content it acts on. The EDD example: the "Add" button (adds a required employer) sits amid Next, Save as Draft and Cancel on the right, so it is hidden.
why: Users glance at one item in a perceived group and assume the other items in it are the same kind.
check: each action cluster contains one kind of action (navigation vs data entry vs cancel).

text: Group controls that belong together (Previous and Next are connected: grouping them would improve usability).
why: The book's suggested fix for the EDD page.
check: Previous and Next adjacent.

text: Put links, buttons and information that users need next to the main content and primary calls to action, not far away in a corner.
why: Task-focused users expect all relevant information and controls to be close together and selectively attend to a focal area; things "in plain sight" outside it are missed (tunnel vision).
check: secondary-but-required controls within the primary action's zone; not in a distant screen corner.

text: Do not put the "skip" or opt-out option far from the main call to action. Mobile example: Kayak puts "Skip" at top-left of a dark screen while the CTA (Sign in with Apple) and "View other sign in options" sit near the bottom; users think they must sign in.
why: Far-away options look unrelated and invisible.
check: distance between skip link and primary CTA; place skip with or beside the CTA group.

text: On large/TV UIs, keep interaction hints next to the content they refer to, and keep them legible over images. Hulu on Apple TV: "Click" / "Click and hold" instructions at the lower right corner, far from the show information on the left, and the photo background hides the text.
why: Distance plus low legibility makes the hints invisible, worse on large screens.
check: hint within the same region as the item; text contrast over imagery.

text: Re-check proximity at every breakpoint. When columns stack, items that were side-by-side comparable become far apart. TfL example: on desktop "Ultra Low Emission Zone" and "Low Emission Zone" links sit side by side; on mobile they are separated by other stacked content and the second may never be seen.
why: Responsive reflow either squeezes the gap or pushes items apart and breaks grouping relationships.
check: screenshot at mobile/tablet/desktop; for each group, confirm members are still adjacent in DOM order and visual order.

text: Show categories/groups visibly so task-focused users scanning fast can locate only what matters to their task.
why: Groups cut scanning cost.
check: visual squint test: with text blurred or replaced by bars, the groups should still be countable (p.133 right panel).

text: Use the standard pattern for any solved problem (top nav on websites, tab bar in apps, 2-field login plus submit button, sequential checkout). Do not invent a new control for a solved task.
why: Learned conventions let users act in seconds without instruction; unfamiliar variants cost cognitive load and conversions.
check: `visual`: does a nav element exist on every page; does a login screen have identifier + password + one submit button; does checkout follow shipping -> payment -> confirmation.

text: Always customise a pattern to the specific case (content, brand, constraints) instead of pasting it unchanged; keep the pattern's structure, change the skin and the parts that the use case demands.
why: Patterns are "not a one-size-fits-all solution"; structure stays, details adapt (t-shirt analogy).
check: `visual`.

text: Do not remove or hide the high-expectation elements of a page type: a visible navigation bar and obvious buttons.
why: Visitors conditioned to see them are puzzled when absent; the book ties this to lost leads and conversions.
applies: landing page | SaaS app UI | mobile.
check: presence of `nav`/header links and at least one clearly styled primary button per view.

text: Describe each pattern you use with the four-part formula: Problem (what the user wants to do), Context (when to use it), Solution (how it is solved), Examples (where it has been implemented before). If one of the four is missing the pattern is not understood well enough to apply.
why: Every library entry has these same elements; they force the designer to decide whether the pattern fits.
check: `visual` / documentation review.

text: Procedure to apply a pattern: (1) define the problem to solve; (2) open a pattern library with that problem in mind and choose the matching category; (3) study ALL samples: intended application, what other designers did, lessons, which element types are used and how they are organised; (4) derive your own solution from those lessons.
why: Patterns "can't be directly applied"; they must be adapted via comparison of several implementations.
check: `visual`.

text: Group patterns by type when thinking about which you need: Social Sharing (promote/share content across networks), Navigation (move through the UI and always be able to return home when disoriented), Input/Output (forms to enter data, feedback in response to an action), Content structuring (site organisation that feels intuitive and accessible).
why: Gives a quick checklist of the pattern families a page/app should cover.
check: `visual`: every product has an answer to each of the four families (even if "not needed").

text: A user must always be able to get back to the homepage (navigation pattern).
why: Disorientation is the failure navigation patterns exist to prevent.
applies: landing page | SaaS app UI | mobile.
check: logo/home link present on every page.

text: Do not use dark patterns: no wording that tricks the user into the opposite of what they intend, no obfuscated terms that lock people into memberships or automatic payments, no luring into email sign-ups as a disguised exchange.
why: They benefit the company at the user's expense and "compromise a company's ability to build trust".
applies: all, especially forms, pricing, cancellation, modals.
check: button labels: reject double negatives ("Don't not opt in"); cost/renewal terms visible near the action; accept and decline options phrased plainly.

text: If no existing pattern solves the problem or can serve as a structure, design a new one, then test it to find pain points and optimise before release.
why: Pattern libraries can create a false sense that innovation is impossible; there is "plenty of room for fresh and innovative solutions".
check: `visual` / user test.

text: A personal/team pattern library needs: (1) familiarity with popular libraries (to know which patterns to use and avoid); (2) a clear hierarchy, separating simple patterns (e.g. sign-in/register) from more involved macro-patterns; (3) real usability: plain language, no heavy jargon, meant for daily use, not decoration.
why: A library is a working tool for everyone on the project, including newcomers.
check: `visual`: library has levels (atom -> macro pattern), plain-language entries.

text: Capture patterns continuously: when an experience delights or frustrates you, screenshot it, note why, and file it in your archive. Study apps you dislike as well as those you like.
why: Understanding why a solution works or fails is what makes a library useful.
check: n/a.

text: In every screen make it unmistakable which area is the figure (what to attend to) and which is the ground (what to ignore). Put the core content on a distinct, lighter/clearer surface over a differentiated backdrop.
why: Visitors decide figure vs ground within moments and subconsciously, on each screen; the decision tells them where to look and what to skip.
check: `visual`; mechanically: the primary content container has a measurable contrast against the page background (surface vs background colour or shadow), and decorative elements are lower in contrast than the content.
source: (p.160-161) - Example: Basecamp 3 homepage. A white content panel (headline "Working with other people? Struggling to keep everyone on the same page?", the illustration and the sign-up form) sits on a warm cream/beige backdrop with illustration and nav in the margin; you know to focus on the white foreground sections. (p.161)

text: Elements that look alike (shape, colour, size, treatment) will be read as one group with the same purpose; so make things that do the same job look the same, and things that do different jobs look different.
why: People group similar items and assume the same function.
check: group controls by role and compare computed styles: same role -> same colour/size/shape; different role -> at least one visible difference.

text: Use one colour consistently for links so all link text is recognisable as the same kind of thing and distinct from body text (GitHub: blue text = links).
why: Similarity signals shared purpose.
check: all `a` elements share a colour distinct from body text.

text: Differentiate page sections by colour/treatment (GitHub: grey top bar, black hero, blue bottom band each serve a different role).
why: Similarity within a band and difference between bands communicates different roles.
check: `visual`; adjacent sections have distinct background treatments.

text: Place related items close together and unrelated items farther apart; the space between groups must be visibly larger than the space within groups.
why: Near items look linked; proximity "overpowers differences in color, form, and other characteristics".
applies: all (cards, forms, lists, footers, pricing, labels with inputs).
check: measure gap inside group vs gap between groups: inter-group gap must clearly exceed intra-group gap (the figure uses roughly 2x-3x or more; the book gives no ratio).

text: Do not rely on colour to bind or separate groups when spacing says otherwise; spacing wins.
why: In the figure, alternating navy/purple dots arranged in three pairs of columns read as three groups, not as a navy group and a purple group.
check: `visual`.

text: When there is not enough space to separate groups with distance, enclose each group in a border, panel or other closed boundary.
why: Elements inside the same closed region are grouped, even when spacing, shape, colour are identical.
check: each logical group shares a container (border or filled background); no container spans unrelated items.

text: Align related items along a clear line or curve (row, column, carousel, stepper) so they read as a connected series; the eye follows the line.
why: Elements on a line/curve look more linked than off-line ones; continuity is a stronger indicator of relatedness than colour similarity.
applies: all (product rows, carousels, steps, timelines, nav).
check: members of a series share a baseline/axis (equal top offsets, equal gaps); off-axis outliers are avoided unless intentional.
source: (p.166-167) - Example: Amazon product carousel: four book cards in one horizontal row with equal width, identical structure (cover, title, author, star rating with count, format, price with prime tick) and left/right arrow controls at the ends; the row tells you the items are comparable and linked. (p.167)

text: You may leave gaps in shapes (logos, icons, illustrations); the viewer's mind completes recognisable forms from past experience. Use it to make simpler, lighter marks.
why: The brain prefers one identifiable pattern and fills the blanks.
check: `visual`: the shape remains recognisable at small size with gaps.
source: (p.167-168) - Examples: a black-shape zebra (no outlines, only stripes and fragments); IBM (blue horizontal stripes), NBC (peacock fan), Zendesk (Z from solid wedge shapes), Funding Circle (circle assembled from separated quarter shapes). (p.168)

text: Give each view one visually dominant element and make it the one you want read/clicked first (usually the primary CTA). What differs most from its surroundings captures attention first.
why: Whatever stands out visually captures and holds attention first; focus then moves to the rest.
check: the primary CTA has the highest contrast/saturation/size difference among interactive elements; at most one such element per view/section.
source: (p.169) - Example: figure of 3 rows by 6 columns of identical navy circles with one tilted saturated red (pink-red) square replacing one circle at row 2, column 4: the red square is seen first. Twilio hero: dark photographic background, white all-caps headline "BUILD APPS THAT COMMUNICATE WITH EVERYONE IN THE WORLD"; two buttons below, an outlined ghost "See Use Cases" and a solid red "Get a free API key": the red CTA is the focal point; nav "SIGN UP" is an outline button, "LOG IN" is plain text. (p.169)

text: Establish hierarchy deliberately using contrast between parts, Gestalt grouping, reading order, colour and shape. Important elements must look more significant than the rest.
why: Viewers scan to judge relative importance; hierarchy is the lever that tells them what to focus on.
check: squint test / `visual`; heading levels differ visibly (h1 vs h4), the primary action is the most contrasted element.

text: Order content for the reading direction of the audience: in a Western setting, left-to-right and top-to-bottom, so the most important content goes top-left/top and flow runs down.
why: Hierarchy is determined by the flow and order of elements.
check: primary heading and CTA appear early in DOM and top-left of the layout; mirror for RTL.

text: Use colour plus shape to force a hierarchy where one item must be noticed immediately: iOS home screen notification badge is a saturated red circle with a white count (e.g. 303, 1,295) on the app icon corner; the eye goes to the badged icons first.
why: A small saturated, distinctively shaped mark among calmer icons becomes the focal point.
applies: mobile | SaaS app UI (badges, unread counts).
check: badge colour is the only saturated red on the screen; keep it small.

text: Differentiate heading levels (h1 vs h4) so the hierarchy reads without the markup.
why: The h1/h4 difference is a direct hierarchy cue.
check: computed font-size/weight steps strictly decrease h1 > h2 > ...

text: Never use colour alone to communicate meaning (status, errors, links in text, chart series); pair with another cue (icon, text, shape, underline).
why: Colour perception varies (colour constancy under different light; colour blindness; tetrachromats see more), so colour-only encoding fails for some users.
check: for every colour-coded state there is a second non-colour indicator; run a greyscale/colour-blind simulation.

text: Test designs with the target audience, because culture and environment affect perception.
why: Perception is shaped by material culture (carpentered-world example).
check: n/a (user test).

text: Use glyph (solid) icons when icons must work at small sizes; accept that they can lack visual interest at larger sizes.
why: Solid fills stay legible when small; large solid shapes look heavy/flat.
check: icon rendered size vs style: filled style at <= UI-size (e.g. 16-24px) fine; flag large (hero-size) glyph-only icons for visual interest.

text: Use colored icons (solid or gradient) sparingly; excessive use is bad for UX.
why: They are hard to fit into a product's style and can distract users from important content; they feel less official and more fanciful.
check: count of multi-colour icons per viewport; icon colours not drawn from the palette tokens.

text: Use duotone icons (two related-but-different colours, built by splitting the icon into two layers e.g. outline + fill and tuning layer opacity) when you want a little more visual appeal without overwhelming the design; avoid them at very small sizes.
why: The second tone adds appeal but becomes unreadable when tiny.
check: icons with two tones are not rendered below the size where both layers remain distinguishable (visual).

text: Outlined icons (vector strokes, empty inside) suit simple, minimalist, professional looks; know that they may take users longer to process and recognise than solid icons.
why: Less mass means slower recognition.
check: visual; for critical/primary actions consider filled or labelled.

text: Represent universal operations (home, print, search, share, delete, menu, settings) with the universal symbol (e.g. search = magnifying glass). You may restyle the icon but keep the core form and concept.
why: Users recognise these instantly; substituting a novel metaphor (binoculars for search) only confuses.
check: an icon-name -> glyph map: search must be a magnifier, home a house, etc.; flag any non-standard glyph on a universal action.

text: Whenever a unique (non-universal) icon is used, add a text label next to it.
why: First-time users cannot decode logo/feature-specific symbols (the Sketch diamond means nothing to a newcomer).
check: every non-universal icon has adjacent visible text.

text: When icons "conflict" (same meaning, several accepted glyphs: thumbs-up, heart, star for "like"), choose the one that suits the interface best and use only that one everywhere in the interface.
why: Consistency within a product matters more than which glyph is chosen.
check: one glyph per concept across the whole UI.

text: Use ambiguous symbols such as the heart with caution: the same heart means "like" on Instagram and Facebook but "favourite/add to list" on Spotify-like sites.
why: Meaning depends on the product context; users carry assumptions from other apps.
check: visual/copy: pair ambiguous glyph with label or tooltip.

text: Consider the audience: icons at their best are simple for a certain group and universal across cultures, ages and backgrounds; choose metaphors and colours that will appeal to your actual users.
why: Abstract symbols are learned; the audience determines what is already learned.
check: visual/judgement.

text: Put every icon in a standard-size container, and make every icon the same size within the container in at least one dimension.
why: Icons differ in size and shape; a standard container makes life easier for developers and stops icons looking like different sizes.
check: all icon SVGs share one viewBox (e.g. 24x24) and each icon's bounding box touches the live area in at least one axis.
section: Icon anatomy: container, grid, padding, keylines

text: Draw icons on a grid and treat padding as the space between the icon and the container border; tweak padding per icon so that all icons look the same size.
why: The grid is a blank canvas with guidelines that keep elements in sync, so fewer mistakes and less time fitting icons together.
check: per-icon padding differs on purpose (circles get less inset than squares); visual.
section: Icon anatomy: container, grid, padding, keylines

text: Use keylines: a starter kit of basic shapes (square, circle, portrait rectangle, landscape rectangle) that keeps proportions aesthetically consistent while leaving room for expression. Draw circular icons to the circle keyshape, square icons to the square keyshape, etc.
why: The shapes are sized by area calculation so different silhouettes appear equally large (circle is larger than square in px, rectangle short side smaller).
check: icon outer bounds fit the keyshape of its silhouette class (see numbers in section 3).
section: Icon anatomy: container, grid, padding, keylines

text: Keep corner radius consistent across a set: if one icon has crisp, sharp corners, all others must too.
why: Border radius is a style parameter that the eye compares between icons.
check: the same corner radius / join style in all icons of a set.
section: Icon anatomy: container, grid, padding, keylines

text: Let context decide which parts of the grid you need: where icons are displayed, how they are masked, and which shapes act as templates.
why: An app-icon grid with masks needs different parts than a UI-toolbar grid (Phosphor's grid evolved from 116x116 with keylines only, to 154x154 with a trim area, to 154x154 with the trim area highlighted and keylines adjusted).
check: visual.
section: Icon anatomy: container, grid, padding, keylines

text: Use grids as recommendations; use the mould directly in some cases and as general guidance in others; delete the grid or parts of it when no longer useful, and review it periodically for obsolescence or misunderstanding.
why: Rules were refined as the family took shape; grids become outdated or misread.
check: process rule: grid reviewed when set is revised.
section: Icon anatomy: container, grid, padding, keylines

text: Check optical balance, do not rely on the metric grid. If a glyph filling the keyshape exactly looks too large next to its siblings (the "G" in the 90px circle keyshape in the figure), scale it down until it feels balanced with the set.
why: Equal metric size does not give equal perceived size.
check: visual: render the whole set in a grid at actual size and squint; also compare filled ink area.

text: Test icons in context before accepting them: on the real home screen / folder / notification / settings view / store listing, in natural settings and not only in design software.
why: Context reveals clarity, readability and stylistic-fit problems that the artboard hides.
check: a screenshot at real device size.

text: Use test sheets: place each new icon next to its sibling icons in various sizes and colours (light and dark backgrounds in the Phosphor sheets) and proof for clarity, readability and stylistic fit directly on a phone.
why: Side-by-side comparison exposes outliers in weight, size and detail.
check: sheet exists per new icon; visual.

text: Combine the icon grid with concise written principles and technical rules for the family.
why: Grids give a visual start but do not convey the technical regulations and principles each icon must follow.
check: a short icon spec exists (canvas, stroke, caps, keylines, trim).

text: Phosphor example principles (adopt as model): Clarity (be clear first; never sacrifice clarity of what the icon represents), Brevity (as few details as possible; reductive; be intentional with every stroke), Character (be quirky; add unique details sparingly to bring warmth and play to an otherwise austere set).
why: They rank the goals so conflicts (detail vs clarity) are decided in advance.
check: visual.

text: Phosphor example technical rules (adopt as a concrete template for a stroke icon set): 48 x 48px canvas; 1.5px centred stroke; rounded end caps; contiguous strokes unless broken segments help comprehension; straight segments, perfect arcs and 15 degree angle increments where possible; adjust curves when necessary to maintain the principles; whole, even-number measurements where possible, folding down to 1px and 0.5px if necessary; start with keylines 28x28px circles, 25x25px squares, 28x22px landscape rectangles, 22x28px portrait rectangles; keep a 6px thick trim area.
why: Hard numbers make the family reproducible by many contributors.
check: stroke-width attr == 1.5 in a 48 viewBox (== 0.03125 of canvas); stroke-linecap round; path coordinates on even integers; outer bounds within 36px (48 - 2x6) live area.

text: The icon must communicate its concept quickly; prefer an expected metaphor to an unexpected one.
why: An unexpected metaphor makes users reach for a guidebook (the car-dashboard symbols p.195 are learned over time and many are not obvious).
check: 5-second test: can a new user name the icon without a label (visual/usability test).

text: Judge confusion by its cost: a confusing nav icon in a low-risk app costs a few taps (VSCO's Feed, Discover, Studio, Profile, Members icons); costly contexts such as driving cost far more. Keep the cost of confusion minimal.
why: Cost of misreading scales with the stakes of the task.
check: judgement; higher-stakes actions get labels.

text: Abstract symbols can become familiar through continuous use and standardisation (Apple's Command key symbol, designed by Susan Kare in 1984, taken from a Nordic place-of-interest sign; the heart, caution/exclamation, music note and up arrow). Use such established symbols; the arrow is a simple, powerful wayfinding symbol.
why: Shared understanding is built by standardisation and repetition.
check: visual.

text: Once the symbol is understandable, make it readable: avoid fine details that vanish at the display size (the Amtrak "Station" icon with very fine details is hard to make out).
why: Detail below the pixel budget turns to noise.
check: render at the real size (e.g. 16-24px) and inspect; minimum gap between strokes must remain visible.

text: Leave enough gap between parts: the Transit app's clipboard icon read as a blob because the space between board and clip was too short; a slight adjustment (widen the gap) fixed it.
why: Narrow gaps fill in at small sizes.
check: gap between adjacent strokes >= about one stroke width at render size (engine inference; the book gives no number).

text: Allow ample space between shapes when an icon has multiple shapes; the icon gets busier and harder to read as strokes get thinner and more numerous. Model: Google Maps transit icons (car, train, walking person, bicycle) stay readable at small sizes beside "01 hr 12 m"-style text.
why: Strokes plus count increase density.
check: visual at actual size.

text: Align the parts of each icon optically, not only metrically. The play icon with the triangle exactly centred in the circle looks off-kilter, because the triangle's wide edge feels heavier than the point and tips it to the left; shift the triangle slightly to the right.
why: Visual mass is not geometric centre; typographers do the same (off-centre dots on "i" and "j", overshoot on round "O" vs "H").
check: visual; compare centroid of ink, not bbox.

text: Do not only trust the figures; double-check with your eyes.
why: Numbers and perception disagree.
check: visual.

text: Express the idea in as few shapes as possible: simplify an icon to just the proper amount of detail. Because canvases are small, brevity is ideal. Material's example: replace a detailed sailboat (two sails, hull with inner detail) with a simple front-view ship silhouette with two waves. Telegram's menu icons (p.204: New Group, Calls, New Secret Chat, Saved Messages, New Channel, Settings, Contacts, Invite Friends) are simple, reductive line icons.
why: A reductive design gets the point across and leaves room for the material (content).
check: node/path count and stroke count per icon; visual.

text: Illustrative multi-tone icons are acceptable when the context calls for it (Yelp cuisine icons: ice-cream, cake, burger and drink, taco, pizza); app icons (mobile, tablet, desktop applications on home screens, docks, app stores) can carry more depth, colour and brand expression because viewers already understand their meaning.
why: Appropriate detail depends on role; app-launch icons are learned brand marks, UI glyphs are not.
check: visual.

text: Keep the same artistic guidelines across the whole icon family.
why: Harmony: set members that differ look like they come from different products.
check: one stroke width, one fill style, one corner radius, one size system per set (computed from SVGs).

text: Control visual weight: weight is affected by fill, stroke thickness, size and shape; keep these parameters consistent across a set. Squint test: if some icons look more powerful than others, the set is inconsistent. Figure on weight: a heart drawn at 75% size, lighter stroke, original, filled, rounder shape runs from lighter to heavier.
why: Heavier icons grab attention unevenly.
check: squint/blur test; ratio of ink area per icon within tight band; same stroke width.

text: Keep fill and outline variants of the same icon consistent with each other (SF Symbols: 9 weights, 3 scales, more consistent between icons and between fill and outline variants than Apple's pre-iOS 13 set, which mixed strokes, fills and sizes). Keep a set of guidelines and norms to follow (and bend) when many authors contribute.
why: Continuity across a large family with many writers is hard and needs explicit norms.
check: each icon has paired .fill variant of same geometry (design-system process).

text: Decide what the icon set says about the brand: what distinguishes it, what image it conveys, what atmosphere it creates. Examples in the book: Waze = quirky, bright, chunky; Twitter = smooth, light, crisp; Sketch = delicate and airy; Freemojis = cute and lovable; Android home-screen icon packs = abstract, pixel, bubbly, neon.
why: An icon set is a visible expression of the brand; it should be chosen, not defaulted.
check: visual.

text: Keep personality in proportion to function: Phosphor adds character only through sparing unique details (see Character rule). Source (p.192)
why: Austere sets get warmth without losing clarity.
check: visual.

text: A complete icon set must be easy for contributors to extend, for designers to use (screen, print, other media) and for engineers to ship; it should be well-organised, well-documented and field-tested, ideally with custom tools.
why: An unusable set will be bypassed and fragment.
check: repo has icon naming convention, master file, usage doc, export pipeline.

text: Organised: keep a clean master file, give assets meaningful names, store in a convenient location, pick the categorisation (alphabetical? by size? by type?).
why: Findability.
check: file/layer naming.

text: Tested: check icons work in context and at the proper sizes, and that they are in sync with the rest of the visual system; place icons close together to proof for clarity, readability, alignment, brevity, consistency and personality (arrow set figure p.212 shows 66 arrow/chevron/refresh icons side by side as a proofing sheet).
why: Proximity makes violations visible.
check: visual proof sheet.

text: Custom tools: if resources allow, provide tooling that makes icons easy to find and export (Material's icon library lets you pick an icon and download different styles/themes, colours and sizes in your preferred file format).
why: Lowers friction for designers and engineers.
check: n/a.

text: Build every layout from three explicit parts: columns, gutters, outer margins. Decide the column count, column width (or stretch), gutter width and margin before placing content.
why: These three values fully define the grid; content placement then becomes mechanical alignment instead of per-element guessing.
check: the page's CSS exposes a single container with defined column count, `gap`/gutter, and horizontal padding/margin tokens; no ad hoc side spacing per section.

text: Make gutter widths a multiple of the base unit (8px, or 4px per the baseline tip).
why: Keeps horizontal spacing on the same rhythm as vertical spacing; the book states it directly: gutters "should be a multiple of the base unit in width".
check: computed `column-gap` / `gap` % 8 == 0 (or % 4 == 0).

text: Before opening the grid tool, answer three questions: how many columns and rows; what column width and row height; whether block size or gutter width must be fixed. Customise grid settings to the layout's needs.
why: Grids control proportions and relationships between page elements, so they must fit the design rather than the other way round.
check: process: grid spec written down (columns, gutter, margin, row height) before visual work.

text: If no bespoke grid is needed, default to a 12-column grid.
why: 12 divides into halves, thirds, fourths and sixths, so most layouts can be built from it (this reason is given for the column grid on p.222-223).
applies: landing page | SaaS app UI | all web.
check: container uses 12 tracks (`repeat(12, 1fr)`) unless a spec says otherwise; spans are in {1,2,3,4,6,12} where possible.

text: Place elements inside grid fields (columns), not inside gutters.
why: Guarantees consistent alignment of all elements on the page; gutters are the separation, not content area.
check: element left/right edges coincide with column edges of the grid (bounding boxes vs column boundaries).

text: Pay attention to the three spacing layers together: spacing between items, margin outside the grid, gutters between grid blocks. Any of them can "significantly impact" how the grid works.
why: A correct column structure still looks wrong if outer margin, gutter and inter-item spacing are not tuned together.
check: visual; also verify gutter, outer margin and item gaps all come from the spacing scale.

text: Define grid and spatial rules early in the project and treat them as agreed across designer and developer; use the same grid on every important page (a layout template for key pages).
why: Uniform sizes/spacing/blocks, fewer misunderstandings between design and dev, faster delivery, quicker hierarchy gains.
check: process: one shared container/grid component reused across pages; page-level layout differs only in spans, not in container definition.

text: Use a symmetric grid (equal columns/rows around a centre axis) to build comfortable, aesthetically acceptable layouts. Use an asymmetric (fractured, "broken") grid when you want a more distinctive, eye-catching presentation and brand statement, while keeping it organised.
why: Symmetry reads as comfortable and ordered; asymmetry reads as creative and unique ("more fascinating and eye-catching", "wow users and advertise product brands"). Both are valid; choose for effect.
check: visual: does the layout have a centre axis (symmetric) or deliberately offset blocks (asymmetric)? Is that a deliberate choice?

text: (opinion) Do not treat a broken grid as chaos: the book's asymmetric examples (p.220 figure, p.247 Altason) keep blocks of different sizes on a shared set of edges, not random placement.
why: Asymmetric grids are "creative yet well-organized"; the organisation is the point.
check: visual: blocks still share edges/alignments.

text: Manuscript grid (a single column spanning the whole content area): use for long text blocks and when specifying margins on a block of text.
why: One column is the simplest layout and suits continuous reading content.
check: one content column with defined side margins.
section: 2.3 Grid types and when each applies

text: Column grid: use as the default for web applications; it splits the frame into evenly spaced vertical fields that objects align to. For responsive work, use 12 columns.
why: "The most prevalent layout for web applications".
check: 12 equal tracks with constant gutter.
section: 2.3 Grid types and when each applies

text: Modular grid: use when you need both column and row rules; vertical columns and horizontal rows meet to form cells (modules) that can be used singly or merged into larger blocks.
