why: Adds layout rules in the second dimension (dashboards, card galleries, image galleries).
check: rows have defined height/step; blocks span whole modules.
section: 2.3 Grid types and when each applies

text: Baseline grid: use dense horizontal rows (the book's sample is 8px rows, alternating red/blue) as text alignment and vertical spacing rules, "in the same way that ruled paper does". Align texts, photos, videos, cards and other objects to it.
why: Gives clear, tight typography and stronger visual hierarchy.
check: vertical positions (top of blocks, paddings, margins) land on multiples of 8px (or 4px).
section: 2.3 Grid types and when each applies

text: Set every line-height to a multiple of the base unit (8px, or 4px) so text sits on the baseline grid.
why: Text lines then fall on the baseline rows, and stacked text blocks keep the rhythm.
check: computed `line-height` px % 4 == 0 (or % 8 == 0) for every text style; computed block heights stay on that step.
section: 2.3 Grid types and when each applies

text: Design the layout in percentages and proportions, not exact pixels, so it works across screen sizes. Always keep responsive design in mind while working with grids.
why: A responsive grid adapts to multiple screens, unlike a fixed-grid layout that "can only be viewed on one device".
check: container and column widths use `%`/`fr`/`minmax()`/`clamp()`; no fixed pixel widths for layout containers beyond a max-width.

text: Fixed behaviour: container width and position stay constant while the viewport changes; the outer margin grows or shrinks. Use it to keep all parts proportional, but watch large screens: it can leave too much vacant space in the margins.
why: Predictable proportions, at the cost of unused side space on extra-large screens.
check: at the widest breakpoint measure side whitespace vs container width.

text: Fluid behaviour: container width is measured in percentages, so it changes with the screen; column width grows or shrinks while margin and gutter stay constant. Use it to make use of the available screen space, but watch for stretched-out items on wide screens.
why: Uses all available space; the trade-off is elements that look stretched.
check: resize across a range: margins and gutters constant px, column widths change; verify cards/images do not look overstretched at the top end.

text: Establish a defined set of breakpoints and say how the design behaves at each one. Express breakpoints in px, as ranges. There is no mandatory set, but use a set.
why: Lets teams describe responsive behaviour consistently and adapt layouts without hurting the experience.
check: stylesheet has a small, finite set of breakpoint tokens; no one-off `@media` widths.

text: At each breakpoint the layout may change a little (e.g. increase gutter size) or a lot (e.g. increase font size, change column count, content layout, and the UI elements used). Design this deliberately per breakpoint.
why: One scaled copy of the desktop layout does not fit mobile; the figure on p.215 shows column count and arrangement changing per width.
check: per breakpoint: column count, gutter, margin, font sizes recorded as tokens.

text: With fluid behaviour, each layout expands until it reaches a breakpoint, then switches to the next breakpoint's layout (example: the "tiny" layout switches to the "medium" layout at 600px).
why: Defines when a layout stops stretching and re-flows.
check: a layout never stretches beyond its next breakpoint; there is a visible layout change at each breakpoint.

text: When documenting or demonstrating responsive behaviour, use the smallest device size inside a breakpoint's range as the representative frame (exception: the "Small" breakpoint).
why: The smallest width in a range is the worst case for that layout.
check: process: test frames taken at the lower bound of each range.

text: Add layout grids to any frame, not only the top-level artboard: top-level frames (desktop, tablet, mobile) and nested frames (framed content areas, components).
why: Alignment rules then apply at component level as well as page level (p.230 figure: three nested frames with 2, 5 and 7 columns holding image tiles).
check: process.

text: Use constraints to control how elements resize relative to their parent frame (e.g. pin a button to a corner and keep its exact size and padding as the frame resizes). With a stretch layout grid, constraints are relative to the nearest column, keeping fixed spacing (gutter) between items.
why: Makes designs behave correctly across device sizes without redrawing.
check: process (CSS equivalent: `position`/`inset` offsets, or grid placement).

text: Customise the on-canvas grid colour and opacity so it is easy to see and distinguish from content.
why: The grid is only useful as an alignment aid if it stays visible against the design.
check: process.

text: (opinion) Do not fear grid constraints; "No order without rules" and creative restrictions "help you not just see your work from a different perspective, but also develop better solutions" and a more original look.
why: Rules produce order; the restrictions force better solutions.
check: visual/process.

text: Break the grid on purpose, only when it emphasises a certain aspect or area of the page. You do not have to start and end work inside a grid field.
why: An element that leaves the grid draws attention; this only works against a visible background of discipline.
check: visual: each grid break has a stated emphasis target; most elements still align.

text: Sketch rough grid layout ideas on pen and paper early (list everything that comes to mind), then move to a precise digital tool as the project progresses and negotiation over details begins.
why: Paper is the fastest way to iterate ideas; precise tools are better for negotiating specifics.
check: process.

text: Keep testing and iterating the grid arrangement; testing cannot be avoided whatever the product.
why: The grid is a design decision and can be wrong like any other.
check: process: grid re-checked at each breakpoint after content changes.

text: Pick the typeface to match the product's tone and theme; deliver page content "in the appropriate mood and tone".
why: Style communicates personality (fun vs serious) before the content is read.
check: `visual`.

text: Map face character to use case as the book does: bold, fat, rounded face for attention on illustrated/cartoon-style sites (shown: heavy slab-like "APPLE / Mac Book M2 Chip" headline); pixelated face for a retro 1980s-90s game-style app ("SABO FRUITS / BUY NOW"); curly, unique script for personal or portfolio sites, not company sites ("Butterflu Kids").
why: Each face carries a context; mismatched context reads as wrong tone.
check: `visual`.

text: If a brand has a very distinctive typeface that is unsuitable for extended reading or small sizes, reserve it for infrequent display sizes (headlines) and pair it with a more legible typeface for the majority of low-size text.
why: Distinctive faces degrade at small size and in long copy.
check: font-family on `h1`/hero vs `p`, `label`, `input`, `small`: distinctive face absent from body-size text.

text: Treat novelty styles (inline, ink/brush, script, whimsical, hand-drawn) as accent only; do not set sustained or functional text in them, and do not try to synthesise bold/italic on them.
why: They "quickly become overbearing"; they exist only as designed, so faux bold/italic is not possible/valid. Script fonts also cannot be tracked much because ligatures split and produce imbalanced spacing.
check: `visual`; computed `font-weight`/`font-style` on novelty face equals the weights actually loaded.

text: Use "cultural" faces (fake-Japanese or fake-Chinese looking letterforms, Disney-style, Coca-Cola-style logotype scripts) only with awareness; they "immediately" give the design a preconceived connotation.
why: They carry strong built-in cultural/brand messages.
check: `visual`.

text: Work with brand/marketing on the typefaces; typefaces are "another way to quietly convey the correct tone and personality" and have to fit into the system.
why: Type is part of brand expression and must be integrated rather than imposed.
check: n/a.

text: Keep the list of font weights/variants short; plan how many weights are needed for clear hierarchy on the most complicated screen, and load only those.
why: Loading all weights of a family is inefficient and costs more to license.
check: count of distinct `font-weight` values in use and of loaded font files (`@font-face`).

text: Before adding a weight, check whether the hierarchy can be achieved by raising type size instead.
why: Size alone can separate levels without adding a font file.
check: `visual`.

text: For rare italic needs (one or two tiny uses), weigh loading an extra webfont against using browser-rendered italics.
why: Cost/benefit of an extra file vs faux-italic rendering.
check: `@font-face` for italic present only if used often.

text: Use bold for headlines, for highlighting crucial areas of text, and for links (makes links stand out and easier to see). Use italics mainly for words in a different language or for reference links.
why: Bold signals importance/clickability; italic signals "foreign / referenced".
check: `visual`.

text: Use a typeface family's range deliberately: a family can have up to ~20 styles (Futura shown with 22: light, condensed, semi-bold, extra bold, bold condensed, book italic...). Use a condensed cut when a lot of letters must fit in a small space; use extra bold (or extra bold condensed) for headline type; light for contrast with bold.
why: Staying inside one family gives hierarchy with unified character.
check: `visual`.

text: Do not use too many typefaces or fonts in one view. The bad example mixes a bold sans, a thin cursive script and a condensed caps face inside one two-line quote ("Happiness is a Direction, not a PLACE"); the good one is a single plain face in one weight.
why: "Too many fonts may emphasize too many elements, creating unnecessary noises to distract users."
check: number of distinct `font-family` values across the page (target: few); `visual`.

text: Start line-height at 1.5 x font size (for body copy at the base size) and derive the rest from it.
why: It is a workable default and gives a base for a baseline grid.
check: computed line-height / font-size on `p` is about 1.5.

text: Use the body line-height as the unit of an underlying baseline grid in which all sizes are mapped or evenly divided; let it also set icon sizes, margins, padding, spacing and general UI component sizing.
why: Ties text rhythm to every other dimension so the layout is systematic.
check: icon sizes, paddings, margins are multiples/divisions of the base line-height.

text: Decide up front how many type sizes you need and which sizes pair with which weights/styles; cover helper text, form labels, body, subheads and headlines.
why: An undefined size set leads to ad-hoc sizes and inconsistency.
check: set of distinct computed `font-size` values is small and matches the scale.

text: Define how sizes behave across devices and viewports; the largest scale differences are on larger displays. Choose the unit deliberately (px, rem, em, vh/vw as a fluid unit) and formalise values as tokens/variables instead of hard-coding.
why: Maintainability and responsive consistency.
check: font sizes come from CSS variables/tokens; no hard-coded one-off sizes.

text: Establish a size for all fonts/typefaces from the start in a type scale and share it with the team for every platform (Android, iOS, Web), stating which platform/context each scale applies to.
why: Scalable type across screen sizes requires one agreed scale.
check: presence of a documented scale.

text: Worked scale shown: H1 Heavy, H2 Bold, H3 Bold, Subtitle Regular, Body 1 Regular, Button Medium (sizes decrease down the list; no px values given). Replicate that structure: weight steps down from Heavy to Regular as size steps down, with Medium reserved for button labels.
why: Weight plus size together make the levels distinct.
check: computed weight order h1 >= h2 >= h3 >= body; button weight 500-ish.

text: Kerning: adjust the space between two specific letters only when that one letter is too far from or too close to its neighbours (e.g. the space after an initial capital looks odd in some typefaces). Kern letter by letter on wordmark logos so the whole word is balanced.
why: Better letter-to-letter balance. In the figure "PX" unkerned leaves a visible gap between P and X; kerned, X tucks in toward P's bowl (dashed guides show the closed gap).
check: `visual`.

text: Tracking: adjust the spacing of all letters in a run to fit more letters into a short space, to open up letters that are too close, or to make a block of words look evenly bordered/justified.
why: One global control for density.
check: computed `letter-spacing` on type classes.

text: Do not track script fonts much.
why: Ligatures split and create imbalanced spaces.
check: `letter-spacing` on script text near 0.

text: Tighten letter spacing on larger type (headings, banners, titles).
why: Large type looks too loose at default spacing.
check: negative/smaller `letter-spacing` on `h1`-`h3`, hero text.

text: Loosen letter spacing on smaller type (body text, error messages, notifications) for improved reading.
why: Small text needs more air between letters to stay legible. The comparison figure "Which one is easier to read...?" puts a small, cramped, tight-leaded paragraph on the left and a larger, looser, more open paragraph on the right; the right is the intended answer.
check: `letter-spacing` >= 0 on body/helper/error text.

text: Leading (line spacing, baseline to baseline) changes the look of a paragraph; do not set lines tight. The figure compares a very tight block (lines almost touching, arrow short) with an open block (arrow longer): open is the readable version. Starting point is 1.5 x font size.
why: Leading and x-height jointly determine how a paragraph appears.
check: line-height / font-size on paragraphs.

text: Take x-height into account when setting leading: a lower x-height relative to cap height leaves more white space between lines; a larger x-height relative to cap height makes the leading look more balanced and orderly.
why: Perceived line gap depends on x-height, not only line-height number.
check: compare font x-height ratio when choosing the face; `visual`.

text: Balance white space with information: enough white space for a clear layout and easier reading, but not so much the page looks "empty" and is hard to use and navigate; and not so little that the interface is congested and packed.
why: Both extremes impede finding information. In the figure, "Less White Space" (marked with a red cross) is a text block packed to the edges with tight leading beside an image; "More White Space" (green check) has the same text shortened with more space between lines and paragraphs and a wider gutter.
check: `visual`; line-height and paragraph spacing present.

text: Pay attention to both white space around elements/blocks of text and text space (letter and line spacing) inside the text.
why: Both affect readability of copy.
check: `visual`.

text: Build visual hierarchy with headings, subheadings, titles and subtitles. The example landing page uses a nav, a centred headline "How Become a UI Designer..?" bigger and darker than its subtitle line, a single filled "Watch More" button, then a section label "UI New Books" above a row of four image cards with small captions.
why: Hierarchical headings "stand out the important information visually" and make reading and scanning easy.
check: computed size ordering h1 > h2 > h3 > body > caption.

text: Use contrast of size and weight plus enough spacing for hierarchy: a big, bold, short title states the service quickly, followed by small body text that explains in detail (example: "All in one solution to your Finance problems" large and bold, small body paragraph below, then two buttons: filled "Get Started" and outlined "Watch Demo").
why: Catches the eye quickly, then explains; the two work together as a clear layout.
check: hero title/body size ratio visibly large; `visual`.

text: Use colour contrast, colour gradients and colour blocks to separate hierarchy levels. Example: a full-bleed saturated blue hero band with white title text "Guide Me Academy" above three equal colour-block tiles (yellow, mint, pink), each with one object.
why: Colour blocks mark sections and levels at a glance.
check: `visual`.

text: Use colour to make crucial text stand out against a neutral background; in the example form, error text is red on white and field states use green (valid) and red (invalid) with check/cross icons: the red top message ("One Of Fields Is Incorrect Or Invalid. Please, Follow The Examples In Order To Continue.") and the red-tinted invalid field cannot be missed.
why: Colour is the most common contrast tool; errors should be hard to overlook.
check: error text colour differs strongly from background; pair with icon (the figure uses icon plus colour, not colour alone).

text: Combine uppercase and lowercase for contrast: the example sets a mixed-case tagline, then a wide-tracked all-caps heading "WE LOVE AND BREATHE CODE ." in the brand slate, then mixed-case body text.
why: Case change signals a different role without a new font.
check: all-caps headings have positive `letter-spacing` (the figure shows widely spaced caps).

text: Use italic, bold or underlined text to pull attention unconsciously to key words. Example: italic purple eyebrow "Composite user interfaces", an all-caps bold line with a script word "Graphical" overlapping, and an italic blue-highlighted acronym "CUI".
why: A different text style draws the eye.
check: `visual`.
source: (p.281) Caution: the figure's overlapping script word collides with the line above (see section 4).

text: Keep UI text as simple and brief as possible, informative but concise ("never make your users think"); but do not go so short or basic that users get confused.
why: Short copy supports scanning; over-short copy confuses and produces a negative outcome.
check: `visual` / word counts of headings and body blurbs. Example shows a headline of two lines, a one-sentence deck and a tiny caption.

text: Keep typography consistent: use consistent colours, font sizes and font kinds so the visitor is not distracted or confused.
why: Consistency is a primary concept of typographic design and of UX overall.
check: the same role uses the same family/size/weight/colour on every page (distinct computed styles per role = 1).

text: Add lightweight animation and interaction to banner/subtitle copy to engage visitors on arrival.
why: Interactive text raises engagement and buys time to make the pitch. (opinion; no durations or easing given in the text; the Figma panel in the next figure happens to show "Smart animate", "Ease in a..." and 600ms, but that is a prototype UI screenshot, not a recommendation)
check: `visual`.

text: Prototype and test type before production. In the prototype: (1) check type scales on a variety of devices, (2) check animations and interactions work as expected, (3) experiment with colours, white spaces and sizes for the desired result. If possible, invite real users to test details and give feedback.
why: Saves time and money; catches typographic problems early.
check: n/a.

text: Use a button (real action control) for actions that change data or state: "submit", "merge", "make new", "upload". Use a link for navigation to another location ("see all" page, a person's profile) and for anything that does not affect the site.
why: Users and assistive tech read the two as different promises; buttons act, links go.
check: `<button>` for actions, `<a href>` for navigation; flag `<a>` without href used as action and `<button>` used only to navigate.

text: Give any custom clickable element that acts like a button `role="button"`; prefer a native `<button>`. Designers must work with developers so screen readers announce a button control.
why: role="button" makes the element appear to a screen reader as a button control.
check: every non-`<button>` clickable has `role="button"` plus keyboard activation; lint with axe.

text: Define six states for every button style: Normal (active and interactive), Focus (keyboard or other input highlighted), Hover (cursor over), Active/pressed, Progress/Loading, Disabled.
why: Each state tells the user what the control is doing now; missing states leave the user guessing.
check: computed styles for `:hover`, `:focus-visible`, `:active`, `[aria-busy]`/loading, `:disabled` all differ from base.

text: Each state needs a distinct affordance, but state changes must not significantly modify the component or add excessive visual noise.
why: The component must stay recognisable across states. The book's figure shows only a darker fill for hover, a lighter/translucent fill for disabled, and a normal-looking fill with no label change for progressing.
check: hover/active change colour/shadow only, not size, layout or label length (no layout shift).

text: Use a loading state when an action is not completed immediately.
why: Signals the component is in the process of completing the action.
check: async handlers set a loading state on the button.

text: Avoid disabled buttons whenever possible. Leave the button enabled; if required info is missing, highlight the blank/invalid fields (red outline, error icon) or show a notification on press.
why: A disabled button gives no reason why; users get stuck "for several seconds or minutes" hunting for what to fix. Figure: bad = greyed Login with no explanation; good = live blue Login and the empty Password field outlined red with a red x.
check: forms: submit not `disabled` by default; invalid fields carry visible error state.

text: (When a disabled button must exist) it signals a component that is currently inactive but may be enabled later; used because removing a button from its natural place and showing it later could confuse.
why: Keeps layout stable.
check: visual: lighter, desaturated fill, no hover.

text: Create a hierarchy of actions: usually one conspicuous primary button, multiple medium secondary, and low-importance tertiary actions. Figure (p.293): primary = filled gradient button; secondary = outlined button (blue border, blue text, transparent/white fill); tertiary = text-only button (blue text, no container). Example composer: Delete as red text tertiary, "Save Draft" outlined secondary, "Send" filled primary with icon, laid out left to right.
why: Style distinguishes more essential from less important behaviours and guides users through many options.
check: per view: count of filled/primary buttons = 1 (per action group); secondary uses outline; tertiary has no fill/border.

text: Make the most frequently used button the default: primary style, and focus it.
why: Helps most users finish tasks faster and directs them down the appropriate route.
check: primary action has primary style and (where sensible) `autofocus`.

text: When all options are equal, or the action is very risky, give no default: show equal-weight buttons so users consciously pick rather than mistakenly select. Figure: Accept/Reject with Accept filled and Reject outlined = steering; both outlined with icons (check, x) = presenting all choices equally.
why: Visual weight is a nudge; remove it when a nudge would cause mistakes.
check: visual.

text: For a CTA, make it the only element on the screen with a distinct colour or design; no other button should compete with it visually or draw attention to it. Keep enough contrast with the background so it does not merge in.
why: A CTA converts a passive user into an active one; competition dilutes it.
check: only one saturated filled button style in the viewport; contrast of button vs its background.

text: CTA size: not too small (users miss it) and not too large ("banner blindness", ignoring elements that look like adverts). Sweet spot 40-60 points of height with adequate separation on both sides.
why: Visibility vs. ad-like dismissal.
check: CTA height 40-60px; clear margin on both sides.

text: CTA shape: pill (highest possible border-radius) works well for CTAs.
why: (opinion/observation) Distinguishes CTA from the standard radius used elsewhere.
check: `border-radius` >= height/2 on CTA.

text: Make buttons look unmistakably like buttons using visual cues; do not rely on a bare icon or a text-only label where recognition matters. The book's quote: the best way to indicate a button is to use visual cues. Figure: filled button with pencil icon and "Edit" = understood in under a second; a circle-outlined "Edit" = people think for a few seconds; "Editable mode" in plain coloured text with a faint pencil = visual confusion, cannot decide quickly.
why: Users expect buttons to look and work as they have for years (Krug, "Don't Make Me Think"); significant departure causes delay and confusion.
check: visual; each interactive element has container, underline, or other affordance.

text: Do not use the same colour for interactive and non-interactive elements.
why: Users cannot tell where to tap.
check: colour of body/label text differs from clickable-text colour.

text: Be consistent: apply the same colour, shape and styling across primary, secondary and tertiary buttons, within the design system and with the platform. Bad figure: Edit as a green gradient pill with glow, "+" as a white circle with shadow, Export as bare text with icon, Done as a square-cornered blue outline: four unrelated styles. Good figure: all four share one violet/blue palette and one corner radius: Edit filled with icon, "+" as filled rounded square, secondary "+" as light tinted square, Export as text button, Done as tinted/lighter-fill button.
why: Predictability: speed, accuracy, fewer errors, users feel in control.
check: unique values of button radius, font, height across the page <= number of defined variants; same hue family.

text: Choose button colours that contrast well with the background to distinguish buttons from other UI elements.
why: Colour is strongly linked to behaviour; contrast makes buttons findable.
check: contrast ratio button vs its background and label vs button fill.

text: Check WCAG contrast of the button label against its fill. Figure: bad = white "Send" on pale mint green fill, plus an outlined "Draft" in the same pale green, rated 1.8:1 (fails AA and AAA); good = white "Send" on strong royal blue, with a blue-outlined "Draft", rated 8.8:1 (passes AA and AAA). Font size, colour and contrast all matter.
why: Low contrast makes the label unreadable.
check: contrast >= 4.5:1 for normal-size button text (WCAG AA); the book shows 1.8:1 as failing and 8.8:1 as passing both AA and AAA.

text: Gestures (swipe to trigger contextual actions, double-tap to like, long-press for menu) are not intuitive to the typical user. Offer them only as an additional route for skilled users; a visible button must still exist for the same action.
why: Hidden actions are undiscoverable. Book is explicit: "I recommend using them as an alternative method" (opinion, author recommendation).
check: every gesture action has a visible control equivalent.

text: Touch targets at least 48 x 48 dp for most platforms (about 9 mm physical, regardless of screen size). Touchscreen elements should be at least 7-10 mm.
why: Mis-taps and accidental taps on neighbours waste time and annoy.
check: bounding box of interactive elements >= 48x48 CSS px (or 44x44 minimum, see rule below).

text: For all interactive elements on mobile start from 44 x 44 points; for smartphone buttons the sweet spot is roughly 50 in height. Width may be any value >= height (including the double-W minimum horizontal padding).
why: Minimum comfortable tap size.
check: height 44-50px on mobile, width >= height.

text: Cursor-based devices: 32 x 32 should work. Even on desktop, the larger the button the easier it is to use.
why: Pointer precision is higher than a finger.
check: min desktop button size >= 32px.

text: Extend the clickable area of icon buttons beyond the visible icon/border (for touch and for mouse). Figure: bad = dashed clickable area hugs the hamburger icon, the chevron of "Click Me >" and the radio dot; good = dashed area extends around the whole "Click Me ->" label plus arrow, around the hamburger with padding, and around the radio plus its label "I'm an option".
why: Visible glyphs are small; a bigger hit area prevents misses.
check: `getBoundingClientRect` of the clickable wrapper larger than the icon; label included in hit area.

text: Set a minimum button size for both web and mobile. Figure series (p.325-326), same heart icon button at four sizes: very small (frustrating), still too small for mobile (fine on laptop/desktop), big enough for both.
why: Too-small buttons are hard to hit; users frustrated and may uninstall.
check: as above.

text: Size communicates importance and builds hierarchy: large enough to be noticed immediately, but not so large that the layout structure is broken. Follow market leaders' (platform) size recommendations.
why: Size is one of the most effective hierarchy tools.
check: primary button larger/heavier than secondary within the same group.

text: Write labels as verbs naming the function the button performs ("Add to basket", "Confirm order"). Test: the button should read as the answer to "Would you like to (Add to basket)?".
why: A good label encourages action; a wrong one causes confusion, time loss, possibly major errors.
check: label begins with a verb (or an imperative noun phrase such as "Learn more"); flag bare "Submit", "OK", "Yes", "No", "Click here".

text: Do not use Yes / No or overly generic labels (Submit). Figure: bad dialog = "Information" link, "No" outlined, "Yes" filled; good = "Learn More" text, "Don't Allow" outlined, "Allow" filled.
why: The user should not have to reread the question to know what the button does.
check: dialog buttons name the action.

text: A text button's text must describe what will happen on touch/click.
why: Without a container, the words are the only cue.
check: visual.

text: Strong button microcopy is constant (consistent) and brief. Capital letters are optional: the decision depends on the font, basic design concept and mood of the message.
why: Brief copy captures attention quickly.
check: label word count (book gives no number; typical 1-3 words, [engine note]).

text: OK/Cancel vs Cancel/OK: either order is fine; pick one and be consistent. Argument for primary first (Windows): matches natural reading order, saves time when it is the likely choice. Argument for primary last (Apple): lets users consider all options before acting, reducing rash choices. Author (opinion) usually puts OK last in dialogue boxes.
why: Neither order produces usability disasters; consistency matters more.
check: same order across all dialogs in the product.

text: Default shape: rectangle with rounded corners; users recognise it immediately and it complements the input field.
why: Studies cited: rounded corners boost data processing, and the element's centre attracts attention.
check: visual.

text: If using unusual button shapes (circle, parallelogram/skewed, one-corner-cut rectangle shown in the p.317 figure), usability-test them and keep UI controls consistent so users can still distinguish buttons.
why: Unusual shapes risk non-recognition.
check: n/a.

text: Choose corner radius to match the brand and the other on-screen objects. Sharp corners fit brands with similar shapes in logo and elements; slightly rounded corners are likely the most popular and most user-friendly; larger radius makes it harder to align text above and below the button; pill (max radius) works well for CTAs.
why: Mixed radii without intent break consistency and readability, and "margin imbalances" appear if the same radius is applied to everything blindly.
check: button radius relates to card/input radius; no more than a deliberate small set of radii.

text: Do not mix several corner radii within one interface unless deliberate. Do not use rounded buttons if the brand image is all sharp corners.
why: Inconsistent UI.
check: collect distinct `border-radius` values on interactive elements.

text: Set padding and safe space from the grid base numbers.
why: Keeps rhythm.
check: padding values are multiples of the base unit (4/8px, [engine note]).

text: Horizontal inner padding = 2x the vertical (example: left padding 2X, vertical 1X). Measured with the capital letter W: vertical padding about 1W (one W above and below the label), horizontal about 2W each side. Minimum: at least one W fits on each side of the label; preferred 2 x W on the sides.
why: Smaller padding makes the label harder to read and comprehend; 2:1 is a "safe choice for better readability".
check: padding-x / padding-y about 2; padding-x >= width of "W" in the label font, ideally 2W.

text: Centre the label horizontally and vertically (equal X on left and right, equal Y on top and bottom); use guides to verify.
why: Misaligned/irregular buttons are one of the most common interface problems.
check: measure label bounding box vs button box: left gap = right gap, top gap = bottom gap (optical caps height).

text: Leave enough space around buttons. When there are several, each button's safe area (margin) must be separate; do not overlap them. Figure: CANCEL (white fill, black caps) and SAVE (blue fill, white caps) with two dotted-outlined safe areas that touch edge to edge and do not overlap.
why: Prevents mis-taps and crowding.
check: gap between adjacent buttons >= sum of their safe margins; no overlap of hit areas.

text: Variants shown (p.292 figure): icon + contained, contained, outlined, text, icon button, floating action button (FAB), toggle button (segmented icons), multiselect button (B / I / U segments), split button ("Save as" + dropdown arrow). Pick from these by importance and context.
why: Each has a fixed role; see below.
check: n/a.
section: Button types: when to use what

text: Dropdown button: tap reveals a list of options; mark the chosen option active (e.g. colour). Settings buttons can behave the same way.
why: Shows current selection.
check: selected item has distinct style.
section: Button types: when to use what

text: Text button: modest emphasis, for less important tasks; no container so it cannot distract from nearby content. Figure shows ADD TO CART (dark) and BUY BOOK (blue) as uppercase, container-less labels.
why: Low visual weight.
check: tertiary actions have no fill.
section: Button types: when to use what

text: Hamburger button: opens a hidden menu; saves space and makes UI lighter/minimalist. Counter-argument: confusing for infrequent web users, can hurt navigation; do user research before using it.
why: Trade-off between space and discoverability.
check: n/a.
section: Button types: when to use what

text: Toggle button: switch between two or more states (on/off switches) or group related alternatives. If grouped, the layout must make clear they belong to a group. In a group there must be at least three toggle buttons (book's wording). Toggle buttons must be labelled with icons, text, or both; single select-or-not toggles (adding or removing a star) require icons.
why: Grouping and labelling prevent ambiguity.
check: grouped toggles share container/border; each has icon or text.
section: Button types: when to use what

text: Floating Action Button (FAB): round (Material Design) button with an icon, floating above the UI, for the single promoted action; has a transferring anchor point, launch and morph motion.
why: Surfaces the promoted action.
check: one FAB per screen, [engine note].
section: Button types: when to use what

text: CTA button: urges the user to take a certain action; can technically be any button type that carries call-to-action text; must stand out from all other buttons. See hierarchy rules above for size and exclusivity. Example (p.308 figure): header "Login" as small filled button, hero "Get Started" as larger filled button under a two-line tagline.
why: Turns passive into active user.
check: see above.
section: Button types: when to use what

text: Ghost (outlined) button: increases the attention and complexity of a text button; denotes crucial actions that are not the page's main action; outline only, no surrounding text indicating an action. Figure: filled "Allow" next to outlined "Don't Allow", with a width dimension marker.
why: Secondary prominence.
check: secondary = outline.
section: Button types: when to use what

text: Raised (contained) button: rectangular with a drop shadow to lift it off the surface; shadow signals it can be pressed. Mostly used to add dimension to flat layouts and for usefulness in large, busy or crowded areas.
why: Shadow separates it from busy backgrounds.
check: box-shadow present, low blur.
section: Button types: when to use what

text: Share button: labelled with icons (recognisable brand emblems). If sharing is not the user's primary activity on the page, do not style it as a button at all (no colour, extra shapes, underlining): show only the icons, which remain interactive.
why: Minimalism, effective negative space.
check: share icons unfilled when secondary.
section: Button types: when to use what

text: Expandable button: opens different alternatives when pressed (figure: round "+" button that becomes "x" with three round teal icon buttons fanning out above it); arranges interaction flow without overburdening the screen, important for limited mobile screens.
why: Progressive disclosure.
check: n/a.
section: Button types: when to use what

text: Plus button: adds new content (contact, post, note, location, product); often goes straight to a creation modal, sometimes offers options first so creation is more focused.
why: Standard add pattern.
check: n/a.
section: Button types: when to use what

text: Delete button: an animation that portrays the action and shows the item being deleted keeps people engaged. Figure sequence: blue trash icon square -> expands to show a red "Delete" -> blue "?" with teal "Are You Sure" -> green check with "Deleted" (four steps left to right, colours blue, red, teal-blue, green).
why: Built-in confirmation and feedback in one control; saves time deleting many files.
check: destructive action has confirm step.
section: Button types: when to use what

text: Hover and interaction effects (animations, frames, opacity, fonts, forms, shadows, colours) can persuade users to click and move to the next stage; tune to action demands. Example: a Framer Play button pops out with a 3D gradient on hover and reverts when the cursor leaves.
why: Hover feedback invites the click.
check: hover effect reverses on leave.
section: Button types: when to use what

text: Flat button: does not lift; fills with colour; main advantage is reduced content distraction. Use with padding so users can locate them, on toolbars, and in dialogues to unify button action with dialogue text.
why: Low distraction.
check: n/a.
section: Button types: when to use what

text: Placement: use common UI patterns and traditional layouts; standard placement improves discoverability, and works even for a button with few visual cues. Combine with ample whitespace and clean visual design.
why: Learned conventions.
check: primary action in conventional position (e.g. bottom-right of dialogs/forms).
section: Button types: when to use what

text: To make an element a focal point, make it heavier than everything around it on at least one weight dimension (size, colour intensity/saturation, contrast, texture, depth, orientation, face, movement). A focal point exists only by relative difference.
why: Weight is the attention-drawing force; "the more weight an object carries, the more attention it attracts" (p.330).
check: visual (blur/squint test or the recall test below); for a script: compare the candidate element's contrast, area and saturation against the page median.

text: Verify hierarchy with the recall test: view the design for a few seconds, close eyes, list what you remember; the remembered items are the heavy ones and must match the intended priorities.
why: Visual weight cannot be measured numerically, only observed. (opinion/heuristic)
check: visual (reviewer step in render-and-critique).

text: Use few strong focal points, not many. If two or more objects carry high weight, they compete (inference: "focal points" are defined as things with more weight than others).
why: Weight is relative; boosting everything flattens the hierarchy. (This is implied by "things with more visual weight than others", p.330; see engine note in section 5.)
check: visual: count of elements that are simultaneously large + saturated + high-contrast above the fold.

text: Model every UI object as four parts: Fill (background: solid, gradient, image or a combination), Border, Outer margin ("margin": space outside, used to place the object safely relative to neighbours), Inner margin ("padding" when talking to developers: safe area inside the object).
why: It is the common language of design tools and CSS.
check: computed `background`, `border`, `margin`, `padding` all explicitly designed per component.
source: (p.334-335; figure p.334: dark slate rounded rectangle with dark border and soft shadow; dashed inner rectangle marks the padding box, dashed outer rectangle marks the margin box; callouts Fill, Outer Margin, Inner Margin, Border)

text: The larger the inner margin (safe area) inside an object, the "safer" it feels; treat padding as a deliberate quantity, not a leftover.
why: Book: "the larger the safe area inside the thing is, the safer it is". (opinion, vague)
check: computed padding vs content.

text: Specify size as W x H on the horizontal and vertical axes in points (the book's example rectangle: W 120p, H 80p). For irregular shapes, W and H are those of the smallest rectangle that contains them.
why: One uniform measurement model across shapes.
check: n/a.
source: (p.336-337; figure p.337: an 80x80 circle and an 80x80 heart, each inside a dotted bounding square)

text: Points are not pixels. A point is a vector unit; on pixel-dense displays one point can be as large as four pixels or more (book wording: "four pixels or more"). Design in points, expect denser rendering.
why: Elements must be large yet sharp and precise on dense screens.
check: compare design units to device pixel ratio.
source: (p.337) [see section 7: the "4 pixels" phrasing is loose; 1 point = 2x2 = 4 px at @2x]

text: Position is the X, Y coordinates of the object's bounding box relative to the artboard (origin 0,0 at top-left, X to the right, Y downward). Circles and blobs are positioned by their bounding box, not their centre.
why: Single positioning rule for every shape.
check: n/a (tool convention).
source: (p.338-339; figure p.338: an 80x80p rectangle at X=0,Y=0 and another 80x80p at X=70,Y=160 on a ruler grid; a circle "ellipse 80x80p" at (0,0) sits in its square bounding box. Note the second rectangle in the figure is labelled 70,160 but plotted near x~130 on the ruler: see section 7)

text: Rotation is a number in degrees; 0 is default; negative values allowed; -15 degrees = 360 - 15 = 345 degrees. Type the exact angle from the keyboard rather than rotating by hand.
why: Hand rotation is imprecise and produces inconsistent interfaces.
check: computed `transform: rotate()` values should be clean numbers (e.g. 15, 45, 90).
source: (p.339; figure: four squares 0 degrees, 15 degrees, -15 degrees, -45 degrees with equivalents -345, 345, 315)

text: Flattening a rotated object resets its angle to 0 while the object stays visually rotated; the new orientation becomes the new rotation base.
why: Tool behaviour; relevant when re-rotating or exporting.
check: n/a.

text: Rotating a circle changes nothing visible unless it has a gradient or photo fill.
why: Rotational symmetry.
check: n/a.

text: Prefer slightly rounded corners over sharp ones: even a radius of 2 to 6 points is read as friendlier than 0.
why: Rounded shapes are perceived as more welcoming than pointy ones (book cites "numerous studies", no citation given).
check: computed `border-radius` on cards/buttons/inputs >= 2px unless a deliberate brutalist/corporate stance.

text: Keep roundness consistent across the UI, define the radius from the grid base unit (e.g. multiples of the base unit such as 4/8), and make it blend with its surroundings (nested elements should look concentric to their containers; inference).
why: Consistent radius reads as one system; random radii read as noise.
check: set of distinct `border-radius` values across the page is small (<= 3-4 tokens) and each is a multiple of the base unit.
source: (p.347). Note: "multiples of base unit" is my concretisation of "defined by the grid base unit"; the book gives no numbers beyond the 2-6p note.

text: Different radii on different corners of one object are allowed (they can make a distinctive button) only if they follow the brand rules (e.g. the logo has the same pattern) and are identical on every screen/display.
why: Asymmetric corners are a brand signature, but inconsistent use breaks it.
check: all instances of the component share the same per-corner radii.
source: (p.347; figure: one wide dark rectangle labelled "Corner radius at 60" on the top-left and "at 02" on the top-right, with the lower corners also differing)

text: Decide four things before drawing a table: cell data type (short numeric strings vs paragraphs/links/files), user task (read/compare vs edit/update/assign), target devices (mobile vs large desktop monitor), and whether view customisation (search, filter, sort, density) is needed.
why: Table UX "varies dramatically" with each answer; the same layout does not serve reading and editing, or phone and monitor.
check: visual / brief review.

text: Left-align every text column (anything made of letters: names, strings, links, paragraphs).
why: Western readers read left to right; a common left edge is a scan line. Do not "reinvent the wheel".
check: computed `text-align` on text cells is `left`/`start`.

text: Header alignment must equal the alignment of its column's data (left header over left text, right header over right numbers).
why: Mismatched headers leave distracting whitespace and superfluous visual noise.
check: header cell `text-align` equals body cell `text-align` in same column.

text: Never centre-align table cells or column text (the book: "Don't (EVER) use center alignment").
why: Centred ragged edges make the eye jump, hurting reading, mental calculation, row comparison, fast scanning and spotting anomalies.
check: no `text-align:center` on `td`/`th` in data tables.

text: Do not repeat the column's word inside every cell. Put the shared word in the header and keep only the qualifier in the rows (e.g. header "Design Category", cells "UI", "Graphic", "UI & 3D" instead of "UI Design", "Graphic Design", "UI & 3D Design"; or header "Lead", cells "Qualified", "Nurturing").
why: Repetition is visual noise; with a fixed header, a user who forgets the column's context can look back at the header instantly.
check: detect a common word/suffix shared by >=80% of cells in a column.

text: Right-align quantitative numbers (amounts: money and quantities; measures; percentages) so digits align by decimal position. Prepare data so every value in the column has the same number of decimal digits.
why: Right alignment makes magnitude comparison and arithmetic across rows easy; it only works if decimals are normalised.
check: numeric cell `text-align:right`; same decimal count per column.

text: Use tabular (fixed-width) digits in numeric columns. The book says "monospace typeface"; the goal is that every digit has the same width, so $1,111.11 does not look smaller than $999.99.
why: Proportional digits (a "1" narrower than a "9") break column alignment and fool comparisons.
check: `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` (or a monospace/tabular font) on numeric cells.

text: Qualitative numbers may be left-aligned: dates, zip/postal codes, phone numbers. If the first column is a date written in digits, left-align it. "Otherwise, all the numbers should be oriented to the right."
why: They are technically digits but not numerical values you compare by magnitude; right-aligning a first-column date looks strange.
check: classify column type; quantitative -> right, identifier-like numbers -> left.

text: Column-management summary: textual data left; numeric data not related to size (date, zip, phone) left; numeric data related to size (count, percent) right; headers aligned according to their column data.
why: One alignment per data type keeps the table predictable.
check: as above.

text: Do not add vertical dividers by default; columns hold the same kind of information so dividers "aren't necessary".
why: Vertical separators make a table look cluttered.
check: no `border-left/right` on cells unless grid style is chosen deliberately.

text: If separators are used: light grey, border no more than 1px.
why: Heavy dark rules (the figure's bad example uses near-black vertical lines) dominate the data.
check: separator width <= 1px and low-contrast grey versus the surface.

text: Default to horizontal lines only (1px hairline between rows, generous whitespace). Book calls this "the most popular and recommended approach for all data sets of any size".
why: Keeps the reader's place with minimal noise.
check: row `border-bottom` only, no vertical borders, no zebra.

text: Use the full grid (horizontal + vertical lines, spreadsheet-style) only for tables with a lot of data.
why: Largest separation between data points, but the extra lines are distracting.
check: grid style only when row x column count is large.

text: Use zebra stripes (alternating row background) for larger data sets, only where the alternating pattern is evident and a highlighted row will not be mistaken for a special/selected row.
why: Helps users retain their place while reading.
check: alternating row backgrounds; confirm stripe tint is distinct from hover/selected colours.

text: Use free form (no dividers at all) only for small data sets where users do not need help keeping their place. A header underline is still present in the figure.
why: Maximum minimalism, lowest noise.
check: no row borders; row count small.

text: Vertically centre cell content when row height varies only slightly (up to 3 lines).
why: Centring distributes the whitespace evenly in the row, which makes the table easier to scan.
check: `vertical-align: middle` when max lines per row <= 3.

text: Top-align cell content when row height fluctuates by more than three or four lines (long multi-line text).
why: Guarantees the start of every cell is visible at first glance.
check: `vertical-align: top` on tables with variable, tall rows.

text: Never bottom-align multi-line cells.
why: Content can be clipped by the browser viewport edge, forcing scroll; if scrolling then jumps to the next row the experience is choppy and jarring, and users may never see the complete cell.
check: no `vertical-align: bottom` in data tables.

text: Provide customised viewing choices for complex tables: at minimum a "Columns Shown" menu and a designated location for a horizontal scrollbar.
why: They are visual cues that the user is in command and can widen the view by scrolling horizontally.
check: column-visibility control present; scroll container visible.

text: Let users freeze (make sticky) the leftmost column when scrolling horizontally, as essential as a fixed header when scrolling vertically. Occasionally freeze the rightmost column too (usually summary text such as totals).
why: Keeps the row identity visible while other columns scroll.
check: `position: sticky; left:0` on first column.

text: Expose per-column preferences through a dropdown on each column heading (small chevron beside the label) with items such as Freeze and Hide; the frozen column is shown with a tinted background and a shadow edge, the column being hidden highlighted in the accent colour.
why: Some preferences are built into the UI, others are user choices; a header menu is where users look.
check: header menu present.

text: Let users hide columns that are irrelevant to their role or goal; do not force them through "dozens of columns".
why: Irrelevant columns create mental strain and dissatisfaction.
check: hide action available for wide tables.

text: Prefer a layout where column resizing is unnecessary (spacing already adequate), which needs clean, regular, predictable data. When data is irregular or the table is user-editable, allow resizing, with a drag handle that appears on hover over the column separator.
why: Resizing is a fallback for unpredictable content.
check: resize handle (col-resize cursor) on header separators for editable tables.

text: Let users switch table density (typical for data-heavy tables). Typical row heights: 40px condensed, 48px regular, 56px relaxed (text list). Control lives as a small icon switcher (three icons) outside the table, near the header controls.
why: Reading styles differ; on a desk monitor a calm, less dense table is fine, but on a smaller screen or when comparing quickly, users need more rows visible.
check: computed `tr` height in {40,48,56}; density toggle exists.

text: Both axes must scroll smoothly. Row visibility tied to scroll position plus very tall multi-line rows makes scrolling jerky.
why: Jerky scroll destroys reading flow.
check: visual / performance test with tall rows.

text: Make the header sticky. If actions live in a control-panel row (filters, dropdowns), include that row in the sticky part. A sticky footer is allowed for totals (figure shows a bottom row with total 50,203).
why: Keeps the user in context while navigating the table.
check: `position: sticky; top:0` on `thead`/control row.

text: Contextual controls may appear only once one or more rows are selected, as a toolbar at the bottom of the window.
why: User keeps context and understands what they are acting on.
check: bulk toolbar hidden at 0 selected.

text: Always tell users how many rows they are seeing out of the total ("universe count").
why: Prevents users from not knowing whether the table is complete.
check: count label like "x of y".

text: Usability-test the table's default view. The author's tests showed users almost always opened the dropdown to choose "see all", so the author sets the default to show all data, shows the line count, and relies on simple horizontal + vertical scroll instead of paging (opinion/author experience).
why: Viewport height and width only allow so much at once; paging adds friction when users want everything.
check: default page size; evidence from testing.

text: At minimum offer column sorting: a small chevron beside the heading is "a quick win with big rewards".
why: Cheapest high-value interaction on any table.
check: sort affordance on sortable headers.

text: Pick a default sort that makes sense for the data: most recent entries (created or edited recently), or the items needing most attention first (lowest inventory, most urgent priority).
why: Surfaces what users most likely need first.
check: default `sort` defined per table.

text: The sort icon must not disturb header alignment relative to column content. For right-aligned numeric columns put the icon to the LEFT of the label so the label's right edge still lines up with the numbers; do not append it on the right where it pushes the text off the numbers' edge.
why: Header text must stay flush with its data (see header-alignment rule).
check: header label right edge == cell text right edge in numeric columns.

text: Standard sort options: alphabetical A-Z / Z-A, recency oldest-to-newest / newest-to-oldest, size largest-to-smallest / smallest-to-largest.
why: Covers the three common data orderings.
check: visual.

text: Do not clutter dense tables with always-visible buttons; reveal actions via hover states where and when needed (row details, bulk actions, inline editing). Discoverability is critical.
why: Tables are dense by nature.
check: row-level actions appear on `:hover`/focus (and must also be reachable by keyboard/touch).

text: Show that a row opens a secondary view by making the entire row react on hover (figure: whole row turns light blue, pointer hand) - it signals clickable details.
why: Affordance without extra buttons.
check: `tr:hover` background + cursor pointer when row is actionable.

text: Choose the row-detail pattern by cost and content volume: - Inline expandable row: technically more expensive; natural; leaves space inside or outside column confines; trigger = whole row or a chevron on the row's left/right edge (p.382-383). - Modal/overlay: more disruptive (pulls user out of table context) but easier to build; trigger = whole row, a "View More" link, or a three-dot menu (p.383-384). - Quick-view sidebar: the most scalable; best when lots of room, scrolling or sub-tabs are needed; same triggers (p.384-385).
why: Trade-off between development resources, amount of data, and context preservation.
check: visual.

text: Multi-select: show a checkbox on row hover to signal the row is actionable; actions (Delete, Export, Duplicate, ...) appear only when one or more rows are selected. Selection state: header checkbox shows indeterminate "minus", selected row checkbox checked, and a bar above the header shows "1 Selected" with an action dropdown.
why: Efficient use of space; limits clutter.
check: bulk bar rendered only when selection count >= 1.

text: Signal editable cells on hover with a text cursor / input-like cell (figure: white raised rounded field with soft shadow appears over the cell). Inline editing in the original view is the low-friction option: reduces friction and preserves context (neighbouring rows/columns still visible).
why: Few clicks to start; context kept.
check: hover style on editable cells; cursor `text`.

text: When friction is wanted (high-stakes data that should not be tampered with excessively), make fields editable only inside the inline expanded row or inside a modal with read-only and/or read-write fields.
why: Having to click through reduces the chance of error; a modal keeps everything in one place and lets you choose which fields are editable.
check: high-stakes fields not inline-editable.

text: Every edit must end with explicit confirmation when leaving the secondary view or inline cell: click-out, Enter, a checkmark icon, or a Save button. Pair with a cancel (figure: red X + green check small buttons on the expanded row; modal has plain "Cancel" text button + filled accent "Save").
why: User needs to know the change was committed.
check: Save/confirm affordance present; Enter submits; Esc/Cancel reverts.

text: Before adding any field, justify it against a defined problem; drop every question that is not absolutely necessary. Keep sign-in and newsletter forms to their natural minimum; for others, aim for as few fields as possible (the book's example reduces a 5-field sign-up (name, email, contact number, designation, company) to 3 (name, email, designation)).
why: Every added question lowers conversion and adds processing work. Asking about workout routine to learn about a store's design is pointless.
check: field count per step; each field maps to a documented use.

text: Word every question so it has one interpretation (specify format and scope).
why: Ambiguous questions yield inconsistent data ("data analysis a nightmare"); integrity means nobody has to second-guess the database.
check: visual/copy review: could two users answer differently while both being "right"?

text: Where a field's answer has several parts, split it into separate inputs (e.g. name into first and last; birth date into day / month / year, either three small dropdowns or one field with a format placeholder).
why: Forces the user to think of one portion at a time, less brain work, fewer errors, less ambiguity (is day before month? 2- or 4-digit year?).
check: multi-part values (name, date, phone, address) are not one free-text field without a format hint.

text: Treat form length as inversely related to conversion: "the longer your form will be, lower will be the conversion rate"; every extra question loses some users.
why: Users will not wait or put in effort; they abandon when patience runs out.
check: count visible fields at first paint; measure completion rate.

text: Make the form look short and easy at first glance. If it looks too long, complicated or time-consuming, users abandon before starting; the first second is "the first and possibly most significant test".
why: First impression decides whether they bother to try (perception of complexity).
check: visual: visible field count and density on load; compare variants via A/B.

text: When a form cannot be short (not every form can have 2-3 fields), reduce perceived complexity by (a) dividing into sections by topic, (b) dividing across multiple screens/pages, (c) saving data frequently on long forms so the user need not restart.
why: Avoids overwhelming at first glance; protects user effort (work is not lost if the connection breaks).
check: step count vs field count; draft persistence exists.

text: Show progress on multi-step forms with a progress bar / step indicator (the book shows 3- and 4-step versions; completed step = filled circle with check, current = hollow ring, upcoming = filled muted circle, joined by a line).
why: Gives a sense of satisfaction per screen and answers "how much is left" ("light at the end of the tunnel"), which otherwise adds mental load from repeatedly checking.
check: an indicator with current step identified is present on every step.

text: On segmented forms, use paired navigation: a secondary (outlined) "Previous" and a primary (filled) "Next", questions in small groups per screen; save the data at each new screen.
why: "Paging back and forth" must be possible without loss; small groups are less daunting than a big list.
check: every step after the first has Previous; state persists on back.

text: Use a breadcrumb-style navigation (e.g. "1. Review house rules > 2. Who's coming? > 3. Confirm and pay") or progress bar so users know where they are in a longer flow.
why: Tells users where they are and how much time remains; gives sense of success nearing the end.
check: visual.

text: Order questions as a face-to-face conversation would: start with easy ones (name, occupation), move later to questions that take minutes (rating a service, suggestions); never open with something personal or heavy.
why: Mirrors natural conversation; easy start builds momentum.
check: visual: first field is the lowest-effort one.

text: Group questions by topic (and into labelled parts, e.g. "Choose Payment Type" then "Fill Details" in the book's checkout).
why: Surrounding questions give context, so users can infer what they do not fully understand.
check: visual; fields of one topic contiguous under one heading.

text: Use a single column. Do not put fields in two side-by-side columns (the book's one flat prohibition: "two columns are a no-no").
why: Usability and responsiveness: users cannot tell which side leads or whether to finish one column first; use a new screen for the second column instead.
check: DOM/layout: input fields stacked, one per row (see exception for tightly related pairs in section 5).

text: Give every field a label: a short, one- or two-word, descriptive description of what to enter that conveys the real question.
why: Users cannot ask for help; the label is the question.
check: every input has an associated visible label.

text: Make labels specific enough to prevent wrong attempts: "Name on Card" not "Name"; "Full name as on card" in a checkout.
why: Appropriate wording reduces the number of attempts people need; the extra words look unnecessary but add appreciated clarity.
check: copy review, no generic one-word label where the meaning is ambiguous.

text: Use placeholders for short format hints/example content (the book's figures show a card number placeholder and a faded example e-mail in an empty field). Do not make the placeholder the only place help lives.
why: Placeholder = in-field guidance of what to write. The book also warns against "labels that vanish": do not give help only to take it away once typing starts; users may need to return to the label mid-answer.
check: label remains visible when the field has a value (not placeholder-as-label).

text: Use masks for fields with a required format (dates, credit card numbers), e.g. `XXXX XXXX XXXX 9870` with the card-network logo at the end of the field.
why: A mask acts as a foundation so users do not have to guess how to convey information.
check: format-bound fields enforce/auto-format their pattern.

text: Every form must have validation; do not leave errors for the final submit. Validate inline, next to each field, as the user goes.
why: Nothing is more irritating than completing a form and receiving a confusing error at the last minute; the user gives up. Inline validation also reassures that everything is going fine and avoids being blocked later.
check: per-field valid/invalid state is shown without submit.

text: Do not validate until the user has finished typing (e.g. on blur / pause), never mark a half-typed value invalid.
why: Partial values are flagged invalid and confuse users.
check: invalid state not shown while the field is focused and mid-entry.

text: Never signal valid/invalid with colour alone. Always add a clearly recognisable symbol (the book uses a check-in-circle for valid and a red x-in-circle for invalid, alongside a red-tinted field), plus text.
why: A red outline alone can be confusing for visually impaired users.
check: each state has an icon or text in addition to colour change.

text: Error messages must say exactly what is wrong and how to fix it, not merely that something is wrong. Example: "Please insert a full email address, complete with @".
why: Nobody likes errors; a useful one turns a time-waster into help. (Exception: system faults, where there is no user remedy.)
check: message contains cause + remedy; no "Invalid input" strings.

text: Inline validation can be a check icon, a field colour change, a text message, or a combination; whichever is used must be continuous and consistent across the form.
why: Constant, consistent communication between form and user is what matters ("usability is the name of the game").
check: same pattern for every field.

text: Where multiple fields fail, a form-level banner at the top may summarise ("One of fields is incorrect or invalid. Please follow the examples in order to continue") while each failing field shows its own icon and short message (e.g. "This mobile number invalid" pointing at the field).
why: Two levels: global notice + local location of the problem (as drawn in the book's figure).
check: visual: banner (red info icon + red text) above title, and per-field markers.

text: Choose input controls that are as obvious as possible; the real concern is the integrity of collected data, not just avoiding confusion.
why: Some UI elements produce unclear data.
check: control matches data type (see D, G).

text: Never pre-check a checkbox that records consent, a preference or a decision. Leave it unchecked, or use an explicit Yes / No pair with nothing selected.
why: With a pre-checked box you cannot know whether the user saw it or understood it, so the data is doubtful; pre-checked boxes to obtain consent to personal-data use are unlawful in the EU and can affect a business based elsewhere.
check: `input[type=checkbox][checked]` on consent/preference/decision fields = fail.

text: Support autofill / use information already stored in the browser so users reach the end faster.
why: A form that does part of the work is appreciated; higher conversion. The book notes there are some security risks but the technique is widely used and accepted.
check: inputs carry proper `autocomplete`/`name` attributes (e.g. email, tel, cc-number, name).

text: One primary button (draws attention; moves to next screen or finishes/submits) and secondary actions styled clearly lower (e.g. "Forgot your password?", "Previous"). Make the order and hierarchy of the buttons unmistakable.
why: Users must not press the secondary action when they meant the primary.
check: one filled primary per form view; secondary styled outline/ghost/link.

text: Do not include a "Clear" or "Reset" button.
why: An accidental reset destroys all the user's work.
check: no `button[type=reset]`.

text: Give button feedback: use a micro-animation after the tap so users know the signal was recognised (no worrying whether it works, no repeat presses).
why: Users who think the form missed their command press the same button repeatedly.
check: pressed/loading state exists.

text: Consider keeping the primary button disabled until all required fields are complete, and change its appearance when enabled (e.g. a brighter colour) to draw the eye. The book's figure: disabled = flat grey button with a faded example in the field; enabled = saturated dark button with real value in the field.
why: Signals readiness and draws attention to the next action. (The book says "might also think about": hedged, see section 5.)
check: button has distinct disabled and enabled styles.

text: Replace generic button text ("Submit") with a label that states the user's purpose / outcome (book examples: "Create New Account", "Pay Now", "Get Premium"-style copy on Spotify's payment button, "Sign Up").
why: Keeps the user focused on the goal that made them start the form; a gentle reminder of the end result.
check: no button with text "Submit".

text: Keep users informed about what is happening: show that something is occurring behind the screen, even if only a simple loading animation; provide a success screen on completion.
why: People like to know what is happening; uninformed users second-guess and rewrite correct data, or re-press the same button.
check: loading state on submit; success state exists.

text: Provide field focus (visible focus state) so users stay focused on the question at hand.
why: Reduces mix-ups.
check: `:focus` style differs visibly from default.

text: Plan every piece of microcopy (buttons, placeholders, labels, errors, helper text under the title such as "Login and enjoy the UI Book, read daily").
why: Every detail is an opportunity to communicate; more information on the form means fewer misunderstandings; users do notice.
check: copy review.

text: Prefer reducing a two-purpose login screen to the essentials: for login ask only email and password, a "Remember me" checkbox and "Forgot password?" link, one primary Login button, then a divider ("Or") with social login buttons (Google, Facebook, Apple, as icon-only squares), then "Not a member? Register".
why: The book's "after" version of a login form removes name, mobile number and date of birth from a login (those belong in sign-up) and moves social options below a labelled divider.
check: login form has at most the credentials fields.

text: Write the content before wireframing navigation; derive the nav structure from the content, and match the structure to the flow/shape of the content. Do not bend content to a pre-made menu.
why: Even perfect navigation won't keep someone on a page whose content is poor; "navigation reveals content".
check: visual / process: nav items map 1:1 to existing content sections or pages.

text: Pick the navigation pattern per context and combine them; never claim one pattern is universally better. Evaluate each against the product before implementing.
why: Patterns perform differently by circumstance (p.435, p.437, p.447).
check: visual.

text: Align navigation with the goals of identified user groups (personas). Derive the nav by asking what these users need, e.g. (Kalbach): How can I locate certain information or a product quickly? How can I be sure the information is current? Is the information reliable? How do I contact the site owner? How can I send information I find to people I know?
why: Nav "reverse engineering": knowing needs tells you what the nav must support.
check: visual: each persona goal has a reachable path.

text: Put the primary menu horizontally across the top or vertically down the left side; those are the most visible locations.
why: Users read pages in an F-shaped pattern (a few horizontal scans across the top, then a vertical scan from top to bottom) (Nielsen).
check: nav bounding box in top band or left rail.

text: Use a horizontal navigation bar as the default for websites.
why: It is easy to scan because we read across the page; users know it and expect it.
check: visual.

text: Remember direction semantics: in Western convention right means progress, left means back/regressive (Bowles quote). Order and direction nav and progress cues accordingly.
why: Number-line / text-direction convention.
check: visual (back/previous left, next/forward right).

text: Use vertical navigation (left rail) when you need a long global list with primary, secondary and tertiary levels; accept that it takes a lot of room. A collapsible variant shows an icon-only rail (avatar + icons, settings and logout at the bottom) that expands to icon + label with nested sub-items.
why: Vertical lists scale to many levels.
check: visual.

text: Use vertical (right-hand) page navigation on long single-page storytelling sites to show where the user is on a linear scroll (Skullcandy "Supreme Sound" example, parallax story).
why: Linear content suits a long vertical page; the side nav orients position and gives access to related information.
check: visual.

text: On mobile put the few most important destinations in tabs at the bottom (or top) of the screen. Bottom space only holds a few tabs, so put only the most crucial panels there.
why: Limited bottom width.
check: count of tab-bar items (book gives no number; its figures show a 5-icon tab bar on p.465 and p.477, and a 4-item bar on p.438 where the active Home item is a white pill with label).

text: A hamburger menu (three-line icon, click/press to reveal more choices) is acceptable on mobile and increasingly desktop. The pattern shown: icon top-left of the header; opens a white full-height drawer over the dimmed app with avatar + name + email at top, a list of text items each with a chevron (My Orders, My Wishlist, Saved Cards, Notifications, Gift Cards, My Rewards, Address, Help), and Settings and Logout separated at the bottom.
why: Reveals secondary navigation without spending screen room.
check: visual.

text: Use breadcrumbs as a supplementary trail showing where the user is, e.g. on an e-commerce product page with many hierarchical sub-categories. They are like chapter titles: they provide context, and matter because many users do not arrive at the homepage.
why: Orientation for deep-linked arrivals.
check: breadcrumb present on pages deeper than level 1. In the figure the trail sits as a pill directly under the header, over the product image: `Grocers / Grocers Category / Snacks & Drink / Jenuin Red...` (long last item is truncated with an ellipsis).

text: Use filters to manage information-heavy sites and links to connect disparate pieces of information; use the menu as the first place visitors look to learn what is on the site.
why: Each is a navigation support for content.
check: visual.

text: A call-to-action button in the navigation/hero must be easily identifiable and given top billing; its job is to convince, motivate and move the audience to act (sign up, purchase, download). In the figures it is a solid lilac-blue `Login` button in the navbar, a dark slate `Watch More` button under the hero headline.
why: Conversion actions need to stand apart from nav links.
check: CTA has a filled background distinct from nav link text.

text: Use relevant, familiar copy for navigation elements and keep it consistent across the design. Name the nav link after what the page is: a museum landing page about Collections is labelled "Collections".
why: Consistency and clarity make navigation easier to understand; users know what to expect before clicking.
check: visual / copy audit: label == page H1 or obvious synonym.

text: Keep navigation simple and conventional. Breaking rules is possible but "it's best to keep things simple".
why: "Past experiences and repeated practices inform user experience"; "any variation from a learnt routine might lead to user errors" (A. Harley, NN/g).
check: visual.

text: Use meaningful, specific labels ("analogue watches", "smart watches"), not generic format words ("products", "items"). Give each such label its own page where possible rather than one page with everything.
why: "Products" tells a user nothing; people search for specific things, so specific labels are clearer and also help SEO.
check: flag nav labels in a stop-list (products, items, stuff, solutions, resources) as generic.

text: Prefer mega menus to plain dropdown menus for sites with many sub-items. A mega menu is bigger, divided into contextual groups, and visible at once; it removes scrolling inside the menu.
why: Dropdowns have poor usability despite ubiquity: (1) crawling dropdown menus can be tough for search engines; (2) users are more likely to skip key pages when using dropdowns (A. Crestodina). Users dislike scrolling.
check: menu panel shows all groups at once without an inner scrollbar and has group headings.

text: Provide navigation cues in addition to the menu: logo and branding, the browser-tab title, visual design changes, the URL, breadcrumbs, and date/time/icons/tags. Highlight the current nav item.
why: They anchor the user and give a sense of place; together they keep the user calm. The browser back button ("lifeline of the online user", "second-most used navigation tool" - Nielsen) is not the whole of navigation.
check: current page item has a distinct active state; `<title>` reflects the page; breadcrumb or section label present.

text: Prototype and test the navigation flow (registration, finding a specific item, purchase patterns, the whole product's nav) before committing. Use a tool with built-in user testing if possible (CrazyEgg, UserTesting, Hotjar). Test with 3-5 people (Laura Klein).
why: An unprototyped guess (e.g. "a breadcrumb will help") is still a guess; data reduces risk. Prototyping also clarifies the product, its direction, users, and what success and failure mean.
check: process.

text: Make animation functional first: it must guide, inform, give feedback, show a relationship between items, or notify of a change. Use decorative/ornamental animation only for storytelling and branding.
why: Excess decorative animation detracted from site quality and made users leave (p.458); functional benefits are what improve UX (p.459).
check: each animation can be tagged with a purpose (navigation, feedback, status, relationship, story).

text: Use "just the perfect amount" of motion; do not use too many different animations.
why: Spice metaphor: one note is dull, many overwhelm and confuse (p.462). Too many animations irritate and users abandon the program (p.473).
check: visual / count of distinct animated elements per view.

text: Do not bother users. An excessive number of animations has the opposite effect.
why: Irritated users leave.
check: visual.

text: Animation must interest visitors rather than distract or frustrate them; beware processing delays or introducing a new design that causes confusion.
why: Animation that does not serve the task becomes friction.
check: visual.
